docs.title: The Anatomy Theatre
docs.text:
(a working title — the anatomy theatre was the room where the anatomy lesson was taught)

This is a reading library: a small number of subjects, each built out to the depth of a good textbook. Every subject opens with an overview and a recommended reading path, then chapters you can read in order or dip into, then deep dives wherever there is real material to go further — the intent is that you can always dig a little deeper, and never hit filler.

Subjects:

  • Dance — choreographers and their works, movement vocabularies and how machines might learn them, notation, the music relationship, chance and algorithmic methods, costume and the staged body, and the fully synthetic dancer. Complete: eight parts, 31 chapters, an atlas of 9 tradition pages, 24 shelf pages, 2 deep dives, 1 plate.
  • Minimal techno — the production craft: groove, the voices, reduction, long-form hypnosis, the artists' documented methods. Queued.

Sources and provenance sit behind tap-able footnotes at the bottom of each page — the text stays clean. Everything here is distilled from a private knowledge commons plus the general knowledge of the agents who write it; where a page draws on the commons' research notes, it says so in a collapsed Field notes block at the end.

docs.title: Dance
docs.text: Choreography solved a problem seventy years before anyone asked a machine to: how to build a limited vocabulary of movement and a set of rules that recombine it into something worth watching. This subject covers the art form whole — the traditions and their makers, the languages of movement and the systems for writing them down, the strange marriage with music, the chance procedures and algorithms, the dressed and lit body on a stage, and the fully synthetic dancer — but that solved problem is its center of gravity, and the chapters radiate out from it.

docs.title: The shape of the subject
docs.text:
Eight parts, all written. Chapters are self-contained — you can read any one cold — but within a part they're ordered, and the parts themselves zoom from the territory down to the machinery:

  • I · The territory — what dance is and what it's for; a world atlas of everything anyone calls dance; ballet's long history; the modern revolt; street and club styles. (complete)
  • II · Movement language — how vocabularies of movement get built, taught, described, and — the open frontier — discovered by machines from video. (complete)
  • III · Writing it down — Labanotation, Benesh, motif notation; video and digital scores. (complete)
  • IV · Music and dance — both directions of the marriage: choreographers using music, composers writing for bodies. (complete)
  • V · Chance, systems, algorithms — Cunningham to code: the generative tradition and the architecture it converged on. (complete)
  • VI · The staged body — costume, props, environment, light. (complete)
  • VII · The synthetic dancer — the plausible body, motion capture, movement generation, rendering, the pipeline end to end. (complete)
  • VIII · The shelf — reference pages on the choreographers themselves. (first wave complete: 24 pages)

docs.title: Available now
docs.text:
The territory (read in order):

  • What dance is; what choreography is — the nouns (dancer, choreographer, score, work, performance; improvisation versus set material) and the four functions — ritual, social, concert, competitive — as the lens for everything after.
  • The world atlas of dance — the hub for everything anyone calls dance: nine tradition-family pages (South Asia, East and Southeast Asia, Africa and the diaspora, the Middle East and Central Asia, European folk and social, Latin America, Oceania and the Pacific, North American vernacular, ballroom), a function index, and a growing first-tier list.
  • Ballet: the long history — court to Romantic to Petipa to the Ballets Russes to now; the schools as dialects; with deep dives on the Ballets Russes and the pointe shoe.
  • The modern revolt and after — Fuller and Duncan to Denishawn, Ausdruckstanz, the Graham generation and the Black modern lineage, Cunningham, Judson, tanztheater, the global contemporary now.
  • Street and club styles — breaking, popping, locking, house, waacking, voguing, krump; cyphers and battles; how a canon forms without an academy, and what the music's loop-and-bar grammar does to the dance.

Movement language (read in order, or dip in):

  • Codified vocabularies — what happens when a tradition names its movements: ballet's lexicon, the mudra systems, hula, flamenco, and the street's uninstitutional canon.
  • Technique as vocabulary — modern dance's alternative: build a training system that produces a body, and let the body be the vocabulary.
  • The craft: composition best practices — Humphrey's principles, phrase-craft, the rehearsal room, editing, and Lerman's feedback protocol.
  • Building a gamut — how a piece-specific movement vocabulary is actually assembled: units, state, operators, and the traps between them.
  • Effort and quality — Laban's answer to a question most vocabularies forget to ask: not what the body does, but how.
  • Machine-discovered vocabularies — can a machine find the units from video, unsupervised? Yes for poses and segments, not yet for named, typed units — what works, and what a working pipeline would look like.

Writing it down (read in order):

  • Notation systems — Feuillet, Stepanov, Labanotation, Benesh, Eshkol-Wachman, motif notation: what each encodes and drops, why none beat video, and why every system is an answer to "what is the unit of movement?"
  • Video, digital scores, and annotation practice — video as working memory and its limits; Forsythe's Improvisation Technologies and Synchronous Objects; Motion Bank and Piecemaker; why an annotation schema is a gamut.

Music and dance (read in order):

  • Choreomusicology: the relationship spectrum — mickey-mousing, visualization, counterpoint, independence; Balanchine, Morris, De Keersmaeker, Cunningham; and the perceptual physics — binding windows, constructive sync, restraint — under each position.
  • How choreographers work with music — counts, breath, cues; the eight-count and where it comes from; additive meters and timelines; groove and the pocket; the rehearsal pianist and the conductor who must anticipate; editing in the studio.
  • Composing for choreography — Tchaikovsky under Petipa's minutage, Stravinsky, Copland for Graham, Cage's durations, Glass and Reich with Childs and De Keersmaeker, the contemporary commission — and the brief a choreographer actually needs.

Chance, systems, algorithms:

  • Chance and rule-based choreography — Cunningham's coin tosses, Brown's accumulations, Childs's permutations, Halprin's cycles: what seventy years of generative choreography actually did, and the two-layer architecture all of it shares.
  • The gamut+rules architecture — the engineering synthesis: transition legality, the three transition policies, the human gate, and why the rendering of a machine's proposal is a design decision.
  • Computational choreography: a history — thirty-five years of choreographers composing with computers, LifeForms to AISOMA, and the five patterns that held the whole way.
  • Choreographing in latent spaces — the continuous counter-position: learned motion manifolds, their pre-mathematical ancestors, and what survives the loss of the unit.
  • Locomotion without a choreographer — where motion comes from when nobody writes it: mechanics, oscillators, evolution, optimization, objectives, rules, repertoires — for humanoid and non-humanoid bodies, and the non-human performers already on stage.

The staged body (read in order):

  • Dance costume: a history — four centuries of what dancers wore, read as a history of what the body was permitted to do: the Sun King's skirts, the tutu as machine, the painters' theatre, the pedestrian revolt, the couture return.
  • Dressing the genre — why each genre wears what it wears: the tutu, the pleated fan, the tracksuit, the tango slit, the fringe — as affordance, signal, and picture; then costume for the camera, and the wardrobe of a rendered dancer.
  • Props and environment — the set as picture, terrain, and partner: Noguchi and Graham, Cunningham's independent events, Bausch's dirt and water, Brown on rooftops, the object as vocabulary — and the rendered stage's one hard rule.
  • Light and the rest of the picture — lighting as dance's second choreography (side light, the cue as time, Rosenthal to Tipton), hair and makeup as genre and as vocabulary, the five rooms, and what the rendered picture inherits.

The synthetic dancer (read in order):

  • The plausible body — what real bodies can and cannot do, as the realism rubric every synthetic dancer is judged against.
  • The captured body: video to skeleton to animation — the state of the art and the free tooling for extracting 3D dance from video, and the clever repairs (learned priors, physics simulation) that make the result look alive.
  • Generating movement — music-to-dance and text-to-motion generation in mid-2026: mechanisms, failure modes, the suspect metrics, and the direct-to-video newcomers.
  • Rendering the dancer — skeleton and keyframes to pixels: how pose-conditioned video generation actually behaves, its motion budget, and how to make it hold still where you need it to.
  • The pipeline, end to end — every stage and its owner, the budgets that bind, composing for the camera, and one phrase walked through the whole chain.

The shelf — reference pages on the choreographers, the first wave complete: Duncan, Nijinsky and Nijinska, Graham, Humphrey, Dunham, Balanchine, Robbins, Cunningham, Ailey, Rainer, Paxton, Brown, Childs, Tharp, Bausch, Forsythe, De Keersmaeker, Naharin, McGregor, Pite, Khan, Hijikata and Ohno, Fosse, Berkeley — each a short factual header, contributions at length, and the major works described.

Plates — contemplation pages: one dense structure, laid out for staring at, not reading:

  • Plate I · The Movement Alphabet

docs.title: The world atlas of dance
docs.text:
This is the library's breadth layer for dance, built on the tiering rule: everything anyone calls dance gets at least a mention; major traditions far from the core get a real description; the core — Western concert dance — gets full depth in the rest of the subject. The atlas groups by region and lineage, because that is how traditions are actually transmitted, and then indexes by function — ritual, social, concert, competitive, the first chapter's lens — because function is what a dance is for, and two dances from opposite ends of the earth with the same function have more in common than two neighbors with different ones.

Each tradition page describes its dances by the same five questions: what it is and where; the movement signature (what you would recognize in a silhouette); the music relationship (which the commons often holds in detail from the music side); the function(s) it serves; and the door — the core chapter it best illuminates. Pages cross-link into the core wherever a tradition teaches something the core needs: the mudra systems into codified vocabularies, flamenco's compás into the choreomusicology chapters, the cypher into street styles.

docs.title: The tradition families
docs.text:
• South Asia — the eight classical forms (bharatanatyam, kathak, odissi, kathakali, kuchipudi, manipuri, mohiniyattam, sattriya), the folk and martial forms, and Bollywood; the tala/raga grammar the dancer's feet recite.
  • East and Southeast Asia — noh and nihon-buyō, Beijing opera's movement, Korean court and folk dance, Balinese legong and kecak, Javanese court dance, Thai khon, Khmer classical; gamelan's nested cycles.
  • Africa and the diaspora — West African ensemble dance (Ewe agbekor, Wolof sabar, Mande djembe dances), Southern African gumboot and pantsula, Ethiopian eskista, the orisha dances of the Afro-Atlantic; the bell timeline and the master drummer's cues.
  • The Middle East and Central Asia — raqs sharqi, dabke, the Sufi sema, Persian classical and folk dance, Central Asian and Caucasian forms; maqam and iqa'.
  • European folk and social dance — flamenco, Irish step and sean-nós, Scottish Highland, Balkan chain dances and aksak, Scandinavian polska, the waltz–polka lineage, Morris and sword dance, the court-to-ballroom line.
  • Latin America — tango, samba, the son–mambo–salsa lineage, rumba, capoeira, folklórico, cumbia, merengue, bachata, the Andean forms; clave.
  • Oceania and the Pacific — hula, haka, Samoan siva and sasa, Tongan lakalaka, Cook Islands ura, Aboriginal Australian and Torres Strait Islander ceremony.
  • North American vernacular — powwow styles, Appalachian clogging and flatfooting, square and contra dance, tap's roots and the Lindy Hop, the jazz dances, cajun and zydeco; the street styles get their own chapter.
  • Ballroom — the Standard five, the Latin five, American Smooth and Rhythm, and the competitive world that shaped the costume, the technique, and the judging.

docs.title: The function index
docs.text:
The same traditions, sorted by what they are primarily for. Most run more than one function; this is the dominant one, and the arrows mark the migrations the first chapter describes.

Function Traditions (dominant use) Ritual Sufi sema; orisha dances (Yoruba, Vodou, Santería, Candomblé); Balinese sanghyang and temple legong; kecak; Kandyan and bharatanatyam's temple ancestors; powwow ceremony; haka as challenge and welcome; Aboriginal ceremony; kathakali's temple theatre; noh's shrine origins; Ethiopian church dance Social Balkan chain dances; dabke; the waltz–polka family; square/contra; céilí; tango's milonga; salsa, cumbia, merengue, bachata; garba/raas; bhangra; sabar at celebrations; gumboot; the Lindy Hop; kizomba; the house-music floor Concert the South Asian classical forms (→ from temple and court); Javanese and Khmer court dance; khon; noh; Beijing opera; flamenco's tablao and ballet flamenco (→ from juerga); Western ballet and modern (the core); Cloud Gate and the contemporary companies everywhere Competitive DanceSport ballroom; Irish step (feis); Highland; powwow contest categories; tap, jazz and "contemporary" competitions; breaking's battles (→ Olympic 2024); krump sessions; voguing's balls; Trinidad's Carnival bands; capoeira's roda (game, not contest, but judged by peers)

docs.title: First tier: the rest of the world, at least by name
docs.text:
A growing list, in the spirit of "everything anyone calls dance gets a line." Each entry is a name, a place, and one clause — enough to know it exists and to search for more. Additions welcome; this list is meant to lengthen.

  • Asia: Bhutanese cham (masked monastic dance); Tibetan cham; Mongolian biyelgee (upper-body, seated); Uzbek and Tajik classical dance; Odissi's cousin Chhau (masked martial, three styles); Sri Lankan Kandyan and low-country dance; Burmese zat pwe; Vietnamese múa rối nước (water puppetry — the puppets dance); Filipino tinikling and singkil (bamboo poles) and pangalay; Malay zapin and joget; Okinawan eisa; Japanese bon odori (festival circle dance), kagura, kabuki dance, butoh (the shelf); Korean salpuri, talchum (mask dance), buchaechum (fan dance); Chinese ribbon, lion and dragon dance, the ethnic-minority stage forms, Tibetan guozhuang; Hmong dance.
  • Africa: Egyptian tahtib (stick); Moroccan ahwash and guedra; Tuareg dances; Hausa and Yoruba bata; Ghanaian adowa, kpanlogo, azonto; Congolese ndombolo and soukous dance; Rwandan intore; Maasai jumping dance (adumu); Zulu indlamu; Xhosa umxhentso; Madagascar's hira gasy; South African kwaito and amapiano dances; Angolan kuduro and kizomba.
  • Europe: Basque aurresku; Galician muiñeira; Portuguese fado has no dance but vira does; Italian tarantella and pizzica; Greek syrtaki (1964, for a film), zeibekiko (solo, male), pentozali; Hungarian csárdás and verbunkos; Polish mazurka and polonaise (the latter an Olympic-opening staple); Czech polka (the original); Russian khorovod and the Cossack squat-kicks (prisyadka); Ukrainian hopak; Georgian kartuli and khorumi (the men on their toes in soft boots); Armenian kochari; Sardinian ballu tundu; Breton fest-noz dances; English Morris, rapper and longsword, maypole; the Faroese chain dance (the oldest surviving European chain dance, to ballads).
  • The Americas: Mexican danza de los voladores (the flying pole), concheros, jarabe tapatío; Guatemalan baile de la conquista; Peruvian marinera and huayno, the scissors dance; Bolivian diablada and caporales; Chilean cueca; Argentine malambo (the gaucho stamping dance) and chacarera; Brazilian frevo, maracatu, forró, bumba-meu-boi, axé; Colombian mapalé and champeta; Dominican palos; Haitian yanvalou and rara; Trinidadian limbo and soca; Jamaican dancehall's named moves; Cuban danzón and casino rueda; Cajun two-step; Métis jigging; Inuit drum dance; Mexican-American quebradita.
  • Oceania: Papua New Guinean sing-sing; Fijian meke; Tahitian ʻōteʻa (the fast hip dance often mistaken for hula); Marquesan haka manu; Kiribati dance; Rapa Nui dance; Torres Strait Islander dance.

The atlas is never finished; the list above is the part of this library most explicitly designed to grow.

Field notes

No commons notes rendered on this hub page; the tradition pages render the music-grammar notes where a dance's music is documented in the commons.

docs.title: Africa and the diaspora
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

Africa is a continent of several thousand dance traditions, and any page is a sampling; what follows picks the families that the rest of the world's dance most descends from — because the Afro-Atlantic diaspora carried West and Central African movement to the Caribbean, Brazil, and the United States, and from there into nearly every popular dance of the last century: the Latin American forms, tap and the jazz dances, the street styles, and by way of them the concert stage. Two structural features recur across the continent's traditions and are worth naming before the survey: polycentric movement (the body's parts — hips, chest, shoulders, head — articulated independently and often in different rhythms, against the European tradition's single upright center) and a call-and-response relationship with music in which the drummer leads the dancer and the dancer answers the drum.

docs.title: The music the dancer answers
docs.text: The commons describes West African ensemble drumming — Ewe, Akan, Mande — in terms that explain the dancing exactly. The ensemble organizes not around a downbeat but around a timeline: a bell pattern (gankogui), most often the seven-stroke pattern over twelve pulses, played as an invariant ostinato the whole ensemble entrains to — held, the commons notes, divisively, as a fixed asymmetric reference, not as a counted sum of cells, despite Western habits of writing it "additively." Supporting drums interlock in hocket, each occupying the others' gaps, and the master drummer shapes the form live — section changes, entrances, breaks, and dance cues — through improvised signal phrases, so that the ensemble's "chart" is a recognized vocabulary of cues rather than a score.1 The dance is built on that architecture: the dancers hold the timeline in the body (often the feet in a duple grouping against the bell's ternary — the cross-rhythm that is the music's identity, performed), the master drum's signal phrase is the cue to change step, and the unstated beats the ensemble leaves open are — as the ethnography of Ewe dance puts it — space for the dancers. It is the working-with-music chapter's cue-based practice taken to its limit: a live control channel from drummer to dancer, with form generated in performance.

docs.title: West Africa
docs.text:
• Ewe dances (Ghana, Togo) — agbekor (a war dance turned social, the canonical teaching repertoire), gahu, kpanlogo (an urban social dance of the 1960s): the drum-ensemble dances above, taught worldwide through the Ghanaian university dance programs and the ethnomusicology literature.
  • Sabar (Senegal, Wolof) — the explosive, high-kicking, leaping women's dance to the sabar drum ensemble at street celebrations, where the dancer enters the circle one at a time to challenge the drummer — participatory and competitive at once; also Senegal's mbalax pop dance.
  • The Mande djembe dances (Guinea, Mali) — dununba, soli, kuku, and the large repertoire carried abroad by the national ballets (Les Ballets Africains, 1952) and by djembe teaching; Germaine Acogny's École des Sables in Senegal built a contemporary technique on this base (the modern revolt).
  • Yoruba and Fon dance (Nigeria, Benin) — the bata drum dances and the orisha dances each deity's characteristic movement, which crossed the Atlantic intact.
  • Hausa, Igbo, Asante (adowa, the Asante funeral and social dance of subtle hand gestures) and Nigeria's popular-dance inventions (azonto from Ghana, shaku shaku, zanku, the Afrobeats dances) complete the region's living edge.

docs.title: Central, Southern, and East Africa
docs.text:
• Congolese ndombolo and the soukous dances — hip-driven, the popular-music dance of Central Africa.
  • Gumboot (South Africa) — the stamping, boot-slapping dance invented by mine workers forbidden to speak, a percussion vocabulary in rubber boots; pantsula — the fast, flat- footed township street dance; Zulu indlamu (the high-kicking warrior dance), Xhosa umxhentso; and the kwaito and amapiano dances that now travel the same routes as the Afrobeats ones.
  • East Africa — Ethiopian eskista (the shoulder-shaking dance, a polycentric signature), the Maasai jumping adumu, Rwandan intore, Kenyan and Tanzanian ngoma.
  • North Africa belongs to the Middle East page as much as here: Egyptian tahtib, Moroccan ahwash, Tuareg dance.

docs.title: The Afro-Atlantic: the orisha dances and after
docs.text: Enslaved Africans carried the Yoruba, Fon, and Kongo religious systems to Cuba (Santería, lucumí), Haiti (Vodou), and Brazil (Candomblé), and with them the dances of the deities: each orisha — Shango, Oshun, Yemaya, Ogun, Eleggua — with a rhythm, a color, a movement signature (Oshun's flowing river hands, Shango's thunder-axe), performed to the bata drums in ceremonies where possession is the goal. These are the first chapter's ritual function in its most vivid surviving form, and they are also the root system of the secular dances around them: Afro-Cuban rumba (guaguancó, yambú, columbia) and from it the son–mambo–salsa lineage (Latin America); Brazilian samba from Bahian samba de roda, capoeira (the Angolan-rooted martial art-dance-game in its roda), maculelê; Haitian yanvalou and rara; Trinidadian and Jamaican forms; and in the United States the ring shout, the juba, the cakewalk, and everything that became tap and the jazz dances (North American vernacular). Katherine Dunham and Pearl Primus (the modern revolt) brought this lineage onto the American concert stage as scholarship and as technique; the contemporary African choreographers — Acogny, Linyekula, Maqoma, Masilo, Chipaumire — are the return journey.

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
That form can be generated live by a cue channel — the master drummer's signal phrases are the clearest example anywhere of the gamut+rules architecture's sequencer being a person issuing tokens the ensemble obeys; that polycentric, polyrhythmic bodies are the normal case, and the single-centered body a regional habit; and that the timeline — a fixed asymmetric reference with no privileged beat — is a third way of addressing time, alongside the hierarchical meter and the breath, that a movement generator modeling "the beat" as a downbeat will get wrong.

Field notes

Renders theory-genre-west-african (the invariant bell timeline; interlocking hocket; the master drummer's signal phrases as the live form-control channel; cross-rhythm as identity; the divisive-not-additive caution). The dance descriptions are confident-knowledge writing.

  1. Locke's analyses of Ewe drumming and Chernoff's African Rhythm and African Sensibility (1979) — the latter's account of an ensemble "leaving space for the dancers" — are the commons note's anchors; it flags that role names (gankogui, kidi, kagan) are Ewe-specific. ↩

docs.title: Ballroom
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

"Ballroom" names two things that share a floor: the social couple dances of the European and American nineteenth and twentieth centuries — the waltz that scandalized Vienna, the foxtrot of the ragtime years, the Latin dances that crossed from Havana and Rio to the hotel ballroom — and the competitive codification of them, DanceSport, which took those dances, fixed their syllabi, and optimized them for a panel of judges. The second is this page's main subject, because it is the clearest case in the world of a dance form engineered by its evaluation — and because its costume, technique, and staging are the dressing-the-genre chapter's textbook of legibility at a distance.

docs.title: The social dances underneath
docs.text: The waltz (the closed, turning couple, c. 1780s–1810s, Vienna), the polka (1840s), the one-step and foxtrot (1910s, ragtime and the Castles — Vernon and Irene Castle, the first dance celebrities, who made social dancing respectable and taught it), the tango as Paris received it (1912–13), the quickstep (1920s, from the foxtrot and the Charleston), and the Latin arrivals — the rumba (the Cuban son slowed and smoothed, 1930s), the samba (Rio's, reinterpreted, 1940s), the cha-cha (1950s), the mambo, the jive (American swing by way of wartime Britain), the paso doble (Spanish march, a French-invented dance), bolero, merengue, swing in its East and West Coast forms — were all social dances before they were syllabus dances, and most still are: the wedding waltz, the Friday-night salsa (Latin America), the senior center's foxtrot. The Arthur Murray and Fred Astaire studio chains (1930s–) built the American social dance industry on teaching them in numbered steps.

docs.title: The codification: English style and the syllabi
docs.text: Competitive ballroom was codified in England in the 1920s — the Imperial Society of Teachers of Dancing's 1924 committee, led by Victor Silvester and others, fixed the English style (later International style) of the waltz, foxtrot, tango, and quickstep with the Viennese waltz added — and the Latin five (cha-cha, samba, rumba, paso doble, jive) were codified after the war. The syllabi name every figure (natural turn, reverse turn, feather step, whisk, chassé, New Yorker, alemana, botafogo), grade them (bronze, silver, gold), and specify footwork, rise and fall, sway, and alignment to the floor — a closed vocabulary as explicit as ballet's. America developed its own American Smooth (waltz, tango, foxtrot, Viennese — with the couple permitted to open the hold) and American Rhythm (cha-cha, rumba, East Coast swing, bolero, mambo) styles, with different technique (Rhythm's bent-knee Cuban motion against International Latin's straight-leg). The World DanceSport Federation (1957 as ICAD) governs amateur competition; the professional circuit runs through Blackpool (the Blackpool Dance Festival, since 1920, the sport's Wimbledon); the Olympic recognition campaign succeeded in making DanceSport an IOC-recognized sport (1997) without ever getting it onto the program — breakdancing got there first, in 2024, under DanceSport's own federation.

docs.title: Standard and Latin: what the judges see
docs.text:
Standard (waltz, tango, Viennese waltz, slow foxtrot, quickstep) is danced in closed hold throughout — the couple's frame never opens — and its technique is the frame: the topline (head and shoulders held wide and still), the body contact at the hips, rise and fall, sway, and swing (the pendulum of the body through the figures), contra body movement and the heel leads. The dance travels counter-clockwise around the floor with up to a dozen couples at once, which is why floorcraft (navigation without collision) is judged. Latin (cha-cha, samba, rumba, paso doble, jive) is danced mostly in open and alternating holds, with hip action (the "Cuban motion" of the settling hip on the straight leg), leg action, and the couple's relationship as the content; the paso doble's bullfight and the jive's kicks and flicks are the outliers.

Judging is comparative and placement-based under the skating system: a panel of judges ranks couples in each dance, majorities decide placings. What a judge can see from the floor's edge in ninety seconds, with twelve couples moving at once, is exactly what the form has been optimized to show — the topline's stillness, the swing's amplitude, the hips' action, the couple's unison — and the dressing-the-genre chapter explains the consequences: the Standard gown's floats to render swing and sway at thirty metres, the tail suit as a worn frame, Latin's fringe to amplify hip action, crystals and tan for visibility under arena light, the number on the man's back. The first chapter's warning about competitive forms — whatever the scoring rewards, the dance becomes — is ballroom's whole modern history: the shapes grew, the speeds rose, the costumes brightened, and the dances moved ever further from the social floor they came from. The evaluation thinking behind the synthetic dancer has no better cautionary tale.

docs.title: The wider competitive world
docs.text: Around DanceSport stand its cousins: Pro-Am (the American industry's amateur-with- professional-partner format that funds the studios), formation dance (teams of eight couples in choreographed patterns), wheelchair DanceSport, same-sex ballroom (the Gay Games circuit and its growing mainstream acceptance), the television formats (Strictly Come Dancing, 2004; Dancing with the Stars, 2005) that made ballroom a mass-audience spectacle again, and the sequence dance and modern jive (Ceroc) scenes of Britain — social forms running alongside the sport.

docs.title: What it teaches the core
docs.text:
That judging is a selection pressure strong enough to redesign a dance in a century; that a closed vocabulary with graded syllabi can be built from social dances in a decade by a committee, as surely as by a king's academy; and that legibility at a distance is a design constraint with its own aesthetics, which the rest of this library's staged-body chapters keep returning to.

Field notes

No commons notes rendered — confident-knowledge writing.

docs.title: East and Southeast Asia
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

The region's great traditions are theatre-dance: forms in which dance, drama, music, mask, and costume are one art, usually with court or temple origins, a codified movement vocabulary, and a theory of the performer's inner state as precise as any in the West. The Western habit of separating "dance" from "theatre" fits them badly, and they repay being read as whole systems.

docs.title: Japan
docs.text: Noh (fourteenth century, Kan'ami and Zeami) — masked, slow, austere music-drama, with a movement vocabulary of kata (fixed forms: the sliding walk suriashi, the stamp, the kamae stance, the small gestures of the fan) so reduced that a single step carries the weight a ballet phrase would. Its mask is the makeup chapter's great mechanism — expression as angle to the light — and Zeami's treatises on hana (the flower, the performer's quality) are a theory of stage presence. Kyōgen, the comic interludes. Kabuki (seventeenth century) is the popular counterpart — kumadori painted faces, the mie held pose, the hanamichi runway — and nihon-buyō, classical Japanese dance, grows out of kabuki's dance scenes into a concert form taught in iemoto schools. Bon odori, the summer festival circle dances, are the participatory stratum; kagura, Shinto shrine dance, the ritual one; butoh (1959–), the modern revolt, is on the shelf. Door: reduction — the technique chapter's lesson that a small vocabulary, deeply done, reads as a world.

docs.title: China
docs.text: Beijing opera (jingju, eighteenth–nineteenth century) organizes performance into four skills — song, speech, acting-dance, and combat — and a role system (sheng, dan, jing, chou) each with its movement conventions: the dan's tiny steps and water sleeves (shuixiu, a metre of white silk extending every gesture — the props chapter's case), the warrior's acrobatics, the painted-face lianpu color code (makeup). Chinese classical dance as a concert form is a twentieth-century construction from opera movement, martial arts, and ballet training; folk and ethnic dance (the ribbon dance, the lion and dragon dances, Tibetan guozhuang, Uyghur sanam, Dai peacock dance) is a vast staged repertoire; and Yang Liping, Tao Ye's numbered works, and Shen Wei are its contemporary edge.

docs.title: Korea
docs.text: Court dance (jeongjae, from the Joseon dynasty) — slow, symmetrical, ceremonial, in layered silk; folk and shamanic dance — salpuri (a solo of suppressed grief with a long white scarf), seungmu (the monk's dance), talchum (masked dance-drama, satirical), buchaechum (the fan dance, a twentieth-century stage creation), and the farmers' percussion dance pungmul with its streamer-hatted drummers. Korea's contemporary scene is large, and K-pop's choreography — precise, unison, camera-built — is the country's most exported movement.

docs.title: Indonesia: Bali and Java
docs.text: Balinese dance — legong (young girls, fast, intricate, eyes and fingers flickering), baris (the male warrior dance), topeng (masked), barong and the trance sanghyang, and kecak (the "monkey chant," a seated male chorus of interlocking cak syllables, staged in its modern form in the 1930s with Walter Spies) — is the region's most kinetic: angular, darting, with the agem base stance and a vocabulary of named positions. Javanese court dance (Yogyakarta and Surakarta bedhaya and srimpi) is its opposite — slow, refined, inward, the dancers nearly floating. Both are inseparable from gamelan, and the commons describes gamelan in terms that explain the dancing: a piece is organized around the gongan, one full gong cycle, punctuated by strictly nested colotomic instruments — the great gong at cycle's end, kenong dividing it, kempul and kethuk subdividing — each a binary division of the level above; a skeletal core melody (balungan) that every elaborating part derives from; and irama, the ensemble-wide density level that shifts in discrete steps at structural points and moves in one direction across a piece.1 The dance rides this exactly: the dancer's phrases end on the gong, the choreography's sections change where irama changes, and Balinese kotekan — interlocking parts each filling the other's gaps at two-to-four times the core rate — is audible in legong's flickering hands. Gamelan is the choreomusicology chapter's strict-hierarchy case in its purest form: hierarchy level is nearly computable from a beat counter, and the dancing knows it.

docs.title: Mainland Southeast Asia
docs.text: Thai khon — the masked dance-drama of the Ramakien (the Thai Ramayana), with its curved-finger, bent-knee vocabulary, the mae bot basic postures, and the demon and monkey roles; lakhon its unmasked cousin; fawn the northern folk forms. Khmer classical dance (Cambodia) — the royal ballet, robam, nearly destroyed under the Khmer Rouge (an estimated ninety percent of its artists died) and rebuilt from the survivors; the hyper-flexed fingers and hands, the slow spiral, the apsara dance; UNESCO-listed. Lao and Burmese court and festival dances complete the family; Vietnamese water puppetry (múa rối nước), in which wooden figures dance on a pond, is the region's most unusual "dancer."

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
Three things. That strict hierarchy in the music produces strict hierarchy in the dance — gamelan's nested cycles are the model for a choreography whose section boundaries are computable. That a mask or a painted face can be a vocabulary as much as a movement can. And that reduction is a technique — noh's handful of kata and the Javanese court's near-stillness are the limit of the "fewer units, more deeply" principle the gamut chapter keeps arriving at.

Field notes

Renders theory-genre-gamelan (gongan and colotomic nesting; balungan; irama as discrete ensemble-wide state; kotekan as joint hocket). The dance descriptions are confident-knowledge writing.

  1. The commons note folds Javanese court gamelan and Balinese kebyar practice into one profile and flags it; the colotomic/balungan/irama frame is shared, kotekan's speed and role vocabulary are Balinese. ↩

docs.title: European folk and social dance
docs.text: title: European folk and social dance summary: Flamenco, Irish step and sean-nós, Scottish Highland, the Balkan chain dances and aksak, Scandinavian polska, the waltz–polka lineage, Morris and sword dance — and two musics the commons holds: the palo's compás and the folk tune's AABB strain. covers: - theory-genre-flamenco - theory-genre-celtic-nordic-folk

docs.title: European folk and social dance
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

Europe's folk and social dances are the substrate under its concert tradition — the court dances ballet codified were village dances first, and the ballroom's waltz and polka were peasant turning dances that scandalized the cities — and they remain, across the continent, the participatory function in full health: every Balkan wedding, Irish céilí, Breton fest-noz, and Andalusian feria is a room full of people who know the steps. Two families are treated at depth because the commons holds their music: flamenco and the Celtic–Nordic tune traditions.

docs.title: Flamenco
docs.text:
Flamenco is the Andalusian art of song (cante), guitar (toque), and dance (baile), with Romani, Andalusian, Moorish, and Sephardic roots and a documented history from the late eighteenth century; cafés cantantes (1860s–1920s) made it a stage art, the tablao its nightclub home, and the twentieth century's ballet flamenco (La Argentina, Antonio Gades, Cristina Hoyos, Sara Baras, Rocío Molina, Israel Galván) its concert form — three functions of one vocabulary, as the first chapter says.

The music the dancer drives. The commons' flamenco note is exact. The atom is the compás — a fixed accent pattern cycling under everything. Most serious palos share a twelve-beat cycle but disagree on the accents: soleá accents 3-6-8-10-12; bulería and alegrías use the same accents but count from twelve, so the accented beat is heard first; siguiriya recasts the twelve pulses as five uneven beats (3+3+2+2+2); tangos run a binary 4/4 family. This is a timeline reference, not a hierarchical meter — the palmas entrain to the asymmetric pattern the way a clave does — and a palo is a frame (compás, tempo range, modal center) within which the singer, guitarist, and dancer negotiate the realization live, cued by micro-gesture: the dancer's llamada calls a section change, the falseta (guitar interlude) and the letra (sung verse) never overlap, and the escobilla (the extended footwork passage) is the dancer's solo within the cycle. Escalation — rhythmic intensification, ornament, dynamic climax — happens inside the unchanging compás, never by restructuring it.1 The dance is that grammar embodied: zapateado (the nailed-heel footwork, a percussion part), the braceo (the arms' carriage, the floreo of the hands), the torso's quiebro, the bata de cola and mantón as apparatus (dressing the genre), and — the point — the dancer as conductor: the baile's llamadas and remates (closing accents) drive the musicians, who watch the feet. Flamenco is the working-with-music chapter's cue-based mode with the dancer holding the cues, and the codified-vocabularies chapter's "grammar with few nouns."

docs.title: Ireland, Scotland, and the tune traditions
docs.text:
Irish step dance — the rigid torso, arms at the sides, and virtuoso feet: hard shoe (the hornpipe, treble jig, and set dances, with fiberglass-tipped shoes) and soft shoe (reel, slip jig, in ghillies); the competitive feis circuit with its solo dresses and wigs; the céilí group dances; and since Riverdance (1994) a global stage form. Beside it, sean-nós ("old style") — the loose-armed, low-to-the-ground, improvisational solo step dance of the Gaeltacht, battering close to the floor. Scottish Highland dance (the Highland fling, sword dance, seann triubhas) — competitive, balletic, at the Highland games — and Scottish country dance (the RSCDS's codified social sets); Cape Breton step dance, the Scottish emigrants' preserved percussive style.

The music the dancers chain. The commons: the atom of Irish and Scottish dance music is the eight-bar strain, near-universally chained as AABB and cycled about three times before the next tune; meter is a separate parameter per tune type — reel (4/4), jig (6/8), slip jig (9/8), hornpipe (dotted 4/4) — and a session chains tunes into a set, negotiated live, with dance-typed contexts fixing the genre sequence.2 The step dancer's vocabulary follows: steps are built to the eight-bar strain, the tune type decides the step family, and the céilí's figures are sized to the AABB round. Scandinavia's polska and Norway's springar are the family's other branch, and the commons' finding about them matters for any generator: the long-medium-short beat of the polska is the meter, not a sloppy triplet — motion-capture studies of the dancers' stamping confirm the asymmetry is systematic — and quantizing it to even triplets erases the dance.

docs.title: The Balkans and the chain dances
docs.text: The chain and circle dances of southeastern Europe — Serbian and Croatian kolo, Bulgarian horo, Macedonian oro, Greek syrtos and kalamatianos, Romanian hora and sârba, Albanian valle, the Jewish hora (from the Romanian) — are the participatory function at its purest: linked hands or shoulders, a leader at the head, steps repeated across an open-ended line to music that is often in the additive meters (aksak, Brăiloiu's term) the working-with-music chapter describes — 7/8 as 2+2+3 (rǎchenitsa), 9/8 as 2+2+2+3, 11/16 (kopanitsa). The dancers' quick-quick-slow is the meter's cells; you can read the time signature off the feet. Bulgaria's state folk ensembles (Philip Koutev, 1951) and the international folk-dance movement turned these into stage and recreational forms worldwide.

docs.title: The turning dances: waltz, polka, and the court-to-ballroom line
docs.text: The waltz (Austro-German Ländler and Walzer, late eighteenth century: the closed couple, turning, scandalous) and the polka (Bohemia, 1830s; a European craze by the 1840s), the mazurka, the schottische, and the galop are the nineteenth century's social dances and the root of ballroom; before them, the court's basse danse, pavane, galliard, minuet, and contredanse (from the English country dance — the ancestor of square and contra) are the dances ballet's lexicon codified. Italian tarantella and Salentine pizzica (the trance-healing dance of the "spider's bite"), Spanish jota and sardana, Portuguese vira, Hungarian csárdás, Polish mazurka and polonaise, Russian and Ukrainian hopak with its squat-kicks, Georgian dance (on the Middle East and Central Asia page) fill out the continent.

docs.title: Ritual survivals: Morris, sword, and the rest
docs.text: England's Morris dance (Cotswold, with sticks, bells, and handkerchiefs; Border and North-West clog traditions; rapper and longsword dances in which the linked swords are woven into a star) are ritual-calendar dances with contested origins and a vigorous revival; Basque ezpata-dantza, Portuguese pauliteiros, and the Faroese chain dance (to ballads, unbroken since the Middle Ages) are their cousins.

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
That a dancer can be the ensemble's conductor (flamenco's llamadas); that the tune's strain length and meter type are the step's grammar (the Celtic tradition's AABB and the polska's uneven beat); and that additive meter is readable from the feet — three reasons a movement generator should model the music's framework, not its onsets.

Field notes

Renders theory-genre-flamenco (the compás accent patterns per palo; timeline not meter; frame/realization with llamada cues; escalation inside the compás) and theory-genre-celtic-nordic-folk (the eight-bar AABB strain; meter per tune type; set chaining; the polska's long-medium-short beat as meter). The dance descriptions are confident-knowledge writing.

  1. The commons note (Manuel, Fernández, practitioner sources) rates the compás patterns and the Andalusian cadence as high-confidence and the cante's estilo system as only loosely analogous to raga/maqam grammar. ↩

  2. The commons note's Scandinavian claim rests on motion-capture studies (Haugen et al.; Kaminsky on polska med kort etta) and flags regional variation in the exact ratios. ↩

docs.title: Latin America
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

Latin America's dances are the Afro-Atlantic diaspora's most elaborate flowering — West and Central African polycentrism and call-and-response, European couple dance and court form, Indigenous ceremony, all recombined in the Caribbean, Brazil, and the Río de la Plata — and they are, by a wide margin, the world's most exported social dances: the waltz aside, no European form travels like salsa, tango, or samba. Most run the first chapter's social function at home and a presentational one abroad, with competitive ballroom versions of several (ballroom).

docs.title: The music every part answers to: clave
docs.text: The commons describes Afro-Cuban music's organizing principle in one sentence, and it governs the dancing of half the continent. Clave — son or rumba clave, five strokes split into a three-side and a two-side, played 3-2 or 2-3 — is a timeline: a fixed asymmetric reference the whole ensemble entrains to, with an internal direction, so that a piece is in 3-2 or 2-3 and every other part's accents are derived from which side of the cell they fall on; the bass tumbao's anticipations, the piano guajeo, the conga pattern are clave-aligned ostinati; the montuno (the short vamp over which coro-pregón call-and-response and solos layer) is a one-clave-cycle cell, and direction changes only at section boundaries, never by drift.1 The dances answer it precisely — and argue about it. Salsa's "on 1" versus "on 2" debate (the break step on the first or second beat; New York's "on 2" mambo timing) is a disagreement about which event of the clave cell the body weights, not about which beat of a measure; the rumba dancer's hips mark the clave's strokes; the son's contratiempo (the step on the off-beat) is clave's anticipation in the feet. A dancer who is "off clave" is wrong in the way a musician is, and everyone on the floor can hear it.

docs.title: Cuba and the Caribbean
docs.text:
• Rumba (Cuba: guaguancó, the courtship game of the vacunao; yambú, slower; columbia, the fast male solo) — the drum-and-voice root form; the orisha dances of Santería (Africa and the diaspora) beside it.
  • Son → mambo → salsa — the son (Oriente, early twentieth century; the casino partner form), the mambo of 1940s Havana and the Palladium in New York (Pérez Prado, Tito Puente — the dance a fast, open, showy partner form), and salsa, the 1970s New York label for the whole family (Fania Records), now danced worldwide in regional styles: Cuban casino and the circle form rueda de casino, Puerto Rican, New York "on 2," LA "on 1," Cali's hyper-fast footwork (Colombia's claim to the world's salsa capital).
  • Cha-cha-chá (1950s, Enrique Jorrín), danzón (the nineteenth-century Cuban ballroom dance, Mexico's too), bolero, mambo; the Dominican Republic's merengue (the two-step hip-sway to tambora and accordion) and bachata (the 1960s bar music, the 2000s global sensual partner dance); Puerto Rico's bomba (drummer follows dancer — the African cue relationship reversed) and plena; Haiti's konpa; Trinidad's soca, limbo, and the Carnival bands; Jamaica's dancehall with its named moves and their inventors, and reggae's skank.

docs.title: Brazil
docs.text: Samba — from Bahia's Afro-Brazilian samba de roda (UNESCO-listed) to Rio's samba no pé, the solo fast-footed Carnival dance of the escolas de samba and their passistas; the partner forms samba de gafieira (the ballroom) and samba-rock; and the ballroom's very different "samba" (ballroom). Capoeira — the Angolan-rooted martial art-dance-game played in a roda to the berimbau: ginga (the swaying base step), kicks, escapes, cartwheels, and acrobatics in a conversation between two players — Angola (slow, low, ritualized) and Regional (Mestre Bimba's 1930s systematization, faster, more athletic); now a worldwide practice and a direct feeder of breaking's power moves and of contemporary dance's floor vocabulary. Forró (the Northeast's accordion couple dance), frevo (Recife's acrobatic Carnival dance with the small umbrella), maracatu, bumba-meu-boi, axé, funk carioca's passinho, and the contemporary companies — Grupo Corpo, Deborah Colker (the modern revolt).

docs.title: The Río de la Plata: tango
docs.text: Tango — Buenos Aires and Montevideo, the 1880s–1900s, the immigrant ports' fusion of habanera, milonga, candombe, and European couple dance: the close embrace, the walk (caminata), ochos, ganchos, boleos, sacadas, the leader's improvised lead and the follower's reading of it — a fully improvised partner dance with a large vocabulary, danced socially at the milonga under its codes (the cabeceo invitation, the tanda of three or four songs, the cortina). Its stage form — tango escenario, the lifts and kicks of Tango Argentino (1983) and Forever Tango — and its ballroom form are different animals; tango nuevo (from the 1990s; Gustavo Naveira, Chicho Frúmboli) re-analyzed the dance's mechanics and opened the embrace. The dressing-the-genre chapter reads its costume; the music (Gardel, Troilo, Pugliese, D'Arienzo, Piazzolla's nuevo tango) is itself a complete art. Milonga (the dance, faster, older) and vals complete the milonga's trio. Argentina's folklórico — chacarera, zamba, gato, the gaucho's stamping malambo (now a competitive male solo with boleadoras) — is the other tradition.

docs.title: Mexico, Central America, the Andes
docs.text: Mexican folklórico — the staged regional repertoire (Amalia Hernández's Ballet Folklórico de México, 1952): the jarabe tapatío (the "Mexican hat dance"), Veracruz's son jarocho and its zapateado on the tarima, Jalisco's skirt-swirling, the danza de los viejitos, the Yucatán's jarana; the pre-Hispanic-rooted concheros and the danza de los voladores (the Totonac flying-pole ritual); and quebradita, banda, cumbia sonidera as living popular forms. Cumbia — Colombia's Caribbean coast (African drum, Indigenous flute, Spanish dress), the continent's most-spread rhythm, with a national style in every country from Mexico to Argentina. The Andes — Peru's marinera (the elegant handkerchief courtship dance) and huayno, the danza de tijeras (scissors dance); Bolivia's diablada, morenada, caporales at the Oruro Carnival; Chile's cueca; Ecuador's sanjuanito. Central America — Guatemala's baile de la conquista, Panama's tamborito, Garifuna punta.

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
That a single global state variable — clave direction — can govern every part's accents, the dancer's included, which is the most concrete possible version of the "shared frame" this subject keeps finding; that fully improvised partner dance (tango, salsa) is a two-body generative system with a lead/follow protocol the gamut+rules architecture has no equivalent for yet; and that a social dance's stage and ballroom versions are different dances wearing the same name — a warning for any corpus labelled "tango."

Field notes

Renders theory-genre-afro-cuban (clave as a directional timeline; clave-aligned tumbao and guajeo; the montuno cell; direction changes only at section boundaries). The dance descriptions are confident-knowledge writing.

  1. The commons note (Peñalosa's Clave Matrix, Mauleón) flags that traditional Cuban players reportedly reject the 3-2/2-3 labeling as a New York-era formalization — treat "the whole arrangement is in one direction" as a generatively useful simplification. ↩

docs.title: The Middle East and Central Asia
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

A region where dance is everywhere and concert dance almost nowhere: the dominant functions are social (the line and circle dances of every wedding from the Levant to the Caucasus) and ritual (the Sufi orders), with solo improvised dance at the center of the social forms and a twentieth-century stage tradition — Egyptian raqs sharqi, Iranian and Soviet "national" ballets — built on top. It is also a region where the music's theory is deep and the dance's theory thin, so the commons' maqam note does unusual work here.

docs.title: The music the dancer inhabits
docs.text: Middle Eastern art music is maqam music, and the commons describes its grammar precisely. The atom is the jins — a three-to-five-note module — not the scale; a maqam chains two or three ajnas at a pivot (ghammaz), and its identity is its sayr, the conventional melodic course: which jins opens, the order the others enter, where modulation is licensed, where the piece resolves. Two maqamat can share a scale and differ entirely in sayr. Time splits by genre: a taqsim (solo instrumental improvisation) or layali/mawwal (vocal) is suspended — no enforced pulse, phrasing by breath — while a metered piece runs against an iqa', a cyclic dum/tak pattern (wahda's plain 4/4, maqsum, sama'i thaqil's 10/8 grouped 3+2+2+3), with cadences aligned to the cycle. The intervals include neutral seconds and thirds no twelve-tone stand-in reproduces.1 For the dancer this produces two distinct modes of moving: to the iqa' — the hips and feet marking a cycle whose accent pattern (dum low, tak high) is the choreography's clock — and to the taqsim — the slow, unmetered section of a raqs sharqi solo in which the dancer follows the melodic course with sustained, continuous movement, phrasing on the singer's or the oud's breath. A raqs sharqi solo is built from exactly this alternation, and the suspended-then-cyclic shape the choreomusicology chapter describes is its form.

docs.title: The Arab world and the Levant
docs.text:
Raqs sharqi ("oriental dance," belly dance in the West's term) — the solo improvised dance of Egypt and the Levant, rooted in social dancing, developed as a stage and nightclub art in Cairo from the 1920s (Badia Masabni's casino, the film stars Samia Gamal and Tahia Carioca, the later Reda Troupe's folkloric stagings) and globalized from there. Signature: polycentric isolations — hip drops, shimmies, undulations, chest and shoulder articulation — over a grounded base, arms framing, the veil and finger cymbals (sagat) as props. Folk cousins: baladi (the urban-folk ancestor), Saidi (Upper Egypt, with the cane — raqs al-assaya, from the men's stick-fighting tahtib), the Persian Gulf's khaleegy hair-tossing dance, Nubian dances, the Moroccan shikhat. Function: social at its root (women dancing for women at weddings), presentational on stage — and contested throughout the region for exactly that migration.

Dabke — the line dance of the Levant (Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, Jordan): linked dancers led by a lawweeh twirling a handkerchief or beads, stamping in synchronized steps to the mijwiz or tabl; the wedding dance of the entire region and a diaspora identity marker. Arab Gulf ardah (the sword line dance), Yemeni bara', Iraqi choubi.

docs.title: The Sufi orders
docs.text: The Mevlevi sema (Turkey; Rumi's order, thirteenth century) — the whirling of the dervishes: white skirts, tall felt hats, the right palm up and left down, turning counter-clockwise on the left foot for long minutes in a ceremony of dhikr (remembrance). It is ritual, not performance, in its own terms — the first chapter's efficacy function — though it is staged for tourists and has been a source for contemporary choreographers (Cherkaoui, Ziya Azazi). Other orders have their own movement — the Moroccan hadra, the Egyptian tanoura (a colored-skirt spectacle form of the whirl), the zar trance rituals of Egypt, Sudan, and the Gulf.

docs.title: Iran and Persian dance
docs.text: Iran's classical dance — the refined, courtly solo of the Qajar and Pahlavi courts, with its soft wrists, upper-body focus, and facial expressiveness — was staged as a national ballet under the Pahlavis and driven underground after 1979, surviving in the diaspora (Los Angeles above all). Regional forms are more robust: the Kurdish halparke (line dances), Azerbaijani dances (shared with the Caucasus), Baluchi, Gilaki, Bandari (the Gulf coast, African-influenced), and the Khorasani stick and bakhtiari dances.

docs.title: Central Asia and the Caucasus
docs.text: Uzbek and Tajik dance — the courtly, lyrical solo traditions (the Bukhara, Khorezm, and Ferghana styles) of wrists, arms, and turning, staged and systematized in the Soviet period. Caucasus — Georgian dance (kartuli, khorumi, mtiuluri): the men's astonishing toe-dancing in soft boots, the women's gliding as if on wheels, the national ensembles (Sukhishvili, 1945) that made it a world stage form; Armenian kochari and shalakho; Azerbaijani yalli; Chechen and Dagestani lezginka — the men's leaping, knife-edge dance of the whole North Caucasus. Turkey — beyond the sema, the folk families (horon from the Black Sea, zeybek from the Aegean, halay the line dance of Anatolia). Afghanistan — the attan, the circle dance of the Pashtuns. The Soviet legacy across this whole zone is a distinctive thing: each "nation" given a staged folkloric ballet, a national ensemble, and a conservatory — which preserved and standardized the dances in the same stroke.

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
That suspended time is a mode of dancing — the taqsim-following solo is continuous movement without a clock, phrased on melody, the clearest living case of the breath mode the working-with-music chapter describes; that the solo improviser inside a grammar (sayr for the musician, the raqs sharqi vocabulary for the dancer) is a complete model of frame-and-realization; and that social line dance is the region's — and perhaps the world's — default form, the participatory function unbroken.

Field notes

Renders theory-genre-maqam (jins and sayr; ghammaz pivots; taqsim as suspended time; iqa' cycles; neutral intervals). The dance descriptions are confident-knowledge writing.

  1. The commons note (Abu Shumays's primer, maqamworld.com, drawing on Racy and Marcus) flags the specific iqa' stroke patterns beyond wahda and sama'i thaqil as practitioner-sourced. ↩

docs.title: North American vernacular
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

North America's vernacular dances are the continent's own fusions — Indigenous ceremony and contest; British Isles step and set dance transplanted to the Appalachians and the prairies; and, above all, the African-American lineage that produced tap, the jazz dances, the Lindy Hop, and, by direct descent, the street styles that have their own chapter. Most are social; several became competitive; and the African-American forms became, through Broadway and Hollywood, the world's idea of American dance.

docs.title: Indigenous: the powwow and the ceremonies
docs.text: The powwow is the pan-Indigenous gathering of the twentieth century — Plains-derived, now continental — whose dances are both ceremony and contest: the Grand Entry; the men's Traditional (the upright, stalking warrior's dance), Grass (the swaying, yarn-fringed dance), and Fancy (the fast, spinning, double-bustled dance of the 1920s–30s); the women's Traditional (stately, the shawl held), Jingle Dress (the Ojibwe healing dance of rolled tin cones, c. 1900s), and Fancy Shawl (the butterfly-like fast dance, mid-century); and the intertribal round dances everyone joins. The drum — a large group drum with singers — is the music, the songs' honor beats the cues, and competition categories with judges and prize money the modern frame (the first chapter's ritual-and-competitive pairing). Beside the powwow stand the nations' own ceremonies, many closed to outsiders: the Pueblo corn and animal dances, the Hopi katsina dances, the Northwest Coast's masked potlatch dances (suppressed by law in Canada 1885–1951 and revived), the Iroquois social dances, the Sun Dance, the Hoop Dance (now a competitive solo form), the Apache Crown Dance; and the Métis jig and the Inuit drum dance in the north. Bangarra's American cousins are companies like Red Sky Performance (Toronto); Indigenous contemporary dance is a growing field.

docs.title: The British Isles transplanted
docs.text: Appalachian clogging and flatfooting — the mountain step dances of the Scots-Irish settlers crossed with African-American rhythm: flatfooting is the loose, low, improvised solo; clogging the later, more codified and competitive team form with taps added (the Green Grass Cloggers, the precision teams). Square dance — the quadrille and contredanse of Europe with a caller chanting the figures (do-si-do, allemande left, promenade), the Western square dance of the 1930s–50s revival standardized into a called vocabulary (Callerlab's lists) that is, in this subject's terms, a spoken sequencer over a fixed gamut; contra dance — New England's longways sets, revived in the 1970s and thriving; the Cajun two-step and waltz and zydeco of Louisiana, danced to accordion and washboard; Cape Breton and Ottawa Valley step dance; Texas's two-step and the country-western line dances of the 1990s (Achy Breaky, the Electric Slide's country cousin).

docs.title: The African-American lineage: tap and the jazz dances
docs.text:
This is the continent's great contribution, and it runs in one line from the plantation to the present. The ring shout, the juba (body percussion — pattin' juba — when drums were banned), the cakewalk (the strutting parody of the masters, become a craze by 1900); minstrelsy's appropriations (William Henry Lane, "Master Juba," the 1840s' first tap star, and the long, ugly history that surrounds him); and tap, the fusion of Irish and English step dance with African rhythm that became a fully codified percussive art by the 1920s — the vaudeville and Broadway hoofers, Bill "Bojangles" Robinson, John Bubbles's rhythm tap, the Nicholas Brothers' acrobatic flash, Fred Astaire's and Gene Kelly's film tap, the bebop hoofers, Gregory Hines, and Savion Glover's Bring in 'da Noise (1996) — tap as percussion first. The dressing-the-genre chapter treats the shoe as instrument. Around it, the jazz dances of the 1910s–40s: the Charleston, the Black Bottom, the Shimmy, the Shag, the Big Apple, truckin', the Suzie Q — and the Lindy Hop, Harlem's Savoy Ballroom, late 1920s (Shorty George Snowden, Frankie Manning's air steps in 1935, Norma Miller, Whitey's Lindy Hoppers), the swing-era partner dance that became jitterbug, boogie- woogie, and the whole swing revival of the 1990s; and after swing, the Bop, the Twist (1960) and the solo social dances of the 1960s (the Mashed Potato, the Watusi, the Jerk), the Hustle (disco, 1970s), and the line that runs into the street chapter.

The music the dances rode. The commons holds jazz and blues form precisely, and the dances are built on it. Jazz's atom is the chorus — one full pass through a tune's fixed form (12-bar blues, 32-bar AABA, "rhythm changes") — cyclic chorus after chorus inside a linear head–solos–head arc, with trading fours as an explicit escalating exchange and varied repeat as the variation mechanism; blues collapses chorus and form into one object, stacks the identical I–IV–V cycle, nests call-and-response two levels deep (the AAB lines; the vocal call and instrumental fill inside each line), and runs on a shuffle triplet feel that is a framework, not a decoration.1 The Lindy Hop's basic is sized to the chorus's phrases; the tap dancer's "trading" with a drummer is trading fours in the feet; the blues dances — the slow drag, the juke-joint grind, the modern blues-dance revival — live in the call-and- response slot and in the shuffle's long-short; and swing's pocket is the working-with-music chapter's groove finding in practice. The jazz dances are the clearest case in the West of vernacular movement shaped bar by bar by a music's form.

docs.title: Stage vernacular: jazz dance and musical theatre
docs.text: Jazz dance as a studio technique — Jack Cole's (the "father of theatrical jazz," 1940s; Indian and Afro-Cuban isolations over jazz rhythm), Katherine Dunham's, Matt Mattox's, Luigi's, Gus Giordano's — is the codified, teachable descendant of the vernacular jazz dances, and musical theatre dance its stage: Agnes de Mille's Oklahoma! dream ballet (1943), Jerome Robbins (West Side Story, 1957), Bob Fosse (Sweet Charity, Pippin, Chicago, the shelf's stylist of hats, hips, and turned-in knees), Michael Bennett (A Chorus Line, 1975), Gower Champion, Tommy Tune, Susan Stroman; and the film musical's choreographers — Busby Berkeley's overhead geometries and Hermes Pan with Astaire — the shelf covers the two Ryan promoted.

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
That a music's chorus structure is a dance's phrase structure (the Lindy, tap's trading); that a caller is a sequencer — square dance is a gamut of figures driven by a spoken control channel, the gamut+rules architecture in a barn; and that the vernacular-to-stage migration (jazz dances → jazz technique → Broadway) is how most of the world's concert vocabularies were made.

Field notes

Renders theory-genre-jazz (the chorus as atom; head–solos–head; trading fours; varied repeat; changes vs. modal) and theory-genre-blues (12-bar-as-form; AAB call-and-response nested two deep; blues tonality; shuffle as framework). The dance descriptions are confident-knowledge writing.

  1. The commons notes rate chorus/AABA/rhythm-changes structure and blues's 12-bar/AAB grammar as high-confidence, and trading fours' strict bar count as common practice rather than universal rule. ↩

docs.title: Oceania and the Pacific
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

The Pacific's dances are, more than any other region's, sung texts made visible. Across Polynesia the dance illustrates a chant or song — the hands and arms say the words, the hips and feet keep the rhythm — and the dances carry genealogy, history, and land claims in societies where they were the archive. Colonization, missionary suppression (hula was banned in public in the 1830s; the haka and many ceremonies were discouraged), tourism's commodification, and then the cultural revivals of the 1970s onward shaped all of them; most now run the first chapter's ritual, social, presentational, and competitive functions at once, with the festival competition (the Merrie Monarch, Te Matatini, Heiva) as the modern institution that keeps the forms rigorous.

docs.title: Hawaiʻi: hula
docs.text: Hula divides into kahiko — the ancient form, danced to chant (oli, mele) and percussion (the ipu heke gourd, the pahu drum), in kapa cloth, ti-leaf skirts, and lei, with the grounded, bent-knee, deliberate vocabulary of the pre-contact tradition — and ʻauana — the modern form that emerged after the missionary ban and King Kalākaua's 1880s revival, danced to song with guitar and ʻukulele, in fabric dresses, softer and more lyrical. Both are built on a small set of named steps — the kaholo (the side-step), ʻami (the hip circle), ʻuwehe (the knee pop), hela (the foot touch), and a dozen more — and on hand gestures that illustrate the text: the rain, the mountain, the lover, the flower. The gesture language is less a fixed lexicon than a descriptive vocabulary shaped by each hālau (school) and kumu hula (master), and the codified-vocabularies chapter treats it as the case between the mudra systems' grammar and improvised illustration. The Merrie Monarch Festival (Hilo, since 1964) is the competitive summit and the engine of the form's rigor. The chant comes first: the dance exists to carry the mele.

docs.title: Aotearoa: the haka and Māori performance
docs.text: The haka is a posture dance with chanted words, performed by men, women, or both — the stamping, the slapped thighs and chest, the pūkana (the dilated eyes) and whētero (the protruded tongue) — as challenge, welcome, commemoration, and, famously, as the All Blacks' pre-match ritual (Ka Mate, composed by Te Rauparaha around 1820). Haka is one genre within kapa haka, Māori performing arts: the waiata-ā-ringa (action song), the poi (the swung balls on cords, a rhythmic and visual skill — the props chapter's case), the mōteatea (traditional chant), the whakaeke entrance and whakawātea exit. Te Matatini, the biennial national competition, is the form's institution, and haka's use in protest and in public ceremony (parliament, funerals, the 2019 Christchurch mourning) makes it the Pacific's most visible dance.

docs.title: Samoa, Tonga, and the Polynesian family
docs.text: Samoa — the siva (the graceful, seated or standing women's dance with hand gestures), the sāsā (a fast, seated or kneeling group dance of slapped rhythms and synchronized gestures to the pātē log drum), the fa'ataupati (the men's slap dance), and the taualuga (the ceremonial finale danced by the taupou, the village maiden of rank). Tonga — the lakalaka (UNESCO-listed: a standing group dance of hundreds, the men's and women's sides with different movements, illustrating a composed poem — the sung-text principle at its largest), the ma'ulu'ulu (seated), the tau'olunga (the solo female dance). Tahiti — the ʻōteʻa (the fast hip-shaking dance to drums that tourists mistake for hula; the men's knee-scissoring pāʻōti), the ʻaparima (the song-dance with hands), the Heiva i Tahiti festival (since 1881). Cook Islands ura (the drum dance; the fastest hips in the Pacific); Fiji's meke (the seated and standing narrative dances with fans and clubs); Niue, Tokelau, Tuvalu (the fatele), Kiribati (the bird-like stance and flicked head); Rapa Nui's sau sau and hoko.

docs.title: Melanesia and Micronesia
docs.text: Papua New Guinea's sing-sing — the great gatherings (Goroka, Mount Hagen) where hundreds of clans in paint, feathers, and shell perform their dances to kundu drums; the Sepik's crocodile and mask dances; Vanuatu's Rom dance and the land-diving of Pentecost (nagol, the bungee's ancestor — a ritual, not a dance, but adjacent); the Solomons' panpipe dances. Micronesia's stick dances (Yap), Palau's ngloik, the Marshall Islands' jobwa — seated and standing chanted dances, many of them lost or reviving.

docs.title: Australia and the Torres Strait
docs.text: Aboriginal Australian ceremony — the oldest continuous dance traditions on earth, tens of thousands of years deep: corroboree is the colonial catch-all; the traditions are the clan-specific songlines' dances, the men's and women's ceremonies, the animal mimesis (the kangaroo, the emu, the brolga), the body paint and the clapsticks and didgeridoo (in the north), and the laws about who may see what. Torres Strait Islander dance — the kab kar, the headdresses (dhari), the distinctive seated and standing dances with their own instruments. Bangarra Dance Theatre (1989; Stephen Page) is the contemporary company that carries this into the concert world, and it sits on the shelf's threshold.

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
That dance can be a text's rendering — the sung-poem principle of hula, lakalaka, and the action song is the most literal music–movement relationship in the choreomusicology chapter's spectrum, visualization of words rather than of structure; that a dance can be an archive — genealogy, land, law — which a system that treats movement as pure form will never see; and that competition preserves as often as it distorts: Merrie Monarch, Te Matatini, and Heiva are why the forms are rigorous today.

Field notes

No commons notes rendered — confident-knowledge writing.

docs.title: South Asia
docs.text:
Atlas page — the world atlas of dance.

South Asia has the world's most elaborated codified dance vocabularies outside ballet — the hand-gesture systems that the codified-vocabularies chapter treats as its second great case — and a theory of performance, the Nāṭyaśāstra (a Sanskrit treatise, roughly 200 BCE–200 CE), older than anything comparable in the West. The classical forms share that theory's vocabulary: nritta (pure dance — rhythm and line), nritya (expressive dance — gesture and face carrying meaning), and natya (drama); the hasta or mudra hand positions; abhinaya, expressive acting, and the nine rasas (aesthetic flavors) it aims to evoke. Each form reconstructed itself as a concert art in the twentieth century from temple, court, or village practice — the first chapter's ritual-to-concert migration — and most are now taught worldwide.

docs.title: The music the feet recite
docs.text: The commons holds the music's grammar in detail, and it is the key to the dancing. The atom of Indian classical music is the avartana — one cycle of the tala, the rhythmic cycle — not a bar. A tala divides into vibhag (groupings: teentaal's sixteen beats as 4+4+4+4), marked by claps and a khali wave, and every phrase resolves onto sam, the cycle's first beat, where tension lands. A full performance is linear at the large scale — the unmetered alap intensifies into jor (pulse) and jhala (fast, dense), then hands off to a metered composition with drums — and strictly cyclic once tala enters; the performer's chief rhythmic freedom is layakari, shifting rhythmic density (double-, triple-time subdivisions) against the fixed cycle, always resolving onto sam. Raga is a phrase-level grammar rather than a scale: ascent and descent rules, a hierarchy of structural notes, obligatory ornament (gamaka), and a short identifying phrase (pakad), over a drone that fixes the tonic permanently.1 The dancer's nritta is layakari for the feet — rhythmic patterns recited as syllables (bols, konnakol; the recitation is padhant) and struck with belled ankles against the cycle, landing on sam with the drummer — and the nritya sits on the raga's melodic phrases. The working-with-music chapter treats this as the paradigm of recited counting.

docs.title: The classical forms
docs.text:
Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu) — descended from sadir, the temple and court dance of the hereditary devadasi communities, reconstructed as a concert form in the 1930s by Rukmini Devi Arundale (Kalakshetra, 1936) and others, with the erotic content muted and Brahmin respectability added. Signature: the araimandi (the half-seated, turned-out plié that is the base position), geometric lines, the adavus (codified step units combining feet, arms, and head — the gamut), stamped footwork with ankle bells, and the elaborate hasta/mudra language of the nritya. Structure: the margam, a concert sequence (alarippu, jatiswaram, shabdam, varnam — the long centerpiece mixing nritta and nritya — padam, tillana). Music: Carnatic, with a nattuvanar conducting with cymbals and reciting the syllables. Door: the mudra system → codified vocabularies; the costume's pleated fan → dressing the genre.

Kathak (North India) — from the kathakar storytellers of the Hindu temples through the Mughal courts, where it acquired its Persianate grace, its gharanas (Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras) and its secular repertoire. Signature: upright spine, fast chakkars (spins, dozens in sequence, ending precisely on sam), intricate tatkar (footwork with a hundred or more bells per ankle), tukras and torasa (rhythmic compositions recited then danced), and a subtle, flirtatious abhinaya to thumri. Music: Hindustani, with tabla; the dancer–tabla dialogue (jugalbandi) is a concert high point. Door: working with music (recited rhythm); Akram Khan's kathak-contemporary on the shelf.

Odissi (Odisha) — the temple dance of the maharis and the acrobatic boys' form gotipua, reconstructed in the 1950s (Kelucharan Mohapatra and colleagues, from temple sculpture and surviving practice). Signature: the tribhangi (three-bend posture: head, torso, hips deflected in opposite directions — the curve of the temple sculptures), the square chauka, fluid torso, soft lyricism. Music: Odissi music, a distinct tradition. Door: the costume's front fan and silver → dressing the genre.

Kathakali (Kerala) — a seventeenth-century dance-drama of the Hindu epics, traditionally all-male, performed through the night. Signature: the vesham — hours-long makeup whose colors and the chutti rice-paste jaw frame encode the character's moral type (light and the picture); enormous skirts and headdresses; an elaborate, precise mudra language (twenty-four basic hastas from the Hastalakshanadeepika) that speaks the sung text; the face's trained muscular virtuosity (navarasa training). Music: Sopana-style singing with chenda and maddalam drums. Institution: Kerala Kalamandalam (1930, the poet Vallathol). Door: makeup as codified vocabulary.

Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh) — a village dance-drama tradition turned concert form in the mid-twentieth century (Vempati Chinna Satyam); close to bharatanatyam in vocabulary, faster and more dramatic, with the famous tarangam danced on the rim of a brass plate.

Manipuri (Manipur) — the Vaishnava Ras Lila dances of Krishna and the gopis, soft, rounded, continuous, the feet never striking the ground hard; the pung cholom drum dance, where the drummers leap and spin while playing, is its virtuoso male form.

Mohiniyattam (Kerala) — the "dance of the enchantress," a female solo form of swaying, circular, lyrical movement, reconstructed alongside kathakali at Kalamandalam.

Sattriya (Assam) — the dance-drama of the Vaishnava monasteries (sattras), recognized as the eighth classical form in 2000 and still partly monastic.

docs.title: Folk, martial, and popular
docs.text:
• Bhangra (Punjab) — a harvest dance to the dhol, shoulders and leaps, now a global diaspora and club form; giddha, its women's counterpart.
  • Garba and raas (Gujarat) — the circling dances of Navratri; garba in concentric circles around a lamp, dandiya raas with struck sticks — the props chapter's prop-as-rhythm case.
  • Ghoomar (Rajasthan), lavani (Maharashtra), bihu (Assam), kalbelia (the Rajasthani "snake-charmer" dance, UNESCO-listed) — a sampling of a vast regional repertoire.
  • Chhau (eastern India) — masked (Seraikela, Purulia) or unmasked (Mayurbhanj) martial dance-drama, leaping and acrobatic.
  • Kalaripayattu (Kerala) — a martial art whose training has fed contemporary dance (Chandralekha; the Akram Khan generation).
  • Kandyan dance (Sri Lanka) — the ves dancers' leaping, drum-driven temple-festival form.
  • Bollywood — the film industry's dance idiom, a century-old hybrid of classical, folk, Western jazz and hip-hop, and whatever is current; the most-watched dance on earth and the one through which most of the world meets South Asian movement. It is a function, in the first chapter's sense — presentational, commercial — laid over every vocabulary above.

docs.title: What the region teaches the core
docs.text:
Two things above all. First, that a gesture language can be a full vocabulary — the mudra systems have grammar, dialect, and drift exactly as the codified-vocabularies chapter argues, and they remain the world's best evidence that meaning can be carried by codified hands.
