The mute test is a standard film-editing heuristic. The dual-metric observation is drawn from several dance-generation papers' reporting practice. ↩

docs.title: Composing for choreography
docs.text: title: Composing for choreography summary: What composers have written for dancers and how — Tchaikovsky under Petipa's minutage, Stravinsky with Nijinsky and Balanchine, Copland for Graham, Cage's durations, Glass and Reich with Childs and De Keersmaeker, the contemporary commission — and what a choreographer actually needs delivered: form, arc, hypermeter, cues. covers: - theory-form-archetypes - theory-tension-energy-arcs - theory-genre-western-classical

docs.title: Composing for choreography
docs.text: Writing music for dance is a discipline of its own, and most of its history is the history of composers learning — sometimes resentfully — what dancers need from a score. The needs are specific: durations that can be danced, phrases that can be counted, climaxes that land where a body can land, forms whose returns a choreographer can stage. This chapter follows the great collaborations for what they reveal about those needs, then states them plainly as a brief — because the commons holds, from its music-theory side, exactly the vocabulary for what a composer delivers: form archetypes, tension arcs, and phrase-level formal function.

docs.title: Petipa's minutage
docs.text:
Before Tchaikovsky, "ballet composer" was a trade: Cesare Pugni, Ludwig Minkus, Riccardo Drigo turned out serviceable, four-square numbers to order, and the order was precise. Marius Petipa gave his composers a minutage — a written plan specifying, number by number, the character, tempo, meter, and bar count of each dance: so many bars of a lively waltz for the entrance, an adagio of such a length for the pas de deux, a variation of sixteen bars, a coda. For The Sleeping Beauty (1890) and The Nutcracker (1892) he handed Tchaikovsky instructions of this kind, down to the measure, and Tchaikovsky — who had admired Delibes's Sylvia (1876) and believed ballet music could be real music — wrote to them and transcended them.1

What the minutage reveals is the nineteenth-century ballet score's form: a suite of closed numbers, each a danceable unit with a stated character, ordered for contrast. The grand pas de deux — entrée, adagio, variation, variation, coda — is itself a small suite with a fixed grammar. In the commons' form vocabulary this is the suite/medley archetype: the composer's contract is ordering, not development — self-contained units chained by tempo and character contrast, nearer to set-sequencing than to symphonic argument. That is also why the scores were so freely cut, reordered, and interpolated by ballet masters: a suite licenses it. Tchaikovsky's achievement was to honor the suite grammar while smuggling in a linear arc above it — the leitmotifs, the tonal plan, the through-line of Sleeping Beauty's Lilac Fairy music — so that the numbers add up to a drama rather than a program. (Adolphe Adam had gestured at this with Giselle's motifs in 1841; Tchaikovsky finished it.)2

docs.title: Stravinsky: the count breaks, then becomes the floor
docs.text:
The Rite of Spring (1913) is the canonical case of music outrunning the dancers' ability to count it. Nijinsky's choreography required the cast to count Stravinsky's irregular, shifting meters aloud; Diaghilev brought in Marie Rambert, trained in Dalcroze eurhythmics, to drill the rhythm into the company; and the dancers still could barely hold it — the riot is remembered, but the counting crisis is the choreographic fact. Additive, shifting meter had arrived in the theatre before the bodies were ready.

Balanchine's Stravinsky is the other half of the story. Apollo (1928) taught Balanchine, by his own account, that he could eliminate — that the score's clarity licensed a stripped choreography. Orpheus (1948) and above all Agon (1957) were written in conversation: the famous exchange in which Balanchine specified durations ("how long?" — "about two minutes") and Stravinsky composed to them is the minutage reborn between equals, and the choreography's structure mirrors the serial score's so closely that the dance is analyzed as a twelve-tone object. Stravinsky's ballet music, from Firebird to Agon, is a forty-year demonstration that the composer who writes to the dance need not write down to it.

docs.title: Graham's commissions and Copland's scenario
docs.text: Martha Graham was the twentieth century's great commissioner. Appalachian Spring (1944) was written by Aaron Copland to her scenario — the manuscript is titled "Ballet for Martha" — and she choreographed to the finished score; the order was scenario, then music, then dance. Samuel Barber (Cave of the Heart), William Schuman (Night Journey), Gian Carlo Menotti, Norman Dello Joio, Paul Hindemith (Herodiade) followed the same pattern. Graham treated the scores as Petipa had treated his — cut, reordered, re-timed to the dance as it emerged — and composers learned that a commission for dance is a commission for material, not for a fixed text.

docs.title: Cage: the composer is given a duration
docs.text: Cunningham's composers were given, in principle, one fact: how long. John Cage's own later scores formalized the idea as time brackets — windows within which a sound may occur, flexible inside, fixed outside — and the Cunningham roster (David Tudor, Morton Feldman, Christian Wolff, Earle Brown, Pauline Oliveros, eventually Radiohead and Sigur Rós for Split Sides, 2003) was asked to deliver a thing of a given length and nothing else. The choreomusicology chapter covered what that did to the relationship; for the composer it meant liberation from the minutage and from the dancer's count alike, and the commons' process form archetype describes much of what resulted: the composer authors a rule and a starting state, and the form is the rule's audible trace. A rule running to completion needs no choreography to agree with it, and for thirty years none did.

docs.title: Process music and process dance: Glass, Reich, Childs, De Keersmaeker
docs.text: The minimalists turned Cage's separation into a new kind of union. Philip Glass and Lucinda Childs met on Einstein on the Beach (1976, with Robert Wilson); their Dance (1979, with Sol LeWitt's film décor) sets Childs's additive, permutational phrase structures against Glass's additive, permutational music — the same archetype on two channels. Steve Reich and Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker never collaborated directly, but Fase (1982), Drumming (1998), and Rain (2001) are the closest the repertory comes to a dance and a score being one process: phasing made visible. This is the composer's process form and the choreographer's accumulation or permutation — the chance chapter's subject — recognizing each other as the same idea, and it is why those works feel inevitable rather than illustrative.

docs.title: The contemporary commission
docs.text:
Today's dance composer works in one of three modes. In the room: Thom Willems with Forsythe, composing electronically as the dance is built; Owen Belton with Crystal Pite; Nitin Sawhney in long partnership with Akram Khan. To a brief: Joby Talbot's full-evening scores for Christopher Wheeldon (Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, 2011; The Winter's Tale, 2014) or Max Richter for Wayne McGregor (Infra, 2008; Woolf Works, 2015), written from a scenario and a timing plan — the minutage in a new suit, with the composer now expected to deliver the arc. As found material: the choreographer who edits an existing recording, or commissions from a producer who delivers stems — Jlin for McGregor's Autobiography (2017) — which the choreographer re-cuts. And a growing fourth: the choreographer-composer — Hofesh Shechter's percussion scores, Ohad Naharin's collages and pseudonymous tracks, Sharon Eyal's live DJ. In the commercial world the question barely arises: the track exists first, and the choreography is made to it.

What composers actually deliver has changed accordingly: a rehearsal mix early, a tempo map and click track for unison and for film, stems so the choreographer can thin or thicken a passage, cue points marked, and — always — a willingness to be cut. The composer who understands dance writes in units that survive surgery.

docs.title: The brief, stated
docs.text:
All of this history reduces to a set of things a choreographer needs from a score, and the commons' music-theory notes supply the vocabulary to ask for them precisely.

  • A declared form archetype. A form is a grammar of what is allowed to recur, contrast, and resolve — strophic, verse-chorus, AABA, rondo, sonata, through-composed, arc, suite, process. Each licenses a different kind of return, and returns are what a choreographer stages: a rondo's refrain is a recurring formation; a sonata's recapitulation is a homecoming the dance must earn; a process form is a ramp with no sections at all. Most real pieces mix archetypes across levels — verse-chorus at the song, sentence/period at the phrase — and the choreographer needs to know the archetype per level to know where the stageable returns are. A score whose archetype is undeclared is a score the dance will fight.3
  • A named arc on a named channel. Every tradition shapes intensity over time, but the shape (monotonic build-and-drop, repeating small lifts, a teleological harmonic resolution, discrete steps, a live-negotiated escalation) and the channel (density, tempo, harmony, texture) both vary — EDM and gamelan arc on density with no harmonic progression at all; the Hindustian jhala arcs on tempo over a static drone; only the sonata family is genuinely harmonic. A choreographer rides the arc, and needs to know which channel is carrying it, so the dance can carry the same one or deliberately a different one. "Where is the climax, and what is building it?" is the single most useful question a choreographer can ask a composer, and the composer should be able to answer it in one sentence.4
  • Regular hypermeter, or marked exceptions. Dancers count in eights because Western music groups bars in fours and eights; a score whose hypermeasures are regular is countable, and one that expands or elides a phrase must say so, because the expansion is exactly where the dancer's count will break. Tchaikovsky's squareness was a virtue; Stravinsky's irregularity needed Rambert.
  • Phrase-level function, not just length. An eight-bar unit is a sentence or a period, and the difference is the difference between an accelerating fragmentation and a question answered; cadence strength tells the dancer how hard a phrase may end. The commons' common-practice note puts it as the score's own contract: a period's antecedent closes weaker than its consequent; never end on a half cadence. A dance that ends a phrase on the music's weak cadence feels unfinished, and the dancer will not know why.5
  • Durations and cue points. Balanchine's two minutes; the oboe the run starts on; the stopwatch length Cunningham's composers were handed. Whatever else the score is, it is a clock the dance shares.

docs.title: What the machine lacks
docs.text:
The music-to-dance generators of Part VII are fed audio features — onsets, beats, spectral energy — which is to say they are handed the bottom of this brief and none of the top. They know where the beat is and nothing about whether this is a rondo's refrain or a sonata's recapitulation, whether the arc is on density or harmony, whether this phrase is a question or an answer. The composer's form knowledge is precisely the structural information the generators lack, and precisely what a choreographer uses. Adding it — a form-level conditioning signal, an arc curve, a phrase-function label — is a research program the commons' own notes already sketch from the music side.

Field notes

Renders theory-form-archetypes (archetypes as recurrence/resolution grammars; suite as ordering; process form; per-level mixing), theory-tension-energy-arcs (arc shape and channel vary by tradition; identify the channel first), and theory-genre-western-classical (sentence/period formal function, hypermeter, cadence-strength hierarchy as the score's contract). The collaboration history is confident-knowledge writing.

  1. Petipa's written instructions for Sleeping Beauty and Nutcracker survive and are quoted in Roland John Wiley's Tchaikovsky's Ballets (1985), the standard study. ↩

  2. The suite-archetype reading is the commons' form vocabulary applied to the nineteenth- century ballet score; the music-historical claim (closed numbers, freely reordered) is standard. ↩

  3. The per-level recommendation — commit to an archetype per hierarchy level rather than globally — is the commons note's synthesis, flagged there as design guidance rather than a cited finding. ↩

  4. The seven arc shapes in the commons note: build-drop, verse-chorus lift, sonata development→recapitulation, alap→jor→jhala, flamenco escalation, gamelan irama steps, blues/jazz chorus-stacking — classified by shape (continuous, repeating, teleological, discrete, live-negotiated) and channel. ↩

  5. Caplin's Classical Form (1998) and Rothstein's hypermeter are the sources; the commons note scopes them to common-practice music and warns that late-Romantic phrase rhythm loosens considerably — which is, not coincidentally, where dancers' counting gets hard. ↩

docs.title: How choreographers work with music
docs.text: The previous chapter was about the relationship; this one is about the room. How do dancers and choreographers actually hold a piece of music in the body, rehearse to it, edit it, and perform with it? The practices are old and mostly unwritten, and they fall into three families — counting, breathing, and cueing — that correspond to three different ways of addressing time. Underneath them sits a small amount of rhythm theory and perception research that the commons holds, and that makes sense of habits dancers usually learn as folklore.

docs.title: Counts
docs.text:
The universal studio unit is the eight: five, six, seven, eight and go. Ballet counts it, jazz and commercial dance count it, hip-hop counts it, the phrase in most Western dance is some number of eights. Why eight? Because most Western music is built in hypermeasures — bars group into fours and eights the way beats group into bars — and an eight-count is two bars of 4/4 heard as one unit. The count is the music's metric hierarchy taken one level up from the beat, and dancers count at that level because it is the level at which phrases begin and end.1

Three things about counts are worth making explicit, because they are where studio practice and music theory disagree productively.

The count is a grid; the phrase is a grouping — and they are independent. Music theory's formal statement (Lerdahl and Jackendoff's Generative Theory of Tonal Music) is that grouping structure — motif, phrase, section — is a separate hierarchy from metrical structure, and a group can begin on a weak beat. Dancers rediscover this constantly: the movement phrase wants to start on and-seven and run across the bar line into the next eight, and a choreographer who chops every phrase to the count produces the squareness that reads as "counting." Good phrasing crosses the counts; the counts are how you find your place, not how you shape the line. Music theory also offers the dancer something sharper than bar numbers: a unit of eight bars is not just "eight bars" but usually a sentence (idea, repeated idea, then a continuation that fragments and accelerates to cadence) or a period (a question-phrase ending weakly, an answer-phrase ending strongly). Choreographers feel this even when they can't name it — the movement that "arrives" on the period's consequent, the accelerating fragmentation that matches the sentence's continuation — and the strongest musical choreographers (Balanchine again) work at exactly this level.2

Not all meter is divisive eights. The commons' rhythm note separates two axes that most people fold into one time signature. Construction: divisive meter halves and thirds a span (4/4 as 2×2); additive meter concatenates unequal cells — the Balkan aksak of 7/8 as 2+2+3 or 9/8 as 2+2+2+3. Reference: hierarchical meter has strong and weak positions around a downbeat; a timeline — the Afro-Cuban clave, the West African bell pattern — is a fixed asymmetric reference the whole ensemble entrains to, with no privileged beat. Dancers in those traditions count differently because the music is built differently: a Bulgarian rǎchenitsa is danced quick-quick-slow because its 7/8 is 2+2+3, and the step pattern is the meter's cells made visible; salsa dancers argue about "on 1" versus "on 2" because they are choosing which event of a timeline to weight, not which beat of a hierarchy; an Ewe dancer whose feet move in two while the arms move in three is performing the music's cross-rhythm, a 3:2 that is the piece's basis rather than its decoration. The same note distinguishes polyrhythm (two groupings in one span), polymeter (different bar lengths realigning at their common multiple — a six-count phrase against eight-count music meets it every twenty-four, the engine of much Childs and De Keersmaeker), and metric modulation (a shared subdivision carrying the dancer across a tempo change). These are separate settings, and a choreographer working outside Western pop had better know which one the music is using before counting anything.3

South Asian counting is recited. Kathak and bharatanatyam dancers learn rhythm as spoken syllables — bols, konnakol — and recite the composition (padhant) before dancing it; the tala's cycle is held by the cycle's first beat, sam, which dancer and drummer must arrive on together. Flamenco's twelve-count compás likewise lives in the palms and the mouth before the feet. Counting there is not a grid laid over the music but the music's own grammar spoken aloud; it is the atlas pages' business and the chance chapter's frame-versus-realization distinction in action.

docs.title: Breath
docs.text: Modern dance's alternative to the count was breath phrasing, and it is a genuine different time-mode, not a softer count. Humphrey's fall and recovery is a breath rhythm — the suspension at the top, the fall, the rebound — and her Water Study (1928) was danced with no music at all, the ensemble phrasing on shared breath. Graham's contraction sits on an exhale. Release technique, contact improvisation, and Gaga all phrase from the body's own durations, and much contemporary work is "counted" only in the sense that dancers share an approximate clock while phrasing internally. Breath time is the choreomusicology chapter's suspended mode: no pulse, placement by gesture and contour. Its cost is ensemble precision — which is why breath-phrased companies rehearse unison for months and why even Humphrey used counts to set the ensemble before releasing them to breathe.

docs.title: Cues
docs.text: The third family keys movement to events rather than clock. Ballet rehearsals are full of it — "go on the oboe," "the run starts on the cymbal" — and it is how dancers survive music whose counts are unreliable or absent. Cunningham's company made the limit case a method: since the music was unknown until performance, the dancers timed their phrases with stopwatches, a clock that was neither musical nor bodily but simply elapsed seconds, and cued one another by sight. Cue-based practice is event-driven; count-based is clock-driven; the distinction will matter when we get to the conductor.

docs.title: Groove, the pocket, and being "on top"
docs.text: Dancers talk about being on top of the beat, behind it, in the pocket — and the perception research the commons holds says something counterintuitive about it. Studies of groove find that exaggerating microtiming does not increase groove; it degrades it. A quantized and a naturally performed version can rate equally; groove falls off as timing is pushed beyond a performance's natural magnitudes; expert listeners reject deviations of roughly forty milliseconds that novices accept; and listeners apply genre-appropriate standards (swing and funk are rated comparably despite different absolute timings). Groove emerges from coherence — timing consistent with genre and context — not from the size of the deviation.4 For the dancer the translation is direct: the pocket is not "slightly late"; it is consistently placed relative to the music's own feel, and a dancer who performs lateness as a style reads as dragging. Combine that with the binding asymmetry — late reads wrong faster than early — and the professional convention falls out: place the accent on or a hair ahead of the beat, with the consistency of the music's own players. Balanchine's "on top of the music" was not taste; it was the perceptual sweet spot.

docs.title: The pianist and the conductor
docs.text:
Two musicians inhabit the dance studio, and each embodies one family of practice.

The rehearsal pianist is the ballet world's great unsung collaborator. In class, the pianist improvises — hears the teacher mark a combination ("and a-one, and plié, and stretch…"), infers its meter, tempo, and character, and plays something that fits, live, dozens of times a day. In rehearsal, the pianist plays reductions of the orchestral score at the tempo the choreographer wants, with counts pencilled above the staff and cues marked ("here the boys enter"). Choreographers who can't read music work through the pianist; those who can (Balanchine, Morris, De Keersmaeker) still rely on one. The pianist is, in effect, a human playback system with zero latency and infinite patience, and a good one shapes the phrasing of an entire company.

The conductor has the harder job, and it is the job the commons' latency note describes precisely. A dance conductor must follow the stage — a ballerina's balance, a jump's preparation — while holding the orchestra together, and the naïve way to do that is to react: watch, then beat. Reaction has a floor. Every stage of any reactive chain costs real time (the note's numbers are for audio-to-visual systems — tens of milliseconds of buffering and analysis, a frame or two of render and display, ~70–100 ms for even a fast chain — but the structure is the same for a human watching a dancer and moving a baton), and by the time the orchestra sounds, the dancer has moved on. The fix is the one the note ranks first: anticipate. A good dance conductor predicts the dancer — reads the preparation and leads the landing — exactly as a predictive beat tracker reports a beat before a causal one could find it. The limit case is also in the note: a pre-authored cue sheet on a known track has zero detection latency, because nothing needs detecting, only playback against a shared clock. That is what a recorded score is, and it is why recorded music, for all its deadness, is so much easier to dance to than a conductor who reacts.5

Which is the real argument in the live-versus-recorded debate. Mark Morris's insistence on live music is not nostalgia: live musicians and dancers form a feedback loop — the players breathe with the dancers, the dancers lean on the players — and the loop is only good if the musicians anticipate. A conductor who merely follows produces the worst of both worlds: the dead tempo of a recording plus the lag of a reaction.

docs.title: The studio: editing, looping, clicking
docs.text:
Modern studio practice is mostly a history of playback technology. The piano reduction gave way to the cassette (rewound a thousand times to the same phrase), then to the CD, then to the laptop and the DAW, where a choreographer now loops eight bars indefinitely, slows a passage without changing pitch, and — increasingly — edits the music: cuts, repeats, reorders, layers. Bausch's collages, Fosse's vamps extended until the number is staged, the contemporary choreographer who trims a commissioned score by a third in the last week: editing is normal, and composers who write for dance know it (the next chapter). Forsythe's practice of having Thom Willems compose in the rehearsal room made the editing simultaneous with the composing.

Commercial dance adds the click track and in-ear monitors, so that forty dancers in an arena hit unison against a mix they can barely hear; music-video and film dance shoot to playback, one phrase at a time, with the count called over it. And the contemporary concert stage has borrowed the DJ: Sharon Eyal's Ori Lichtik plays live, Hofesh Shechter composes and mixes his own percussion scores, Ohad Naharin assembles and sometimes writes (under a pseudonym) the collages Batsheva dances to. The line between choreographer and music editor has become thin, and the studio's working memory is now a timeline in software.

docs.title: Silence
docs.text: Every family of practice has a silent form — the counted silence, the breathed silence, the cued silence — and choreographers use silence as a musical resource: the held stillness before the drop, the section danced to feet and breath only, Robbins's Moves in its entirety. Silence is where the dancer's own time becomes audible, and where the mute test is run on the audience in real time: does the movement carry its own pacing?

docs.title: For the generated dancer
docs.text:
The music-to-dance generators of Part VII count — they consume beat and onset features and learn to accent them — but they neither breathe nor cue, and they are reactive by construction: a frame is generated from the audio up to that frame. This chapter's lessons apply without translation. A generator that accents on the detected beat is late by its detection latency and reads late faster than early; the fix is prediction or a pre-authored cue sheet, which for a known track is trivially available. A generator that exaggerates microtiming for "feel" degrades groove, exactly as a human does. And a generator that cannot phrase across the counts — that cannot begin a movement on and-seven — will produce the squareness every dance teacher has spent a career correcting.

Field notes

Renders theory-structural-hierarchy-grouping (hypermeter as the origin of the eight; grouping independent of meter; sentence and period), theory-meter-rhythm-frameworks (divisive/additive construction, hierarchical/timeline reference, polyrhythm/polymeter/ cross-rhythm, metric modulation), theory-microtiming-and-groove (exaggeration degrades groove; experts reject ~40 ms; genre-coherent magnitudes), and theory-anticipation-vs-reaction-latency (the reactive chain's floor; anticipate, hide, or pre-delay; the cue sheet as zero-latency). Studio practice is confident-knowledge writing.

  1. Rothstein's Phrase Rhythm in Tonal Music (1989) is the standard account of hypermeter; the eight-count as "two bars heard as one" is the dance-studio consequence. ↩

  2. Lerdahl & Jackendoff, A Generative Theory of Tonal Music (1983); William Caplin, Classical Form (1998) for sentence and period — "formal function," not just length. ↩

  3. Brăiloiu and Bartók for aksak; Toussaint for timelines; the commons notes a caution (Agawu) that reading West African timelines as "additive" may itself be a Western imposition — the patterns may be better understood as rotational/divisive in their own logic. ↩

  4. Multiple independent groove-perception studies, summarized in the commons: quantized vs. natural rate similarly; degradation is monotonic past natural magnitudes; expert sensitivity around +40 ms; genre-appropriate standards; and recent work finding syncopation predicts groove more than microtiming in common meters. ↩

  5. The commons' figures are for audio-reactive visual systems (buffer, analysis window, detector, render, display: ~70–100 ms floor for a fast chain, 150+ ms for an ordinary one); the predictive beat tracker (Meier, Chiu & Müller 2024) cancels its own latency by offsetting the decision line forward at negligible accuracy cost. The conductor analogy is this chapter's; the structure of the argument is the note's. ↩

docs.title: Plate I · The Movement Alphabet
docs.text: Ann Hutchinson Guest's fifteen prime actions — the classes from which, she claimed, all movement derives. This plate is for staring, not reading: the small words are prompts, not definitions. The thinking behind it lives in Building a gamut.

docs.title: Action itself
docs.text: ANY ACTION the wildcard — something, anything, happens STILLNESS a rest — with duration, level, shape

docs.title: The body changing shape
docs.text: FLEXION fold · curl · close in EXTENSION unfold · open · reach ROTATION turn · spiral · twist

docs.title: Moving through space
docs.text: TRAVELLING cross the floor · go DIRECTION gesture into a line of space

docs.title: Meeting the ground
docs.text: SUPPORT take weight · stand, sit, lie SPRING leave the ground

docs.title: Against gravity
docs.text: BALANCE hold the center · suspend FALLING give in to gravity

docs.title: Ways of defining a movement
docs.text:
MOTION TOWARD defined by its approach MOTION AWAY defined by its departure DESTINATION defined by where it ends RELATING defined by its relationship

Solid cards: the ten performable verb classes. Dashed cards: not performables — ways of specifying a movement (by approach, departure, endpoint, relationship) plus the wildcard. One notation-world caveat travels with the plate: every system in this family under-serves floorwork — if the floor matters to you, imagine each solid card lying down too.

docs.title: The shelf
docs.text:
The chapters of this subject are ordered by zoom — territory, language, notation, music, systems, staging, the synthetic dancer — and they carry the ideas. The people are here. Each page is an encyclopedia entry in the library's sense: a short factual header (dates, lineage, company), then an extensive account of what the choreographer contributed and descriptions of the major works, with links back into the chapters where the ideas are developed. The shelf browses as its own collection and is linked from everywhere the chapters name someone.

The first wave, with the emphasis on modern and contemporary dance that the subject's core tier calls for.

docs.text:

docs.text:

  • Busby Berkeley — the overhead kaleidoscope; the camera as the only viewpoint.

Second-wave candidates, as the chapters demand: Hofesh Shechter, Sharon Eyal, Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, Rennie Harris, the Nicholas Brothers, Savion Glover, Michio Ito, La Argentina, Mary Wigman, José Limón, Pearl Primus.

docs.title: Akram Khan
docs.text: Born London (Wimbledon), 29 July 1974, to a Bangladeshi family. Trained kathak from age seven with Sri Pratap Pawar (Academy of Indian Dance); performed in Peter Brook's Mahabharata (1987–89) as a child; De Montfort University and the Northern School of Contemporary Dance; X-Group at P.A.R.T.S. (Brussels, 1999). Company Akram Khan Company, founded 2000 with producer Farooq Chaudhry. Key collaborators Nitin Sawhney, Jocelyn Pook, Vincenzo Lamagna and Ben Frost (composers); Michael Hulls (lighting); Tim Yip, Kimie Nakano (design); Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui (Zero Degrees), Sylvie Guillem (Sacred Monsters), Juliette Binoche (In-I), Israel Galván (Torobaka), the Shaolin monks' Cherkaoui cousin Sutra (lit by Hulls), Antony Gormley; the writers Karthika Naïr and Ruth Little (dramaturg).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Kathak as contemporary language. Khan's body is a kathak body — the spins, the rhythmic footwork, the articulate hands, the speed and the stillness, the upright spine — and his contribution was to make that vocabulary a source for contemporary dance rather than a flavor applied to it. The early solos (Loose in Flight, Polaroid Feet, 2001; Ronin, 2003; Gnosis, 2010, with the kathak repertory performed straight in the first half) establish the grammar; the codified-vocabularies chapter and the South Asia atlas page treat kathak's recited rhythm, and Khan is its contemporary carrier. His Giselle (2016, English National Ballet — the Romantic ballet reset among migrant garment workers behind a wall, Lamagna's reworked Adam) is the most successful new full-length ballet of its decade and the proof that the language scales to a company.

The duet as encounter. Zero Degrees (2005, with Cherkaoui; Gormley's casts of their bodies; Sawhney's score) — two men of migrant background telling a border story — made both men stars and set the form of the collaborative duet that defined a decade: Sacred Monsters (2006, Guillem), In-I (2008, Binoche), Torobaka (2014, Galván — kathak meets flamenco on the bull and the cow).

Narrative and the world. Desh (2011 — a solo on Bangladesh, his father, the shipbreaking yards, Tim Yip's animated projections; Olivier Award), Until the Lions (2016 — the Mahabharata from Amba's view, in the round), Xenos (2018 — his last full-length solo, a colonial Indian soldier in the First World War), Outwitting the Devil (2019 — Gilgamesh), Jungle Book reimagined (2022), the London 2012 Olympic opening-ceremony section: Khan made the migrant, the colonial subject, and the mythic the matter of British dance at scale.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • Fix (2000), Rush (2000), Kaash (2002 — Anish Kapoor, Sawhney; the first ensemble work), Ronin (2003), ma (2004), Zero Degrees (2005), Sacred Monsters (2006), bahok (2008, with the National Ballet of China), In-I (2008), Gnosis (2010), Vertical Road (2010), Desh (2011), iTMOi (2013 — in the mind of igor, for the Rite centenary), Torobaka (2014), Kaash revival, Until the Lions (2016), Giselle (2016), Chotto Desh (2015, for children), Xenos (2018), Outwitting the Devil (2019), Creature (2021, ENB), Jungle Book reimagined (2022), Gigenis (2024 — a return to the classical Indian forms with an ensemble of masters).

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt (Britain); the South Asia page; the codified-vocabularies chapter; the lighting chapter (Michael Hulls); the ballet history (Giselle).

docs.title: Alvin Ailey
docs.text: Born Rogers, Texas, 5 January 1931 · died New York, 1 December 1989. Trained Lester Horton's school and company, Los Angeles (from 1949; he took over the company at Horton's death in 1953); in New York with Graham, Holm, Charles Weidman, Karel Shook, and acting with Stella Adler. Company the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, founded 1958 (artistic directors after him: Judith Jamison, 1989–2011; Robert Battle, 2011–23; Alicia Graf Mack from 2025); the Ailey School (1969); Ailey II. Key collaborators Judith Jamison (the dancer Cry was made on), Carmen de Lavallade, Dudley Williams, Donna Wood; the lighting designers Nicola Cernovitch and Chenault Spence; Duke Ellington (a dozen ballets to his music); the repertory's guest choreographers.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Revelations. Made in 1960, when he was twenty-nine, to spirituals, gospel, and blues — "Pilgrim of Sorrow," "Take Me to the Water," "Move, Members, Move" — Revelations is the most widely seen modern dance work in the world: the "I Been 'Buked" opening cluster, "Fix Me, Jesus," "Wade in the Water" with its billowing cloth, "Sinner Man," the fans and stools of "Rocka My Soul." It closes nearly every Ailey program and has since 1960; audiences who know no other dance know it. Its vocabulary — Horton's long lines and lateral T, Graham's contraction, Dunham's isolations, social and church movement — is the modern-revolt chapter's Black modern lineage made into one piece.

The repertory company. Ailey's second contribution is institutional: a company built not on one choreographer's work but on a repertory — his own ballets alongside Horton, Dunham, Beatty, McKayle, Primus, and then the living field (Ulysses Dove, Bill T. Jones, Ronald K. Brown, Rennie Harris, Kyle Abraham, Camille A. Brown, Jamar Roberts). He called the company a museum of Black dance and a home for American dance of every kind; it is the model other repertory companies followed, and the largest modern dance institution in the world — a school, a second company, a building, a television presence, a State Department touring history, and a New York City Center season every December.

Blood memories. His own works drew on what he called "blood memories" of Texas — the church, the juke joint, the fields — and on jazz and blues: Blues Suite (1958, the first), Revelations, Cry (1971, for Jamison, "for all Black women everywhere, especially our mothers"), Night Creature (1974, Ellington), Masekela Langage (1969), The River (1970, for ABT, Ellington), Memoria (1979, for Joyce Trisler), For "Bird" — With Love (1984). The Ellington ballets and the jazz scores put the vernacular music of the atlas's North American page at the center of a concert repertory.

docs.title: Major works

docs.text: The modern revolt; the lighting chapter (Cernovitch; Revelations' light); the North American vernacular page; the what-dance-is chapter (the company as institution; the round and the arena).

docs.title: Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker
docs.text: Born Mechelen, Belgium, 11 June 1960. Trained Mudra, Maurice Béjart's school in Brussels (1978–80); Tisch School of the Arts, New York (1981). Company Rosas, founded 1983; resident at La Monnaie opera house (1992–2007); founded the school P.A.R.T.S. (Performing Arts Research and Training Studios, Brussels, 1995), the most influential contemporary dance school in Europe. Key collaborators Thierry De Mey and Peter Vermeersch (composers; De Mey also her filmmaker), Steve Reich's music (never the man — the works to his scores are hers alone), the ensemble Ictus (resident musicians), Ann Veronica Janssens and Michel François (visual artists), Dries Van Noten (costumes), Bojana Cvejić (dramaturg and co-author of her books), Boris Charmatz (duets), and the Rosas dancers across forty years.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Music made visible, structurally. De Keersmaeker's work is the choreomusicology chapter's central contemporary case: choreography derived from the architecture of the score — its phrases, canons, phase relationships, geometric proportions — and made visible as floor pattern and ensemble structure. Fase: Four Movements to the Music of Steve Reich (1982) — Piano Phase, Come Out, Violin Phase, Clapping Music — phases two dancers as the music phases two tapes; Drumming (1998) and Rain (2001, Music for 18 Musicians) derive their spirals, circles, and pentagrams from the scores' structure so rigorously that her books (A Choreographer's Score, with Cvejić, 2012–) are part musical analysis, part geometry. The Bach works — Toccata (1993), Zeitung (2008), Partita 2 (2013, with Charmatz), Mitten wir im Leben sind (2017, the cello suites), the Goldberg Variations solo (2020), the Brandenburgs (2018) — continue the method on a different grammar. She is the composing chapter's case of process form on two channels, and the gamut chapter's case of a small vocabulary exhaustively permuted.

Rosas danst Rosas. The 1983 breakthrough — four women, chairs, repeated everyday gestures (the hand through the hair, the tug at the shirt), sections of violent repetition to De Mey and Vermeersch's score — made her famous and the repetitive, task-like, feminine-but-unsentimental vocabulary a European signature; Beyoncé's 2011 "Countdown" video lifted it and De Keersmaeker said so publicly.

Geometry as composition. Circles, spirals, the golden section, pentagons, the Fibonacci sequence drawn on the floor — her method (taught at P.A.R.T.S.) is to build a dance as a drawing in space and time, the dancers walking, running, and turning along the lines. Vortex Temporum (2013, Grisey, with Ictus playing among the dancers), Work/Travail/Arbeid (2015, a museum version of Vortex run for nine hours a day), En Atendant and Cesena (2010–11, ars subtilior, danced at dusk and dawn at Avignon) — the structure is the content.

P.A.R.T.S. The school (with Cvejić's theory, Rosas's practice, and guest artists from the whole field) trained a generation of European choreographers (Salva Sanchis, Noé Soulier, Eleanor Bauer, Andros Zins-Browne, many more) and set the contemporary European standard.

docs.text: The choreomusicology chapter; the composing chapter; the chance chapter (the systems generation's heir); the costume history (Van Noten); the modern revolt (the Belgian wave).

docs.title: Bob Fosse
docs.text: Born Robert Louis Fosse, Chicago, 23 June 1927 · died Washington, D.C., 23 September 1987. Trained the Chicago Academy of Theater Arts (Frederic Weaver); a teenage vaudeville and burlesque hoofer (the Riff Brothers); dance in Hollywood (Kiss Me Kate, 1953 — his partnered solo caught Jerome Robbins's eye). Career Broadway choreographer from The Pajama Game (1954); director-choreographer from Redhead (1959); film director from Sweet Charity (1969). Key collaborators Gwen Verdon (dancer, wife, muse, and the keeper of the style), Ann Reinking, Chita Rivera, Liza Minnelli, Ben Vereen; the composers Cy Coleman (Sweet Charity), Stephen Schwartz (Pippin), Kander and Ebb (Cabaret, Chicago); Tony Walton (design), Jules Fisher (lighting); the editor Alan Heim.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
A vocabulary from limitations. Fosse's style — turned-in knees and feet, rolled and hunched shoulders, the pelvis thrust, the isolated hip and finger and head, the "Fosse hands" (spread fingers, the "jazz hand"), the bowler hat tipped over the face, white gloves, the sideways shuffle, the angular stillness broken by a single tiny move — is famously built around his own body's limits (bad turnout, rounded shoulders, early baldness) turned into signatures. It is a codified vocabulary invented by one man and now taught as "Fosse" in every jazz class, and the dressing-the-genre chapter reads the hat and gloves as props and distance-legibility devices.

The number as camera. His choreography is built for the frame: small isolations the camera can read, groups arranged in flat, symmetrical, frontal pictures, the body held still except for one moving part — a limited-animation principle (the rendering chapter's "small deviations carry the acting") applied to bodies. On film he cut dance to the beat (Cabaret, 1972, eight Oscars including his, over The Godfather; All That Jazz, 1979, the autobiographical musical of his own heart attack; Lenny, Star 80) and proved that editing could be choreography — the dance-for-camera tradition the pipeline chapter inherits, and the reason Ryan promoted him to the shelf's first wave.

The director-choreographer and the concept musical. Sweet Charity (1966 — "Big Spender," "Rich Man's Frug"), Pippin (1972 — the "Magic to Do" hands in the dark), Chicago (1975 — the vaudeville-as-murder-trial; the 1996 revival, choreographed "in the style of Fosse" by Ann Reinking, became the longest-running American musical on Broadway), Dancin' (1978 — the plotless dance musical), Big Deal (1986): Fosse held book, staging, and dance in one sensibility, dark, sexual, cynical, and precise, and his influence is everywhere a hat tips or a hip snaps — from Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean" (which quotes him) to Beyoncé's "Single Ladies" (which quotes his 1969 "Mexican Breakfast" with Verdon).

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • The Pajama Game (1954 — "Steam Heat," the bowler hats' debut), Damn Yankees (1955 — "Whatever Lola Wants"; film 1958), New Girl in Town (1957), Redhead (1959), How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying (1961), Little Me (1962), Sweet Charity (1966; film 1969), Pippin (1972), Liza with a Z (1972, TV), Cabaret (film, 1972), Lenny (film, 1974), Chicago (1975), Dancin' (1978), All That Jazz (film, 1979), Star 80 (film, 1983), Big Deal (1986); posthumously Fosse (1999, the revue) and the Chicago revival's quarter-century.

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The North American vernacular page (musical theatre); the dressing-the-genre chapter; the props chapter (hats, canes, chairs); the rendering and pipeline chapters (dance for the frame).

docs.title: Busby Berkeley
docs.text: Born Berkeley William Enos, Los Angeles, 29 November 1895 · died Palm Desert, California, 14 March 1976. Trained none in dance; military drill (a lieutenant in the First World War, conducting parade drill for thousands of men — the origin, by his own account, of the patterns); Broadway dance director from the 1920s (A Connecticut Yankee, 1927). Career Hollywood from 1930 (Eddie Cantor's Whoopee!); Warner Bros. 1933–39 — 42nd Street, Gold Diggers of 1933, Footlight Parade, Dames, Gold Diggers of 1935 (his first as director) — then MGM (Babes in Arms, For Me and My Gal, The Gang's All Here, the Esther Williams films); the late revival (Jumbo, 1962; the 1971 No, No, Nanette Broadway supervision). Key collaborators Harry Warren and Al Dubin (songs), Ruby Keeler, Dick Powell, Joan Blondell, Carmen Miranda, Esther Williams; the cameramen who built his monorail and crane rigs.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
The camera is the choreographer. Berkeley did not choreograph dances so much as compositions for a lens: the chorus girls are elements — legs, arms, violins, pianos, neon-lit instruments, water — arranged in patterns that resolve only from the camera's position, above all the overhead shot, where a hundred dancers become a kaleidoscope opening and closing. He cut holes in studio roofs for the crane, built a monorail for the moving camera, and shot with one camera, editing in the head; the number has no stage — it exists nowhere but on film. The light-and-the-picture chapter names the screen as the room with a single viewpoint, and Berkeley is the limit: a picture that could not be seen by any audience present.

The chorus as pixels. In the overhead geometries ("By a Waterfall" in Footlight Parade, "The Shadow Waltz" with its neon violins in Gold Diggers of 1933, "I Only Have Eyes for You" in Dames, "The Lady in the Tutti Frutti Hat" in The Gang's All Here), the individual body disappears into the pattern and the pattern is the dance — the dressing-the-genre chapter's costume designed to be read from above, the gamut chapter's units reduced to a single pose repeated in formation. Critics read the numbers as the Depression's dream-machine, as erotic abstraction, as proto-computer graphics; all three are right, and the emergent-locomotion chapter's swarms and the rendering chapter's generated crowds are his grandchildren.

The narrative number. The other Berkeley — "Remember My Forgotten Man" (Gold Diggers of 1933, the breadline of veterans), "Lullaby of Broadway" (Gold Diggers of 1935, the showgirl's death), "42nd Street" — staged a whole story in a number, with the camera tracking through sets no stage could hold. His method — design for the shot, not the room — is the pipeline chapter's premise, seventy years early, and the reason Ryan promoted him to the first wave: a synthetic dancer's stage is always a Berkeley stage, seen from one lens and existing only there.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • Whoopee! (1930), 42nd Street (1933), Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933 — "We're in the Money," "Pettin' in the Park," "The Shadow Waltz," "Remember My Forgotten Man"), Footlight Parade (1933 — "Honeymoon Hotel," "By a Waterfall," "Shanghai Lil"), Dames (1934 — "I Only Have Eyes for You"), Wonder Bar (1934), Gold Diggers of 1935 (1935 — "Lullaby of Broadway," "The Words Are in My Heart"), Gold Diggers of 1937 (1936), Hollywood Hotel (1937), Babes in Arms (1939), Strike Up the Band (1940), Ziegfeld Girl (1941), For Me and My Gal (1942), The Gang's All Here (1943 — "The Lady in the Tutti Frutti Hat," the neon finale), Take Me Out to the Ball Game (1949), Million Dollar Mermaid (1952 — the Esther Williams water ballets), Jumbo (1962).

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The light-and-the-picture chapter (the screen as room); the dressing-the-genre chapter (costume for the overhead lens); the pipeline chapter (composing for the shot); the North American vernacular page (the film musical).

docs.title: Crystal Pite
docs.text: Born Terrace, British Columbia, 15 December 1970. Trained Pacific Dance Centre, Victoria; danced with Ballet British Columbia (1988–96) and with William Forsythe's Ballett Frankfurt (1996–2001). Company Kidd Pivot, founded in Vancouver, 2002 (with a Frankfurt residency 2010–12); associate choreographer of Nederlands Dans Theater, associate artist at Sadler's Wells, associate dance artist of Canada's National Arts Centre; works for the Royal Ballet, the Paris Opéra, NDT, Cullberg, Cedar Lake, Ballet BC. Key collaborators Jonathon Young (actor-writer, Electric Company Theatre — Betroffenheit, Revisor, Assembly Hall), Owen Belton (composer), Jay Gower Taylor (design), Tom Visser and Robert Sondergaard (lighting), Nancy Bryant (costumes), Simon Fisher Turner.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Articulation and the crowd. Pite's body — from Forsythe, hyper-articulate, fast, every joint speaking — is put to two uses. In the duets and small works it is character and psychology; in the large works it is the mass: Emergence (2009, National Ballet of Canada — a hive of thirty-eight dancers, swarming, insectile, the emergence chapter's boids on a stage), Polaris (2014, sixty-four dancers to Thomas Adès), Flight Pattern (2017, Royal Ballet — thirty-six dancers to Górecki's Third Symphony, on the refugee crisis), The Seasons' Canon (2016, Paris Opéra, fifty-four dancers to Max Richter's recomposed Vivaldi), Angels' Atlas (2020), Light of Passage (2022). She is the contemporary master of the corps as organism — unison that ripples, breaks, and re-forms — and the gamut chapter's operator logic (canon, cascade, delay) at ensemble scale.

Dance-theatre with text. With Jonathon Young she made the century's most celebrated dance-theatre works: Betroffenheit (2015 — Young's own grief after the deaths of his daughter and her cousins, a man in a room with addiction as a cabaret troupe; Olivier Award), Revisor (2019 — Gogol's The Government Inspector, the dancers lip-syncing a recorded play, then the same material abstracted), Assembly Hall (2023 — a medieval re-enactment society's meeting). Recorded speech drives the body — the dancers lip-sync and embody voice — a technique that makes her work the most legible in the field and a direct descendant of Bausch's theatre with Forsythe's body.

The mainstream of contemporary ballet. The Statement (2016, NDT — four executives around a table, a recorded play), Solo Echo (2012), Plot Point (2010, to Bernard Herrmann's Psycho), The Tempest Replica (2011), Dark Matters (2009 — puppetry), Lost Action (2006), Grace Engine (2012): the repertory that every major company now dances, and that made Pite — with McGregor and Forsythe — one of the three choreographers who define the ballet-contemporary blur the modern-revolt chapter ends on.
