docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt; the emergent-locomotion chapter (the swarm); the gamut chapter (ensemble operators); the working-with-music chapter (Belton in collaboration); the ballet history.

docs.title: Doris Humphrey
docs.text: Born Oak Park, Illinois, 17 October 1895 · died New York, 29 December 1958. Trained Denishawn (1917–28), where she also taught and made her first "music visualizations." Companies Humphrey-Weidman (with Charles Weidman, 1928–44); artistic director of the José Limón Dance Company (1946–58). Key collaborators Charles Weidman, José Limón, Pauline Lawrence (designer, manager), Wallingford Riegger and Vivian Fine (composers), and the Bennington School of the Dance, where she taught with Graham and Holm (1934–42). Students Limón, Sybil Shearer, Eleanor King, and through the Juilliard dance division (which she helped found, 1951) a generation of teachers.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Fall and recovery. Humphrey's technique derives movement from gravity: the body's "arc between two deaths" — the stillness of standing and the stillness of lying down — with the fall (yielding to gravity), the recovery (the rebound), and the suspension at the top of the arc as the expressive moment. Breath rhythm, weight, momentum, the swing: the technique chapter sets it beside Graham's contraction as the other foundational principle of American modern dance, and the one whose physics (pendulum, momentum, the moment of suspension) maps most directly onto the plausible-body chapter's dynamics.

The ensemble and the group form. Where Graham built on the solo heroine, Humphrey built on the group: Water Study (1928), sixteen dancers breathing and surging as one body, without music; The Shakers (1931), the religious community's ecstatic order; New Dance (1935) and the trilogy (Theatre Piece, With My Red Fires), the individual and the society danced as counterpoint. Her sense of the stage as a field of forces — the craft chapter's stage geography — came from composing for masses.

The theorist. The Art of Making Dances (1959, finished just before her death) is modern dance's canonical text on composition — the stage map, symmetry as death, "all dances are too long," the eye faster than the ear, design the ending early — and the craft chapter is largely an exposition of it. She was the first modern choreographer to write down how.

The Limón company. Crippled by arthritis, she stopped dancing in 1944 and became the artistic director of her protégé's company, choreographing for it (Day on Earth, 1947; Night Spell, 1951; Ruins and Visions, 1953) and shaping Limón's own masterpieces (The Moor's Pavane, 1949) — the model of the choreographer as director and outside eye.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • Air for the G String (1928 — Bach, the Denishawn visualization style perfected), Water Study (1928), Life of the Bee (1929), Drama of Motion (1930 — in silence), The Shakers (1931), Dionysiaques (1932), New Dance (1935), Theatre Piece (1936), With My Red Fires (1936), Passacaglia and Fugue in C minor (1938 — Bach; her ensemble masterpiece), Inquest (1944), Day on Earth (1947 — Copland), Night Spell (1951), Ruins and Visions (1953), Dawn in New York (1956), Brandenburg Concerto No. 4 (1959, completed by Ruth Currier).

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The technique chapter (fall and recovery); the craft chapter (The Art of Making Dances); the modern revolt; the working-with-music chapter (breath phrasing; Water Study); the choreomusicology chapter (music visualization).

docs.title: George Balanchine
docs.text: Born Georgi Balanchivadze, St Petersburg, 22 January 1904 · died New York, 30 April 1983. Trained the Imperial Theatre School, Petrograd (graduated 1921); the Petrograd Conservatory (piano and composition). Companies Diaghilev's Ballets Russes (ballet master, 1924–29); Les Ballets 1933; with Lincoln Kirstein the School of American Ballet (1934), American Ballet, Ballet Caravan, Ballet Society, and New York City Ballet (1948–83). Key collaborators Igor Stravinsky (from Apollo, 1928, to Agon, 1957, and the 1972 Stravinsky Festival), Lincoln Kirstein (the institution), Barbara Karinska (costumes), Jean Rosenthal and Ronald Bates (lighting), Jerome Robbins (co-ballet master at NYCB), and the dancers he made ballets on — Tanaquil Le Clercq, Maria Tallchief, Diana Adams, Allegra Kent, Suzanne Farrell, Patricia McBride, Edward Villella, Arthur Mitchell, and the generations of the "Balanchine ballerina."

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
The plotless ballet. Balanchine did not invent dancing without a story — Fokine's Les Sylphides did — but he made it the central form of the century: ballets that are the music made visible, with no characters, no mime, no narrative, and the structure of the score as the structure of the dance. Serenade (1934), Concerto Barocco (1941), The Four Temperaments (1946), Symphony in C (1947), Agon (1957), Jewels (1967) — the choreomusicology chapter treats him as the master of structural visualization, the kind that renders the music's architecture rather than its surface, and the composing chapter describes the Stravinsky conversation in which the choreographer specified durations and the composer wrote to them.

The American classical style. Speed, attack, energy, extension, off-balance and syncopation, the weight forward, the hips allowed to open, the line pushed past the Petipa norm — the "Balanchine technique" is a dialect of the classical lexicon built for a new body (long-legged, fast) and a new music; his company class and the School of American Ballet reproduce it, and his injunctions ("don't think, dear, just do," "what are you saving it for?") are its folklore. The "leotard ballets" (the costume history) stripped the costume to let it be seen.

The institution. With Kirstein he built the model American company — school first ("but first, a school," 1934), then the company; a repertory of his own work performed in repertory; the Ford Foundation grants that seeded American ballet schools; the Balanchine Trust after his death, licensing the ballets with répétiteurs who set them — the mechanism by which his repertory became the most-performed in the world.

Broadway and Hollywood. On Your Toes (1936, "Slaughter on Tenth Avenue"), Babes in Arms, Cabin in the Sky, the Goldwyn films — Balanchine made the musical's dance numbers integral, a line that runs to Robbins and Fosse.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Apollon musagète (Apollo, 1928) and The Prodigal Son (1929) — the Ballets Russes works; Apollo the one he said taught him to eliminate.
  • Serenade (1934) — to Tchaikovsky, for his first American students; the fallen dancer, the hair coming down; the most-performed Balanchine ballet.
  • Concerto Barocco (1941), Ballet Imperial (1941), The Four Temperaments (1946), Symphony in C (1947), Orpheus (1948, Noguchi), La Valse (1951), Scotch Symphony (1952), The Nutcracker (1954 — the American Christmas institution), Western Symphony (1954), Allegro Brillante (1956), Divertimento No. 15 (1956), Square Dance (1957).
  • Agon (1957) — Stravinsky's twelve-tone score, twelve dancers, the pas de deux for Diana Adams and Arthur Mitchell; the century's central plotless ballet.
  • Stars and Stripes (1958), Episodes (1959, Webern), Liebeslieder Walzer (1960), A Midsummer Night's Dream (1962), Bugaku (1963), Movements for Piano and Orchestra (1963), Don Quixote (1965), Jewels (1967 — Emeralds, Rubies, Diamonds: the first full-evening plotless ballet), Who Cares? (1970, Gershwin), Stravinsky Violin Concerto and Duo Concertant and Symphony in Three Movements (1972, the Stravinsky Festival), Chaconne (1976), Vienna Waltzes (1977), Ballo della Regina (1978), Mozartiana (1981, the last major work).

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The choreomusicology chapter (visualization); the composing chapter (Stravinsky); the ballet history (neoclassicism; the schools); the costume history (Karinska; leotard ballets); the working-with-music chapter ("on top of the music").

docs.title: Hijikata Tatsumi and Kazuo Ohno — butoh
docs.text: Hijikata Tatsumi (Yoneyama Kunio) · born Akita, northern Japan, 9 March 1928 · died Tokyo, 21 January 1986 · studied Neue Tanz (German expressionist lineage) with Masumura Katsuko, Eguchi Takaya; in Tokyo from 1952; the Asbestos-kan studio (Asbestos Hall) with his wife Motofuji Akiko from 1962. Ohno Kazuo · born Hakodate, Hokkaido, 27 October 1906 · died Yokohama, 1 June 2010 · saw La Argentina (Antonia Mercé) dance in Tokyo in 1929; studied with Ishii Baku and Eguchi Takaya; a gymnastics teacher and a soldier (nine years, a prisoner of war) before his first recital at forty-three (1949); worked with Hijikata from 1959; his son Yoshito Ohno his partner and heir. Lineages Sankai Juku (Amagatsu Ushio, 1975), Dairakudakan (Maro Akaji, 1972), Hakutobo, Byakko-sha, Min Tanaka's Body Weather, Carlotta Ikeda, Ko Murobushi, and the international butoh of Europe and the Americas.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Ankoku butō. Kinjiki (Forbidden Colors, 1959 — after Mishima; Hijikata and the young Yoshito Ohno, a chicken, a homoerotic encounter in near-darkness) is conventionally butoh's birth: a performance that got Hijikata expelled from the modern dance association and announced the "dance of darkness" (ankoku butō) — an anti-dance against both Western modern and Japanese classical forms, rooted in the postwar body, the grotesque, the Tōhoku countryside's mud and crouching peasants, Genet and Artaud and Bataille, the body as a thing that is acted upon. The modern-revolt chapter places it as the parallel Japanese revolt; the makeup chapter treats the white body — rice powder over shaved heads and skin, the individual erased, the surface a screen for light — as the form's signature and as a lighting decision.

Butoh-fu. Hijikata's compositional method was a notation of images: the butoh-fu, scrapbooks and scrolls of words and pictures (Bellmer, Bacon, Klimt, Wols, Michaux) that the dancer internalizes as sequences of transformations — "a thread pulls the top of the head; the eyes are in the back of the skull; you are an old woman walking in ash; you are smoke." The body is choreographed by image rather than by step, and the notation chapter would place butoh-fu as a fifth kind of score — a score of states. His late 1960s–70s works (Hijikata Tatsumi and the Japanese People: Rebellion of the Body, 1968; 27 Nights for Four Seasons, 1972) and his choreography for others (the Hakutobo women, Ashikawa Yoko) built the style's repertoire of slow, distorted, hyper-controlled movement.

Ohno: the improvised body. Ohno's butoh was the other pole — improvisational, tender, comic, devotional, built from memory and from the body's own life rather than from a system. Admiring La Argentina (1977, directed by Hijikata — Ohno at seventy-one in a dress, channeling the Spanish dancer he had seen fifty years earlier) made him famous worldwide at the end of his life; My Mother (1981), The Dead Sea (1985), Water Lilies (1987) followed, and he performed into his nineties, in a wheelchair, moving his hands. His teaching — "do not dance your technique; dance your life" — shaped the international butoh more than Hijikata's system did.

The export. Sankai Juku's polished, visually exquisite stagings (Kinkan Shonen, 1978; Jomon Sho, 1982; the hanging-from-the-building Sholiba; Amagatsu's later works) took butoh to Paris and the world's festivals; Dairakudakan's spectacle, Min Tanaka's farm-based Body Weather, Carlotta Ikeda's Ariadone (the first all-woman company) and the European butoh scene spread it; it is now a worldwide practice, and a standard reference for every choreographer who works with slowness, distortion, and the white body.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Hijikata: Kinjiki (1959), Hijikata Tatsumi DANCE EXPERIENCE no kai (1960–61), Anma (The Masseur, 1963), Barairo Dansu (Rose-Colored Dance, 1965), Hijikata Tatsumi and the Japanese People: Rebellion of the Body (1968), 27 Nights for Four Seasons (1972), the Hakutobo works (Hitogata, 1976), and the direction of Admiring La Argentina (1977).
  • Ohno: Jellyfish Dance (1949), the Hijikata collaborations (1959–68), Admiring La Argentina (1977), My Mother (1981), The Dead Sea (1985), Water Lilies (1987), Ka Chō Fū Getsu (1990), The Road in Heaven, the Road in Earth (1999), Requiem for the 20th Century (2000).

docs.title: Where they are in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt; the makeup and light chapter (the white body); the dressing-the-genre chapter; the East and Southeast Asia page; the notation chapter (butoh-fu as a score of images).

docs.title: Isadora Duncan
docs.text: Born Angela Isadora Duncan, San Francisco, 26 May 1877 · died Nice, 14 September 1927 (the scarf, the car). Trained largely self-taught; social and "fancy" dancing in California; briefly Augustin Daly's company and the ballet of Marie Bonfanti in New York. Career solo and small-ensemble concerts in London, Paris, Budapest, Berlin, Russia, and America from around 1900; schools at Grunewald (Berlin, 1904), Bellevue (Paris, 1914), and Moscow (1921, at the Soviet government's invitation). Legacy carriers the "Isadorables" (Irma, Anna, Maria-Theresa, Lisa, Margot, Erica — her adopted pupils) and the reconstructed repertory they transmitted.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
The refusal. Duncan's achievement was to make a whole art out of what she rejected: the corset, the pointe shoe, the tutu, the ballet lexicon, the story ballet, the commercial stage. In their place — a Greek tunic, bare feet and legs, a vocabulary of walking, running, skipping, leaping, reclining, and gestures welling from the solar plexus (her word for movement's source), danced to concert music that had never been danced to (Chopin, Gluck, Beethoven's Seventh, Wagner, Schubert). The Dance of the Future (1903) declared ballet "deformed" and nature the model; the modern-revolt chapter opens with her because every later revolt repeated the gesture, and the costume history treats the tunic as ideology.

Music as partner. Duncan danced to symphonic music as an equal — she was the first to treat the concert repertory as choreographable — and was attacked for it by musicians; the choreomusicology chapter's visualization debate begins with her.

The legend and the schools. Her life (the children drowned in the Seine in 1913; the marriage to Yesenin; the Soviet school; the death) became the first modern-dance myth, and her schools — run on her belief that dance education was the education of the free body — seeded the German and Russian modern movements as much as the American. What survives of the repertory is small (the dances were improvised into shape and set by the Isadorables), but the idea of the solo concert dancer as artist and the idea that a new dance could be made from principle rather than inherited steps are hers.

docs.title: Major works (as transmitted)
docs.text: • The Chopin dances — the mazurkas, waltzes, and preludes; Mother (a Scriabin étude); Revolutionary (Scriabin); The Three Graces and Bacchanal (Gluck's Iphigénie dances); the Marche Slave (Tchaikovsky — the slave freed); the Brahms waltzes; Marseillaise (1915, the war years); the Schubert Ave Maria (after her children's deaths); the Beethoven Seventh and the Wagner Liebestod (the symphonic dances, lost in their details). The Duncan repertory is reconstructed and taught today by the Isadora Duncan Dance Foundation and the lineage from the Isadorables.

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt; the costume history; the choreomusicology chapter; the what-dance-is chapter (the soloist as inventor of a concert form outside the only existing one).

docs.title: Jerome Robbins
docs.text: Born Jerome Rabinowitz, New York, 11 October 1918 · died New York, 29 July 1998. Trained with Gluck Sandor and Felicia Sorel; ballet with Ella Daganova, Antony Tudor, Eugene Loring; modern with Alys Bentley; danced with Ballet Theatre (1940–44). Companies Ballet Theatre (American Ballet Theatre); New York City Ballet — associate artistic director under Balanchine from 1949, ballet master-in-chief (with Peter Martins) after Balanchine's death; Ballets: U.S.A. (1958–61). Key collaborators Leonard Bernstein (Fancy Free, On the Town, West Side Story), Stephen Sondheim, Arthur Laurents, Oliver Smith, Jean Rosenthal (lighting), Irene Sharaff (costumes), and Broadway producers who gave him total control as director-choreographer.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Broadway as dance theatre. Robbins made the musical's choreography carry story and character — the sailors of On the Town (1944), the gangs of West Side Story (1957), whose "Prologue," "Cool," and the rumble are danced drama; Fiddler on the Roof (1964), whose bottle dance and the village's movement are its world. As director-choreographer he held the whole show, and his methods (the West Side Story cast kept apart as rival gangs) are Broadway legend. Jerome Robbins' Broadway (1989) anthologized it.

The American ballet. Fancy Free (1944, Bernstein, Ballet Theatre) — three sailors on leave in wartime New York — brought vernacular gesture, jazz rhythm, and character into classical ballet in one stroke and made Robbins famous at twenty-five. From Interplay (1945) and The Cage (1951) to Afternoon of a Faun (1953 — two dancers in a studio, watching themselves in the invisible mirror, the audience as mirror) and The Concert (1956 — the comedy of concertgoers' fantasies, a piano onstage), he gave NYCB its other voice.

The Chopin ballets and the plotless Robbins. Dances at a Gathering (1969), an hour of Chopin piano pieces for ten dancers in a field of implied relationships, is the postwar repertory's warmest masterpiece; In the Night (1970), The Goldberg Variations (1971), Other Dances (1976, for Makarova and Baryshnikov), Glass Pieces (1983 — the pedestrian grid crossing to Philip Glass, the street crowd as corps), Ives, Songs (1988), and West Side Story Suite (1995). Moves (1959) — a ballet in silence — is the choreomusicology chapter's control condition.

The classical-vernacular bridge. Robbins's contribution to the subject is the demonstration that ballet's lexicon and American social movement — the walk, the shrug, the jazz step, the hands in pockets — can be one vocabulary, which is the codified-vocabularies chapter's dialect argument as a career. His ballets' light, precise musicality and his Broadway storytelling have separate descendants (Justin Peck explicitly the first; every director-choreographer the second).

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Fancy Free (1944), On the Town (1944, Broadway), Interplay (1945), Facsimile (1946), The Guests (1949), Age of Anxiety (1950), The Cage (1951), Afternoon of a Faun (1953), Fanfare (1953), The Concert (1956).
  • The King and I (1951 — "Small House of Uncle Thomas"), Peter Pan (1954), West Side Story (1957; film 1961, co-directed, two Oscars), Gypsy (1959), Fiddler on the Roof (1964).
  • Moves (1959), N.Y. Export: Opus Jazz (1958 — Ballets: U.S.A., the sneaker ballet), Les Noces (1965, ABT), Dances at a Gathering (1969), In the Night (1970), The Goldberg Variations (1971), Watermill (1972 — the slow, Noh-influenced meditation), Dybbuk (1974), Other Dances (1976), Opus 19/The Dreamer (1979), Glass Pieces (1983), Antique Epigraphs (1984), In Memory Of… (1985), Ives, Songs (1988), Jerome Robbins' Broadway (1989), West Side Story Suite (1995), Brandenburg (1997, the last).

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The ballet history; the choreomusicology chapter (Moves); the North American vernacular page (musical theatre); the lighting chapter (Rosenthal).

docs.title: Katherine Dunham
docs.text: Born Glen Ellyn, Illinois, 22 June 1909 · died New York, 21 May 2006. Trained the University of Chicago (anthropology, under Robert Redfield and Melville Herskovits; fieldwork in Jamaica, Martinique, Trinidad, and Haiti, 1935–36, on a Rosenwald fellowship); ballet with Ludmilla Speranzeva and Mark Turbyfill; initiated into Haitian Vodou. Companies Ballet Nègre (1930), the Negro Dance Group, the Katherine Dunham Dance Company (1940–60s, touring fifty-seven countries); the Dunham School of Dance and Theatre, New York (1944–57); the Performing Arts Training Center, East St. Louis (1967–). Key collaborators John Pratt (designer, her husband), her dancers (Talley Beatty, Janet Collins, Eartha Kitt, Lucille Ellis, Vanoye Aikens), and the Haitian drummers and artists she brought into the company.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Dance anthropology as choreography. Dunham's fieldwork — the first by a dancer- anthropologist — documented the sacred and social dances of the Caribbean (her master's thesis on Haitian dance, Dances of Haiti, 1947) and then staged them: not as ethnographic display but as concert theatre with the forms' movement intact. L'Ag'Ya (1938, the Martinique fighting dance), Shango (1945), Rites de Passage (1941) brought the Afro-Atlantic lineage onto the American stage with authority and respect, and the first chapter's ritual-to-concert migration has no better documented case.

The Dunham technique. A codified training that fuses ballet's structure, modern's torso, and the isolations, polycentrism, and grounded flexibility of Caribbean and African dance — the first technique to treat the diaspora's movement principles as a foundation rather than a flavor. It is taught worldwide and is the technique chapter's under-credited fourth lineage beside Graham, Humphrey, and Horton; Ailey, Beatty, and the whole Black modern line passed through it or its graduates.

The company and the revue. Tropics and Le Jazz Hot (1940), Cabin in the Sky (1940, with Balanchine), Tropical Revue (1943), Bal Nègre (1946), Caribbean Rhapsody — Dunham made the Black dance company a commercial and artistic success on Broadway, in Hollywood (Stormy Weather, 1943; Carnival of Rhythm), and on world tours, decades before Ailey, and paid for the seriousness with the revue.

Activism. She refused segregated theatres on tour (the 1944 Louisville protest), made Southland (1951, a lynching) in Chile against State Department pressure, and in 1967 moved to East St. Louis to build a community arts center and a training program for the city's youth; her 1992 hunger strike at eighty-two protested US policy toward Haitian refugees.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • L'Ag'Ya (1938), Tropics and Le Jazz Hot (1940 — "Rara Tonga," "Barrelhouse"), Rites de Passage (1941), Tropical Revue (1943), Choros (1943), Shango (1945), Bal Nègre (1946), Veracruzana (1948), Southland (1951), Afrique (1950s), Ode to Taylor Jones (1968), the films Stormy Weather (1943), Casbah (1948), and the Metropolitan Opera's Aida (1963 — the first Black choreographer at the Met).

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt (the Black modern lineage); the Africa and the diaspora page; the technique chapter; the what-dance-is chapter (ritual to concert).

docs.title: Lucinda Childs
docs.text: Born New York, 26 June 1940. Trained Sarah Lawrence College; studied with Merce Cunningham; Robert Dunn's composition class (1962). Company the Lucinda Childs Dance Company, founded 1973. Key collaborators Robert Wilson and Philip Glass (Einstein on the Beach), Sol LeWitt, Frank Gehry, John Adams, and from the 1990s the European ballet companies that commissioned her.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Judson's conceptualist. Childs's Judson-era works — Pastime (1963), Carnation (1964, a solo with a colander, sponges, and a plastic bag), Street Dance (1964, in which the audience looked out a window at dancers in the street while a tape described what they saw) — were among the most rigorously conceptual of the period: objects, text, and the relation between description and action.

Pattern permutation. After a hiatus she returned in 1973 with the work that defines her: dances built from a small set of simple movements — walking, skipping, turning, a step and a half-turn — arranged in permutations along geometric floor paths (diagonals, grids, circles), repeated and phased with a rigor that makes the audience see the structure rather than the dancer. Radial Courses (1976), Melody Excerpt (1977), Katema (1978) — the chance chapter treats these with Brown's accumulations as the systems generation, and the gamut chapter as the purest small gamut in the repertory: a handful of units, a large, exhaustively explored operator space.

Process music, process dance. Einstein on the Beach (1976, with Robert Wilson and Philip Glass; she performed the solos and later choreographed the two "Dance" sections, 1984) and Dance (1979; Glass's score, Sol LeWitt's film of the dancers projected at full scale over the live dancers, so that the piece doubles itself) are the composing chapter's case of additive process on two channels at once. Dance is the minimalist masterpiece of the form: ninety minutes of permuted phrases in white against their own filmed image, and the clearest demonstration anywhere that a rule made visible is an aesthetic experience.

Return to the institutions. From the 1990s Childs choreographed for ballet companies (Paris Opéra, Lyon, Bavarian State Ballet, Les Ballets de Monte-Carlo), directed opera, and revived Dance (2009) and Available Light (2015) for a new generation — the postmodern vocabulary, like Brown's, absorbed by the opera house.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Pastime (1963), Carnation (1964), Street Dance (1964), Museum Piece (1965) — Judson.
  • Untitled Trio (1968/1973), Calico Mingling (1973 — four dancers on a city grid, filmed from above by Babette Mangolte), Radial Courses (1976), Melody Excerpt (1977), Katema (1978), Interior Drama (1977).
  • Einstein on the Beach (1976; "Dance 1" and "Dance 2" choreographed 1984) — the "Field" dances.
  • Dance (1979) — Glass, LeWitt; Relative Calm (1981 — Jon Gibson, Robert Wilson's light), Available Light (1983 — John Adams, Frank Gehry's two-level set, at MOCA Los Angeles), Cascade (1984 — Steve Reich), Portraits in Reflection (1986).
  • Mad Rush (1990), Rhythm Plus (1991), Concerto (1993 — Górecki; the work ballet companies dance), Chamber Symphony (1994), Commentaire (1997), Largo (2001), Ten Part Suite (2001), Songs from Before (2009 — Max Richter), Canto Ostinato (2015), Distant Figure (2022).

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The chance chapter (pattern permutation); the gamut chapter (the small gamut); the composing chapter (Glass; process form); the choreomusicology chapter; the modern revolt.

docs.title: Martha Graham
docs.text: Born Allegheny (Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania, 11 May 1894 · died New York, 1 April 1991. Trained Denishawn (Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn), Los Angeles, 1916–23. Company the Martha Graham Dance Company, founded 1926 — the oldest modern dance company in America — and its school. Key collaborators Louis Horst (musical director and composition teacher, 1926–48), Isamu Noguchi (sets, 1935–66), Erick Hawkins (dancer, her husband 1948–54), Aaron Copland, Samuel Barber, William Schuman, Gian Carlo Menotti (composers), Halston (costumes, 1970s–80s). Students and dancers who became choreographers include Merce Cunningham, Erick Hawkins, Anna Sokolow, Paul Taylor, Pearl Lang, Yuriko, Bertram Ross, and — at one remove through Batsheva, which she helped found in 1964 — much of Israeli dance.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
A technique built on a principle. Graham's first and deepest contribution is the idea that a dance technique can be derived from a single physical-expressive premise rather than inherited as a lexicon. Hers was the breath made visible: contraction — a deep hollowing of the pelvis and torso on the exhale, curving the spine — and release — the return on the inhale, the body lengthening. From that opposition she built the spiral (the torso's rotation around the spine), the falls (to the knee, to the floor, and the recoveries), the floor work that occupies the first half of every Graham class (the seated and kneeling sequences that train the torso before the legs are asked for anything), the cupped hand, the flexed foot, the contracted leap. The technique chapter sets this beside Humphrey, Cunningham, and Gaga as the paradigm of modern dance's alternative to codification: build the body, and the body is the vocabulary. It is still taught, essentially unchanged, in conservatories worldwide, and it remains the most dramatic of the modern techniques — every movement motivated from the center, every phrase an emotional event.

The dramatic torso. Where ballet's expressiveness lives in the limbs and the line, Graham relocated it to the trunk. Her dancers' torsos contract, spiral, and arch with an intensity that can read as agony or ecstasy, and her subject matter followed: the interior life — sexuality, guilt, terror, rapture — dramatized through the body's center. This is the source of modern dance's reputation for seriousness and of the cliché ("angst") that the next generation revolted against; it is also the reason her work still reads.

The repertory. Graham made some 180 works across sixty-five years, and their arc is a history of American modern dance's ambitions: the austere early abstractions and the "American" period of the 1930s–40s; the Greek cycle of the 1940s–60s, in which myth (Medea, Jocasta, Clytemnestra, Ariadne, Phaedra) became the vehicle for psychological drama, told from the heroine's interior through flashback, split characters, and Noguchi's symbolic objects — a dance-theatre form she invented; and the late works made after she stopped dancing (1969), lighter and more lyrical. She danced into her mid-seventies, which shaped the roles (the solo heroine, the company around her) and later the company's difficult transition to dancing her works without her.

The institution and the commissions. Graham built the model of the modern dance company: a founder-choreographer, a technique, a school, a repertory, a board, a home, a succession crisis. She was the twentieth century's great commissioner of music for dance (the composing chapter) — Copland's Appalachian Spring to her scenario, Barber, Schuman, Hindemith, Menotti, Dello Joio — and the props chapter's exemplary case of set as terrain, through Noguchi's twenty-odd sculptures that her dancers climbed and entered. The costume history tells how she designed her own costumes for decades, and how Lamentation's jersey tube made a technique visible.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Heretic (1929) — Graham in white against a wall of women in black who repel her: the first statement of the lone figure against the group, and of her early starkness.
  • Lamentation (1930) — a solo seated on a bench inside a tube of stretch jersey; grief as the fabric's strain. The most-reproduced image in modern dance.
  • Primitive Mysteries (1931) — a ritual for the Virgin and a chorus of women, in three sections; austere, processional, to Horst's score. Often called her first masterpiece.
  • Frontier (1935) — a solo before Noguchi's fence and ropes: the pioneer woman facing space. Her first Noguchi set, and the American period's emblem.
  • Chronicle (1936) — a massed women's work against war and fascism, made the year she refused to perform at the Berlin Olympics; partly reconstructed in the 1990s.
  • Letter to the World (1940) — on Emily Dickinson, with spoken text; Deaths and Entrances (1943), on the Brontës: the literary-psychological works of the early 1940s.
  • Appalachian Spring (1944) — Copland's score, Noguchi's Shaker house frame; a bride, a husbandman, a pioneer woman, a preacher and his followers, at a wedding on the frontier. The most-performed Graham work and the one the general public knows.
  • Cave of the Heart (1946) — Medea, Barber's score, Noguchi's wire "dress": jealousy as a spiral of the torso, the sorceress entering her brass sculpture at the end.
  • Errand into the Maze (1947) — Ariadne and the Minotaur (the Creature of Fear), Menotti's score, a duet of terror overcome; the rope-path set.
  • Night Journey (1947) — Jocasta at the moment of her death, the story of Oedipus told in her flashback; Schuman's score, Noguchi's bed.
  • Diversion of Angels (1948) — a rare plotless, joyful ensemble work, three couples in white, red, and yellow; the lyrical Graham.
  • Clytemnestra (1958) — her only full-evening work, the Oresteia from the queen's interior; Halim El-Dabh's score. The Greek cycle's summa.
  • Acts of Light (1981) and Maple Leaf Rag (1990, to Joplin) — the late works, the last made the year before her death, a self-parodic, affectionate company piece.

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The technique chapter (contraction–release as derived vocabulary); the modern revolt (the Graham generation); the costume history and props chapter (Lamentation; Noguchi); the composing chapter (the commissions).

docs.title: Merce Cunningham
docs.text: Born Centralia, Washington, 16 April 1919 · died New York, 26 July 2009. Trained Cornish School, Seattle (where he met John Cage, 1938); soloist with Martha Graham, 1939–45. Company the Merce Cunningham Dance Company, founded at Black Mountain College, 1953; dissolved by his own plan in 2011, two years after his death, after a final "Legacy Tour." Key collaborators John Cage (music director and partner until Cage's death in 1992), David Tudor, Robert Rauschenberg (resident designer 1954–64), Jasper Johns (artistic adviser 1967–80), Mark Lancaster, Charles Atlas and Elliot Caplan (film), and composers from Feldman, Wolff, and Brown to Radiohead and Sigur Rós. Dancers who became choreographers include Paul Taylor (briefly), Viola Farber, Steve Paxton, Karole Armitage, Trisha Brown (a student), Lucinda Childs (influenced), and a large share of the Judson generation.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Chance as a compositional method. From the early 1950s Cunningham used chance operations — coin tosses, dice, the I Ching — to decide the order of phrases, the number of dancers, the directions, the durations, and the timing of a work, while keeping the material (the movements themselves) entirely his own. The chance chapter makes the structural point at length: chance decided continuity, never invention; the gamut was authored and the sequencer was random. Its purpose, in his telling, was to get past his own habits — to produce transitions and juxtapositions his taste would never have chosen and his dancers' bodies then had to solve. The result was a new kind of stage: many things happening at once, no narrative, no climax, movement that began and ended without preparation, and a literalness (a leap is a leap) that made expression the viewer's business.

The independence of the elements. Music, dance, and décor were made separately and met at the performance (the choreomusicology chapter). The dancers rehearsed in silence and timed their phrases by stopwatch; the composer was given a duration; the designer was given a stage; the first performance was often the first time any of them saw the whole. Cage's word for the relationship was coexistence, and the audience's irrepressible habit of finding connections anyway became one of the work's subjects.

The decentralized stage. Following Einstein's remark that there are no fixed points in space, Cunningham declared every point on the stage equally important: no front, no center, no hierarchy of soloist and corps, movement facing any direction, the viewer free to look anywhere. His Events (from 1964) — ninety-minute, unbroken assemblages of excerpts from the repertory, performed in gyms, museums, and piazzas, often with dancers facing several ways — made this literal, and they are the props chapter's case of the set as co-present rather than depicting.

A technique. The Cunningham technique — a long, erect, flexible spine (Graham's torso freed of its drama) over fast, intricate, balletic legs, with the back's own vocabulary of curves, tilts, twists, and arches — produced what the technique chapter calls the chance-ready body: one that can go anywhere from anywhere, because the sequence may demand it.

The computer and the camera. In 1989 he began composing with LifeForms (later DanceForms), the first choreographer to make dances on software — Trackers (1991) was the first result — and the computational-choreography chapter opens with him; in his last years he used motion capture (BIPED, 1999, with Paul Kaiser and Shelley Eshkar's projected figures; Loops for the hands). With Charles Atlas he made video-dances (Channels/Inserts, 1981) that were choreographed for the camera rather than filmed.

The company as crossroads. For half a century the Cunningham company was where the New York avant-garde met: Rauschenberg, Johns, Warhol, Stella, Morris, Nauman, Paik; Cage's circle of composers; and a roster of dancers who went on to found the next generations. Its dissolution by design — the Legacy Plan, with the works licensed through a trust and the company closed — is itself a contribution: the first choreographer to decide, in advance, how his work would outlive his company.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Sixteen Dances for Soloist and Company of Three (1951) — the first use of chance, for the order of sections.
  • Suite by Chance (1953) — the first work fully composed by chance operations, to Christian Wolff's electronic score; the chance chapter's founding document.
  • Summerspace (1958) — to Feldman, in Rauschenberg's pointillist costumes and backdrop: dancers dissolving into a field; later staged for New York City Ballet.
  • Crises (1960), Aeon (1961), Winterbranch (1964, to La Monte Young, with Rauschenberg's harsh lighting — the work audiences walked out of).
  • Variations V (1965) — with Cage, Tudor, Paik, and Stan VanDerBeek: photocells and antennas triggered sound as the dancers moved; the first interactive dance.
  • RainForest (1968) — Warhol's helium Silver Clouds, Tudor's score; Walkaround Time (1968) — Johns's Duchamp Large Glass, Behrman's score; Scramble (1967) — Stella's banners; Canfield (1969) — Morris's light column.
  • Torse (1976) — the technique at its most rigorous, made entirely by chance from a gamut of sixty-four phrases; Sounddance (1975) — to Tudor, a fast, dense ensemble erupting from a curtain.
  • Roaratorio (1983) — to Cage's Roaratorio, with Irish jigs; Pictures (1984) — the dancers forming still pictures in Lancaster's light.
  • Points in Space (1986) — made for television with Elliot Caplan, then for the stage.
  • Trackers (1991) — the first LifeForms work; Beach Birds (1991); CRWDSPCR (1993) — the computer years.
  • Ocean (1994) — in the round, 112 musicians around the audience, Cage's posthumous plan; BIPED (1999) — Gavin Bryars's score, motion-captured projections, the late masterpiece.
  • Split Sides (2003) — with Radiohead and Sigur Rós, the order decided by dice on stage; Nearly Ninety (2009) — the last work, for his ninetieth birthday.

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The chance chapter (the method); the choreomusicology chapter (independence); the technique chapter (the body); the computational-choreography chapter (LifeForms); the costume and props chapters (Rauschenberg, Johns, Warhol); the modern revolt (the break).

docs.title: Vaslav Nijinsky and Bronislava Nijinska
docs.text: Vaslav Nijinsky · born Kyiv, 12 March 1889 (o.s.) · died London, 8 April 1950 · Imperial Theatre School, St Petersburg (graduated 1907); the Mariinsky (1907–11); Diaghilev's Ballets Russes (1909–13, 1916–17); choreographed four ballets; institutionalized for schizophrenia from 1919. Bronislava Nijinska · born Minsk, 8 January 1891 · died Pacific Palisades, California, 21 February 1972 · Imperial Theatre School (graduated 1908); the Mariinsky; the Ballets Russes (1909–13, 1921–24); her own school in Kyiv (1919–21) and companies; Ida Rubinstein's company, the Paris Opéra, de Basil's Ballets Russes, Ballet Theatre, the Marquis de Cuevas's company; teacher in Los Angeles from 1938; revived Les Noces and Les Biches for the Royal Ballet (1964, 1966).

docs.title: Nijinsky: contributions
docs.text:
The dancer. Before the choreography there was the dancing — the leap in Spectre de la rose, the puppet in Petrushka, the Golden Slave in Schéhérazade: by every account the greatest male dancer of his era, restoring the male role ballet had lost in the nineteenth century (the ballet history).

The three ballets. L'Après-midi d'un faune (1912) — twelve minutes in profile, a frieze in motion, no ballet steps, rehearsed a hundred times; the first ballet whose movement was invented whole for one work. Jeux (1913) — tennis, modern dress, a triangle; puzzling then, prophetic now. The Rite of Spring (1913) — turned-in feet, stamping, the hunched and earthbound body, the sacrificial solo, Stravinsky's rhythms the dancers could barely count: the riot, the eight performances, the loss, the 1987 reconstruction (Hodson and Archer). The Ballets Russes deep dive and the composing chapter tell it. What the three established — that the classical lexicon could be discarded and a vocabulary built for the piece — is the premise of everything in Part II. Till Eulenspiegel (1916, New York) was the fourth and last.

docs.title: Nijinska: contributions
docs.text:
The modernist ballet. Nijinska is the under-credited figure of the Ballets Russes' second decade and one of the century's major choreographers. Les Noces (1923) — Stravinsky's cantata-ballet of a Russian peasant wedding; Goncharova's brown-and-white austerity; massed, stamping, architectural ensembles, the women's braids, pyramids of bodies — is the modernist masterpiece of the company and a direct ancestor of every constructivist and minimalist ensemble since. Les Biches (1924 — Poulenc, Marie Laurencin) — a 1920s house party of ambiguous flirtations, the hostess with her cigarette holder, the girl in blue — is the first ballet of modern sensibility and irony. Le Train Bleu (1924 — Milhaud, Cocteau, Chanel's sportswear) completed the trio.

The teacher and the carrier. Her Kyiv school (1919–21) was an experimental laboratory (Serge Lifar was a student); her treatise On Movement and the School of Movement set out a theory of movement as continuous line. She choreographed for Ida Rubinstein (Boléro, 1928 — the original, with Ravel; La Valse), for the Paris Opéra, for de Basil, for Ballet Theatre, and for Hollywood; she taught in Los Angeles for thirty years (Cyd Charisse, Maria Tallchief, Allegra Kent among her students); and her late revivals of Les Noces and Les Biches for Ashton's Royal Ballet returned the works to the repertory, where they remain. Her Early Memoirs (1981, posthumous) is a primary source for her brother and the company.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Nijinsky: L'Après-midi d'un faune (1912), Jeux (1913), The Rite of Spring (1913), Till Eulenspiegel (1916).
  • Nijinska: Les Noces (1923), Les Biches (1924), Les Fâcheux (1924), Le Train Bleu (1924), Boléro (1928), La Valse (1929), Les Cent Baisers (1935), Chopin Concerto (1937), La Fille mal gardée (1940, Ballet Theatre staging), Brahms Variations (1944), the Royal Ballet revivals (1964, 1966).

docs.title: Where they are in this subject
docs.text: The Ballets Russes deep dive; the composing chapter (Rite's counting crisis); the costume history (Bakst's Faune; Chanel's Train Bleu); the ballet history.

docs.title: Ohad Naharin
docs.text: Born Kibbutz Mizra, Israel, 22 June 1952. Trained began dancing at twenty-two with Batsheva (1974), invited by Martha Graham to New York; Juilliard and the School of American Ballet; danced with Graham, Béjart's Ballet of the 20th Century, and his own New York company (1980–90). Company Batsheva Dance Company, Tel Aviv — artistic director 1990–2018, house choreographer since; Batsheva's junior company. Key collaborators his dancers; Avi Yona Bueno (lighting); Rakefet Levy (costumes); Maxim Waratt (music — his own pseudonym); the Gaga teaching community; Sharon Eyal, Hofesh Shechter, Bobbi Jene Smith, and others who came through Batsheva.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Gaga. Developed from the late 1990s (partly through his own recovery from a back injury), Gaga is a movement language — taught in classes without mirrors, in which the teacher speaks continuous imagery ("float the flesh," "connect to the bones," "thick and thin," "quake," "lena" — the pleasure of effort) and the dancers move continuously, researching sensation — not a technique with codified steps. The technique chapter treats it as the "anti-vocabulary with a vocabulary problem": it produces a highly recognizable body (available, grounded, liquid, explosive, the spine articulate, the groove constant) without a lexicon, and its vocabulary is sensation words. Taught to dancers (Gaga/dancers) and to the general public (Gaga/people), it is practiced worldwide, and the latent-spaces chapter reads it as navigation of a sensation space rather than a step space.

The Batsheva style and its lineage. Under Naharin Batsheva became one of the world's defining contemporary companies: collective, pulsing, groove-driven ensembles, extreme individual solos inside them, a frank sensuality and humor, Israeli pop and world music collaged with his own scores. The choreographers who came out of the company — Sharon Eyal (L-E-V), Hofesh Shechter, Yasmeen Godder, Noa Zuk, Roy Assaf, Bobbi Jene Smith — are the modern-revolt chapter's Israeli wave.

Decadance and the audience on stage. Decadance (2000–), an evening assembled from excerpts of his repertory, reconfigured for each company that performs it, is his most- travelled work and a deliberate gamut of his own pieces recombined — the chance chapter's architecture applied to a career; Minus 16 (1999) contains the "Echad Mi Yodea" chair semi-circle (from Anaphaza, 1993 — the dancers in black suits rising, collapsing, stripping to the Passover song in accumulation) and the section in which dancers bring audience members onstage to dance cha-cha — participation inside the concert.

Collage scores. He assembles his own music — Israeli pop, Vivaldi, techno, mambo, the "Hava Nagila" cha-cha — and writes tracks under the name Maxim Waratt; the working-with-music chapter cites him as the choreographer-as-music-editor.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • Kyr (1990), Mabul (1992), Anaphaza (1993), Z/na (1995), Zina (1995), Sabotage Baby (1997), Naharin's Virus (2001 — after Peter Handke's Offending the Audience), Mamootot (2003 — in a studio, the audience on four sides), Three (2005), Telophaza (2006), Max (2007), Hora (2009 — in a green box, to film music), Sadeh21 (2011 — the leaps from the wall), Last Work (2015 — a woman running on a treadmill throughout), Venezuela (2017 — the same choreography performed twice to different music: the swap test as a piece), 2019 (2019), Yag (1996/2022), MOMO (2022), and Decadance (2000–) and Minus 16 (1999) in versions worldwide.

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The technique chapter (Gaga); the latent-spaces chapter; the modern revolt; the working-with-music chapter; the choreomusicology chapter (Venezuela).

docs.title: Pina Bausch
docs.text: Born Solingen, Germany, 27 July 1940 · died Wuppertal, 30 June 2009. Trained Folkwang School, Essen, under Kurt Jooss (1955–59); Juilliard, New York (1959–61: Antony Tudor, José Limón, Paul Taylor); danced with the Metropolitan Opera Ballet and with Jooss's Folkwang-Ballett. Company Tanztheater Wuppertal, director from 1973 until her death (the company continues). Key collaborators Rolf Borzik (designer, her partner, d. 1980), Peter Pabst (designer from 1980), Marion Cito (costumes from 1980), Matthias Burkert and Andreas Eisenschneider (music), Raimund Hoghe (dramaturg, 1980–90), and the dancers — Dominique Mercy, Malou Airaudo, Jo Ann Endicott, Lutz Förster, Nazareth Panadero, many others over decades — whose answers to her questions are the pieces.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Tanztheater. Bausch made a form that is neither dance nor theatre and that every European stage has had to reckon with since: evening-length, non-narrative pieces assembled from fragments — repeated everyday gestures, social dances, spoken confessions, songs, games, cruelties, tendernesses — that accumulate into a portrait of how men and women treat one another. The modern-revolt chapter places her; the method is the thing to understand. From around 1978 she made pieces by asking the dancers questions ("what do you do when you're sad?" "show me a gesture of your mother's"), collecting the answers, and composing from them — so the material is the dancers' own and the authorship is hers; the dancers are credited as co-creators, and the works are remade, not restaged, on new casts. It is the craft chapter's tasking method at its most radical, and the chance chapter's frame-and-realization split with the frame being a question.

Repetition as form. Her signature device — a gesture or scene repeated until it changes meaning, from charming to unbearable to funny to grief — is a structural principle: the piece is a set of motifs, returning with variation, and the audience's changing response to the same thing is the content. The gamut chapter's operator logic (repeat, vary, accumulate) is here turned on social behavior rather than movement.

The difficult stage. With Borzik and then Pabst she made the set a terrain the dancers must negotiate — peat, water, turf, carnations, a collapsing wall, a rock — the props chapter's central case, and with Cito's gowns and suits (the costume history) she made costume a social fact the terrain ruins.

Music as collage. Tango, blues, Purcell, pop, folk song, cut together, each fragment's relation to the movement chosen locally — the choreomusicology chapter's off-axis position.

A lineage. The Folkwang line (Reinhild Hoffmann, Susanne Linke), the Belgian and French waves, Alain Platel, the whole European dance-theatre of the 1980s–2000s, and beyond dance the directors who learned from her (Pedro Almodóvar's Talk to Her opens with Café Müller; Wim Wenders's 3-D Pina, 2011, is the memorial).

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Fritz (1974) and the opera-dance works (Iphigenie auf Tauris, 1974; Orpheus und Eurydike, 1975) — the first Wuppertal years, still "dance."
  • The Rite of Spring (Le Sacre du printemps, 1975) — on a stage covered in peat, the Chosen One in a red dress, the ensemble's terror; the last work made as pure choreography before the method changed, and the most-performed.
  • The Seven Deadly Sins (1976, Brecht/Weill) — the turn toward theatre.
  • Blaubart (1977) — Bartók's opera on a tape recorder the protagonist stops and starts; a room of dead leaves. Komm tanz mit mir (1977); Renate wandert aus (1977).
  • Café Müller (1978) — a café of chairs; a sleepwalking woman (Bausch herself) in a slip; a man clearing chairs from her path; a couple repeatedly posed and dropped by a third. The emblem.
  • Kontakthof (1978) — a dance hall, the ensemble in evening clothes presenting themselves, courtship as humiliation and hope; remade with seniors over 65 (2000) and with teenagers (2008).
  • Arien (1979) — water across the stage, a hippopotamus; Keuschheitslegende (1979).
  • 1980 — Ein Stück von Pina Bausch (1980) — on turf, after Borzik's death; mourning, games, childhood.
  • Bandoneon (1980), Walzer (1982), Nelken (Carnations, 1982 — thousands of silk carnations, a man signing "The Man I Love," guard dogs).
  • Auf dem Gebirge hat man ein Geschrei gehört (1984), Two Cigarettes in the Dark (1985), Viktor (1986 — the first of the "city pieces," co-produced by and made about Rome), Ahnen (1987).
  • Palermo Palermo (1989) — the wall that collapses in the first minute; Tanzabend II (1991, Madrid), Das Stück mit dem Schiff (1993), Ein Trauerspiel (1994), Danzón (1995), Nur Du (1996, the American West), Der Fensterputzer (1997, Hong Kong), Masurca Fogo (1998, Lisbon), O Dido (1999, Rome), Wiesenland (2000, Budapest), Água (2001, Brazil), Für die Kinder von gestern, heute und morgen (2002), Nefés (2003, Istanbul), Ten Chi (2004, Japan), Rough Cut (2005, Korea), Vollmond (2006 — the rock and the water), Bamboo Blues (2007, India), Sweet Mambo (2008), and "…como el musguito en la piedra, ay si, si, si…" (2009, Chile) — the last, premiered weeks before her death.

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt (tanztheater); the props and costume chapters; the choreomusicology chapter (collage); the craft chapter (tasking; Hoghe as dramaturg).

docs.title: Steve Paxton
docs.text: Born Phoenix, Arizona, 21 January 1939 · died Vermont, 20 February 2024. Trained gymnastics; danced with José Limón and then with Merce Cunningham (1961–64); Robert Dunn's class. Groups a founder of the Judson Dance Theater (1962) and the Grand Union (1970–76); from 1972 the Contact Improvisation community (no company — a practice, jams, Contact Quarterly founded 1975); Touchdown Dance (with Anne Kilcoyne, for visually impaired dancers); lived and taught at Mad Brook Farm, Vermont.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Walking. Proxy (1961), Satisfyin Lover (1967 — forty-two people walking, standing, and sitting across a stage at their own pace), State (1968): Paxton made the pedestrian the material, more rigorously than anyone at Judson. A person walking, unperformed, watched as dance — the modern-revolt chapter's postmodern premise stated as plainly as possible.

Contact Improvisation. In January 1972, at Oberlin College, Magnesium — men hurling themselves at each other and falling on mats — and then in June at the John Weber Gallery, New York, the first performances under the name: a duet form in which two bodies share a moving point of contact, give and take weight, roll, lift, fall, and follow the physics of the encounter without a plan. No steps, no music, no leader, no audience required. Contact spread through jams and workshops rather than companies; it is practiced on every continent, it reshaped contemporary partnering (the lifts and floorwork of release-based technique descend from it — the technique chapter treats it with release as the subtraction of the vocabulary), it is a social and somatic practice as much as an art, and it is the first chapter's cleanest case of a dance form with a participatory function invented inside the concert tradition. Its rules are physical, not choreographic — the chance chapter's frame reduced to gravity and attention — and it has no author in the ordinary sense, which Paxton insisted on.

Material for the Spine and the solos. His later decades produced the improvised solos to Bach (Goldberg Variations, 1986–92, performed over years; English Suites) and Material for the Spine (from 1986; the DVD-ROM, 2008), a technical study of the spine's and pelvis's movement in rolling and spiraling — a somatic pedagogy that is the Contact form's technical residue. Flat (1964), Bound (1982), Ave Nue (1985, with Lisa Nelson), Night Stand (2004, with Nelson) are the performance landmarks; the Golden Lion of the Venice Biennale (2014) recognized the whole.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • Proxy (1961), Transit (1962), Flat (1964), Jag vill gärna telefonera (1964), Satisfyin Lover (1967), State (1968), Magnesium (1972), Contact Improvisations (1972 onward — the form itself), Backwater: Twosome (1977, with David Moss), Bound (1982), Ave Nue (1985), Goldberg Variations (1986–92), Material for the Spine (1986–), Night Stand (2004), Quicksand (2016, with Nelson and Jurij Konjar).

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt; the technique chapter (release and contact); the chance chapter; the what-dance-is chapter (a participatory form from the concert tradition).

docs.title: Trisha Brown
docs.text: Born Aberdeen, Washington, 25 November 1936 · died San Antonio, 18 March 2017. Trained Mills College (dance, 1958); Anna Halprin's summer workshop (1960); Robert Dunn's composition class in New York (1961–62). Company the Trisha Brown Dance Company, founded 1970 (still performing). Key collaborators Robert Rauschenberg (from Glacial Decoy, 1979), Laurie Anderson, Donald Judd, Nancy Graves, Fujiko Nakaya, the Judson group (a founding member), the Grand Union (1970–76), and her dancers (Stephen Petronio, Diane Madden, Vicky Shick, and others who carried the technique).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
The equipment pieces and the site. Brown's early work literally rotated the stage: Man Walking Down the Side of a Building (1970), Walking on the Wall (1971), Roof Piece (1971) — the props chapter's canonical site works, in which gravity was a sideways force, the city a set, and the viewer's assumptions about up and down the material.

Accumulation and the rule-made dance. Accumulation (1971) — a gesture, then the gesture plus a second, then those plus a third, in a rotating solo of thirty minutes — is the cleanest rule-generated dance in the repertory, and the chance chapter treats it as the second-generation answer to Cunningham: not randomness but a visible procedure. Primary Accumulation (1972, lying down), Group Primary Accumulation, Accumulation with Talking plus Watermotor (1979 — the dance performed while telling two interleaved stories) extended it. Locus (1975) mapped the alphabet onto a cube around the dancer and spelled a text in movement; the Unstable Molecular Structure works (Opal Loop, 1980) built ensembles from individually rule-driven parts. Brown is the proof that a rule system can become an aesthetic rather than a demonstration.

The released vocabulary. In the 1980s the rules produced a style: loose, sequential, initiated from anywhere, weight dropped and caught, the limbs flung and the spine liquid — the technique chapter's release lineage at its most articulate. Set and Reset (1983), with Rauschenberg's translucent set and costumes and Laurie Anderson's score, made on five instructions ("keep it simple," "play with visibility and invisibility," "stay on the edge," "act on instinct," "line up") is its masterpiece and the work companies worldwide learn her idiom through.

The Valiant cycle and the opera house. Newark (Niweweorce) (1987, Donald Judd's colored drops), Astral Convertible (1989), Foray Forêt (1990, with a marching band passing outside the theatre), then M.O. (1995) to Bach's Musical Offering — the turn to classical music — and the operas (L'Orfeo, 1998, which she directed; Winterreise, 2002; Pygmalion) took the postmodern vocabulary into the institutions Judson had refused. She drew all her life; her drawings and "It's a Draw" performances (drawing on paper with her whole body) are in museum collections.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Trillium (1962) — the first; Rulegame 5 (1964); Homemade (1966 — dancing with a projector strapped to her back, projecting a film of herself doing the dance).
  • Planes (1968), Man Walking Down the Side of a Building (1970), Floor of the Forest (1970 — a grid of ropes and clothes the dancers dress into), Walking on the Wall and Roof Piece (1971), Leaning Duets.
  • Accumulation (1971), Primary Accumulation (1972), Locus (1975), Line Up (1976), Watermotor (1978 — the solo that shows the style being born, famously filmed in slow motion by Babette Mangolte).
  • Glacial Decoy (1979 — Rauschenberg's first set for her; the dancers exiting and entering as if the stage were wider than the frame), Opal Loop (1980 — Nakaya's fog), Son of Gone Fishin' (1981), Set and Reset (1983), Lateral Pass (1985), Newark (1987), Astral Convertible (1989), Foray Forêt (1990), For M.G.: The Movie (1991), If you couldn't see me (1994 — a solo danced entirely with her back to the audience, Rauschenberg's music and costume).
  • M.O. (1995), Canto/Pianto (1997), L'Orfeo (1998), Five Part Weather Invention (1999), Rapture to Leon James (2000), Geometry of Quiet (2002), PRESENT TENSE (2003), O zlozony / O composite (2004, Paris Opéra), I love my robots (2007 — with Kenjiro Okazaki's moving poles), L'Amour au théâtre (2009), I'm going to toss my arms — if you catch them they're yours (2011 — the last, with industrial fans).

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The chance chapter (accumulation; rules as style); the props chapter (the site works); the technique chapter (release); the modern revolt (Judson and after); the costume history (Judson's pedestrian clothes; Rauschenberg).

docs.title: Twyla Tharp
docs.text: Born Portland, Indiana, 1 July 1941. Trained Barnard College; the American Ballet Theatre school; studied with Richard Thomas, Graham, Cunningham, Erick Hawkins, Luigi, Matt Mattox; danced with Paul Taylor (1963–65). Companies Twyla Tharp Dance (founded 1965; merged into ABT 1988–91; reformed); works for the Joffrey, ABT, NYCB, the Paris Opéra, the Royal Ballet, and nearly every major company. Key collaborators Mikhail Baryshnikov (Push Comes to Shove, 1976, and the ABT years), Milos Forman (Hair, Ragtime, Amadeus), Jennifer Tipton (lighting), Santo Loquasto (design), Sara Rudner, Rose Marie Wright, Kenneth Rinker and the early company; Billy Joel (Movin' Out), Bob Dylan, Frank Sinatra (recordings).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Structure first. Tharp began as a rigorous postmodernist — Tank Dive (1965), Re-Moves (1966), The Fugue (1970, in silence, three dancers, a twenty-count theme put through contrapuntal variation on a miked floor) — and never stopped building on structure: her loose, slouching, jazzy, quicksilver style rides on counts and canons as tight as any in the repertory. The gamut chapter and the chance chapter both could cite The Fugue as the operator catalog performed; the working-with-music chapter cites her polymetric counterpoint against pop songs.

The crossover. Deuce Coupe (1973, for the Joffrey, to the Beach Boys, with graffiti artists painting a backdrop live) put her company and a ballet company onstage together — the first "crossover" ballet; Push Comes to Shove (1976, Baryshnikov in a bowler hat to Haydn and Joseph Lamb) made classical virtuosity funny and American; In the Upper Room (1986, Philip Glass, the dancers in Norma Kamali's stripes and red pointe shoes emerging from fog) is the most-performed contemporary ballet in the world. Tharp taught ballet companies to move like Americans and modern dancers to respect the classical instrument, and the blur the modern-revolt chapter ends on is partly her doing.

Pop, Broadway, film. Eight Jelly Rolls (1971, Jelly Roll Morton), Sue's Leg (1975, Fats Waller), Nine Sinatra Songs (1982), the Dylan and Billy Joel shows (Movin' Out, 2002, the Tony), Come Fly Away (2010); choreography for Hair (1979), Ragtime, Amadeus, White Nights — Tharp made the recorded pop song a legitimate score for concert dance and the concert dancer a Broadway draw.

The book. The Creative Habit (2003) — the box for each project, the ritual of the morning, "scratching," the spine of a piece — is the most-read practical book by a choreographer and an unofficial companion to the craft chapter; Push Comes to Shove (1992) is the memoir; Keep It Moving (2019) the late one.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text: • Tank Dive (1965), Re-Moves (1966), Generation (1968), Medley (1969, outdoors), The Fugue (1970), Eight Jelly Rolls (1971), The Bix Pieces (1971), The Raggedy Dances (1972), Deuce Coupe (1973), As Time Goes By (1973), Sue's Leg (1975), Push Comes to Shove (1976), Baker's Dozen (1979), The Catherine Wheel (1981, David Byrne), Nine Sinatra Songs (1982), Bach Partita (1983), In the Upper Room (1986), Brief Fling (1990), Known by Heart (1998), The Beethoven Seventh (2000), Movin' Out (2002), Come Fly Away (2010), Preludes and Fugues (2015), Minimalism and Me (2018).

docs.title: Where she is in this subject
docs.text: The modern revolt; the working-with-music chapter; the choreomusicology chapter (counterpoint); the costume history (sneakers in the opera house); the craft chapter.

docs.title: Wayne McGregor
docs.text: Born Stockport, England, 12 March 1970. Trained Bretton Hall College (dance and drama); the José Limón School, New York. Companies Random Dance (founded 1992; Studio Wayne McGregor from 2017, resident at Sadler's Wells and then at its own East London studios); Resident Choreographer of the Royal Ballet since 2006 — the first from outside the classical world. Key collaborators the scientists and technologists (Open Ended Group, the Google Arts & Culture Lab, cognitive scientists at Cambridge and UCSD), composers (Max Richter, Joby Talbot, Jlin, Jon Hopkins, Thom Yorke), designers (Lucy Carter, lighting; Gareth Pugh, Moritz Junge, costume; the artists Olafur Eliasson, Tacita Dean, Julian Opie, Edmund de Waal, Ben Cullen Williams), and his dancers, who are trained into his thinking-body method.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
The hyper-articulate body. McGregor's movement language is immediately recognizable — extreme extension, spinal undulation and hyper-flexion, speed, the limbs folding and unfolding at angles the classical line doesn't use — applied equally to his own company and to the Royal Ballet's dancers, whom he re-wired. It is a technique in the sense that it produces a distinctive body, and it is the most imitated contemporary vocabulary in ballet companies worldwide.

Choreography as cognition. His deepest contribution is to have treated choreography as a problem in thinking — how dancers generate material, how a "creative body" can be studied, how tools might extend it. Long collaborations with cognitive scientists (the "Choreographic Thinking Tools" research with David Kirsh and others; the Mind and Movement resource for schools) produced a documented method of imagery-led generation: dancers given mental tasks (imagine the body as a drawing, move a point through space, subtract a limb) produce movement no direct instruction would — the technique chapter's operator idea from the cognitive side.

The computational collaborations. Three projects carry the computational-choreography chapter: the Choreographic Language Agent (2004 onward, with Open Ended Group) — software that proposes abstract movement ideas in response to a dancer's; Living Archive (2019, with Google Arts & Culture) — a model trained on twenty-five years of the company's video that generates new phrases in his idiom, used live in Living Archive: An AI Performance Experiment; and AISOMA (2025) — the public version, a tool that lets anyone work with his archive the way the company does. McGregor is the field's clearest case of a choreographer treating a generative model as a collaborator whose proposals he gates — the gamut+rules architecture's human gate, with a learned sequencer. The latent-spaces chapter reads Living Archive as navigation of a learned space of his own work.

Scale and institution. As the Royal Ballet's resident he made full-evening narrative ballets (Woolf Works, The Dante Project) that reconciled his abstraction with the house's storytelling; as a company director he built a studio that hosts research, residencies, and education; he has choreographed for film (Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, Fantastic Beasts, Mary Queen of Scots), opera, Radiohead, and the Paralympic ceremony.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Xeno (1994), Sulphur 16 (1998), Nemesis (2002 — the dancers with prosthetic arm extensions) — the early Random Dance works, technology already present.
  • AtaXia (2004) — from research on the neurological condition: movement built from disrupted coordination; Amu (2005) — the heart, with scientists and a cardiac surgeon.
  • Chroma (2006, Royal Ballet) — Joby Talbot and Jack White's music, John Pawson's white box; the work that got him the residency and that ballet companies worldwide now dance.
  • Entity (2008) — Random Dance, with the Choreographic Language Agent; Infra (2008, Royal Ballet) — Max Richter's score, Julian Opie's walking LED figures above the dancers.
  • Limen (2009), Live Fire Exercise (2011), Carbon Life (2012 — Mark Ronson, Gareth Pugh), Raven Girl (2013 — a narrative ballet after Audrey Niffenegger).
  • FAR (2010) — after Roy Porter's Flesh in the Age of Reason; UNDANCE (2011); Atomos (2013 — in 3-D glasses; the dancers' material generated partly from a film).
  • Woolf Works (2015, Royal Ballet) — Max Richter, three Virginia Woolf novels; Alessandra Ferri's return; the Olivier Award and the proof that his idiom could carry narrative.
  • Tree of Codes (2015) — Jamie xx, Olafur Eliasson, Jonathan Safran Foer's cut-up book: the Paris Opéra and his company together.
  • Obsidian Tear (2016), Multiverse (2016), Autobiography (2017 — twenty-three sections ordered each night by an algorithm working from his genome sequence; Jlin's score), Yugen (2018), Living Archive (2019), The Dante Project (2021, Royal Ballet — Thomas Adès, Tacita Dean; the Divine Comedy full-length), MaddAddam (2022, National Ballet of Canada — Atwood), UniVerse: A Dark Crystal Odyssey (2023), Deepstaria (2024), and the 2025 AISOMA performances.

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The computational-choreography chapter (the Agent, Living Archive, AISOMA); the latent-spaces chapter; the technique chapter; the modern revolt (the contemporary now); the lighting chapter (Lucy Carter).

docs.title: William Forsythe
docs.text: Born New York, 30 December 1949. Trained Jacksonville University; Joffrey Ballet School; danced with the Joffrey and then the Stuttgart Ballet (1973–80), where John Cranko's company made him a choreographer. Companies Ballett Frankfurt, director 1984–2004 — the twenty years that made the city a world center — then The Forsythe Company (2005–15); since then freelance, with works for the Paris Opéra, Boston Ballet, English National Ballet, and installations for museums worldwide; professor at USC's Glorya Kaufman School. Key collaborators Thom Willems (composer, in the rehearsal room, from 1985), Stephen Galloway (costumes), the Frankfurt dancers themselves (Dana Caspersen, Jone San Martin, Antony Rizzi and many others — Forsythe's method makes them co-authors), ZKM Karlsruhe and Ohio State's ACCAD (the digital projects), Motion Bank. Designs his own lighting.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Ballet deconstructed. Forsythe's first contribution was to take the Balanchine line — speed, off-balance, the classical vocabulary pushed — and push it past the point where it remained classical: the épaulement exaggerated into torsion, the arabesque tipped past recovery, the line broken on purpose, the preparation removed, the dancers falling and catching. In the Middle, Somewhat Elevated (1987, for the Paris Opéra) is the work the whole ballet world took as the announcement: Willems's pounding electronic score, nine dancers in green, a competition of extremes. The ballet companies that program him — nearly all of them — program this and the works around it, and "Forsythe" became a style: the ballet body at maximum articulation. He has said, consistently, that he was never against ballet; he was interested in what it was made of.

An operator vocabulary. The deeper contribution, and the one this library cares most about, is that Forsythe made operations rather than steps the unit of his work. His Improvisation Technologies — developed in the studio from the late 1980s and published as a CD-ROM in 1999 — are a vocabulary of things to do to movement: draw a line in space with a limb and fold it; extrude a point; drop a curve; avoid an imagined obstacle; collapse a shape; reorient the body's own geometry; "room writing." The technique chapter treats this as the clearest case of a vocabulary of transformations rather than positions — the kind of thing the gamut chapter's operator catalog formalizes — and the video chapter treats the CD-ROM as the first digital score that teaches a generative method rather than recording a piece. His dancers improvise with these tools inside structures he sets; his pieces are, in the chance chapter's terms, frames with designed realizations.

Structure made visible. Synchronous Objects (2009) extracted the cue and alignment structure of One Flat Thing, reproduced as data and rendered it as twenty visualizations — the video chapter's centerpiece — and the essay "Choreographic Objects" (2008) stated the thesis behind it: a choreographic idea can exist in forms other than a body. From that came the choreographic objects themselves — installations (Nowhere and Everywhere at the Same Time, the pendulums; The Fact of Matter, the gymnastic rings; Scattered Crowd, the balloons; City of Abstracts, the delayed-video wall) that choreograph the visitor, and that put Forsythe in art museums as often as theatres. Motion Bank (2010–13) generalized the digital-score idea to other choreographers, and its Piecemaker tool is now the dance world's durable annotation stack.

The rehearsal room as a compositional instrument. Willems composing live in the room, the dancers generating material from operations and tasks, the lighting designed by the choreographer, the dramaturgy of several things at once — Forsythe's process is itself a contribution, and the working-with-music chapter cites it as the case where neither music nor dance leads.

docs.title: Major works
docs.text:
• Gänge (1983) and the early Frankfurt years' full-evening experiments, where the deconstruction began.
  • Artifact (1984) — his first full-evening Frankfurt work: a deconstructed ballet with a woman in historical costume reciting, a curtain that falls repeatedly mid-phrase, the corps in unison lines; Artifact Suite (2004) is the excerpt ballet companies dance.
  • Steptext (1985) — to Bach's Chaconne, fragmented, with the lights cutting the music; In the Middle, Somewhat Elevated (1987) — the canonical one.
  • Impressing the Czar (1988) — the full-evening work that contains In the Middle as its second act, framed by baroque pageantry and a final act (Bongo Bongo Nageela) of the whole company in schoolgirl uniforms.
  • The Loss of Small Detail (1991) — Issey Miyake's costumes, snow, text, fragmentation; Limb's Theorem (1990); Enemy in the Figure (1989) — a light on wheels, a rope, a wall: the dancers in and out of darkness.
  • Eidos: Telos (1995) — the large, dark, three-part meditation with text; Self Meant to Govern (1994) — the Improvisation Technologies on stage.
  • One Flat Thing, reproduced (2000) — seventeen dancers and twenty steel tables dragged downstage; the cue-driven counterpoint later mapped by Synchronous Objects; filmed by Thierry De Mey.
  • Kammer/Kammer (2000) — live video, text, a room within the stage; Decreation (2003) — after Anne Carson, voices and bodies wrenched.
  • Three Atmospheric Studies (2005) — the Iraq-war work, a mother searching for her son; Heterotopia (2006); I don't believe in outer space (2008); Sider (2011).
  • Quintett (1993) — five dancers to Gavin Bryars's Jesus' Blood Never Failed Me Yet, made as his wife was dying: the tender Forsythe, and the most-revived.
  • Blake Works I (2016, Paris Opéra; to James Blake) and Playlist (Track 1, 2) (2018, ENB) — the late return to pure, joyous classical dancing to pop music.

docs.title: Where he is in this subject
docs.text: The technique chapter (operations as vocabulary); the video chapter (Improvisation Technologies, Synchronous Objects, Motion Bank); the computational-choreography chapter; the working-with-music chapter (Willems in the room); the lighting chapter (designing his own light); the ballet history (the Balanchine line's limit).

docs.title: Yvonne Rainer
docs.text: Born San Francisco, 24 November 1934. Trained Martha Graham School, Cunningham studio; Anna Halprin's workshop (1960); Robert Dunn's composition class (1960–62). Groups a founder of the Judson Dance Theater (1962) and of the Grand Union (1970–76). Second career filmmaker (seven features, 1972–96: Lives of Performers, Film About a Woman Who…, Journeys from Berlin/1971, Privilege, MURDER and murder); returned to choreography in 2000 at Baryshnikov's invitation and has made work since with her Raindears. MacArthur Fellow (1990).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Trio A. The Mind Is a Muscle, Part I (1966) — four and a half minutes of continuous movement with no phrase accents, no repetition, no climax, the gaze averted, the energy level even, every movement given the same weight as every other: the emblem of the postmodern dance, performed by anyone who learns it (it was taught deliberately to non-dancers) and now in museum collections. The modern-revolt chapter and the technique chapter treat it as the limit of subtraction: a dance made entirely of what it refuses.

The "No Manifesto." "No to spectacle no to virtuosity no to transformations and magic and make-believe no to the glamour and transcendency of the star image no to the heroic no to the anti-heroic no to trash imagery no to involvement of performer or spectator no to style no to camp no to seduction of spectator by the wiles of the performer no to eccentricity no to moving or being moved" (1965) — the creed of the whole generation, which she later said was meant as a provocation and a clearing, not a program, and which she half-retracted in 2008.

Task, rule, and the ordinary body. We Shall Run (1963, twelve people jogging to Berlioz), Parts of Some Sextets (1965, with mattresses), Terrain (1963 — game structures, rules read aloud), the "Continuous Project–Altered Daily" (1969–70) that dissolved into the Grand Union's improvisations: Rainer's work treated movement as task and the performer as worker, the chance chapter's rule-based lineage on the side of the pedestrian. Her writings (Work 1961–73; the essay "A Quasi Survey of Some 'Minimalist' Tendencies…") gave the period its self-description.

Film and return. Her films of the 1970s–90s made her a founding figure of feminist and structural cinema; the return to dance (After Many a Summer Dies the Swan, 2000; AG Indexical, with a little help from H.M., 2006, a Agon reworking; RoS Indexical, 2007, after the Rite; Assisted Living, 2010s; Hellzapoppin', 2022) re-enters the canon with the tools she left it with.
