Lifting 2D detections to a 3D body was never really the hard part per-frame; the hard part is world grounding — recovering the global trajectory and orientation so that a dancer who travels, turns, and jumps does so in the world instead of swimming in place at the camera's origin. This is precisely the dance-relevant half: travel and facing are choreography.

The state of the art (single ordinary camera, no markers, no suit):

  • WHAM (CVPR 2024) made world grounding respectable — motion context plus learned foot-contact cues to pin trajectory to the ground.2
  • GVHMR (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024; TPAMI 2026) is the current default. Its trick is a coordinate system: predict pose in gravity-view coordinates — a frame defined by gravity plus the camera ray, uniquely inferable per image — which removes an ambiguity the network otherwise wastes capacity resolving. It emits SMPL-X, grounds camera-space motion more accurately than WHAM, and its core network is roughly seven times faster (~0.28 s vs ~2.0 s); on the standard per-pose accuracy benchmark the two are within a fraction of a millimeter.3
  • OnlineHMR (CVPR 2026) does the same job causally — streaming, for live settings.

All of this is research code: free on GitHub, real to run (a GPU, a Python environment, no support desk), and worth it when you want the best monocular result on footage you don't control — archival dance video being the canonical case.

When you do control the room, triangulate instead. Multiple cheap cameras beat one clever network. FreeMocap — free and open source — turns two or more ordinary webcams into a markerless rig: MediaPipe's 553 landmarks per frame (body, both hands, face) triangulated into 3D, exported to native Blender, FBX, or CSV; its April 2026 release added reprojection-outlier rejection, so one badly placed camera no longer corrupts the whole solve.4 Its sibling Pose2Sim takes any camera mix (phones, GoPros) into an OpenSim biomechanical skeleton — the tool when joint kinematics need to be right, not just plausible-looking.5

docs.title: What dance does to all of this
docs.text:
Dance is close to a worst case for capture, and the failure modes are specific enough to plan around:6

  • Floorwork breaks the priors. Standing-biased pose priors and foot-contact heuristics misfire when weight is on the back, side, or hands — the same standing bias the notation systems carry, now baked into models trained on walking-heavy data. Rolls and inversions are where monocular methods hallucinate hardest; multi-camera capture is the honest fix.
  • Spins flip orientation. Left/right ambiguity under fast rotation produces the characteristic snap where the body turns 180° between frames. (Recall that near-symmetric skeletons carry limb identity almost entirely in subtle appearance cues — at speed, those cues blur away.)
  • Fast motion blurs and jumps. Large inter-frame displacement defeats tracking; power moves defeat it so thoroughly that BRACE — the breakdancing dataset — had to be partly annotated by hand because automatic capture failed on exactly the material it exists to cover. Shoot 60 fps or better for anything percussive.
  • Costume occludes. Skirts, coats, long hair, hats — everything the staged-body chapters will celebrate is an occlusion generator. Capture passes want fitted clothing; wardrobe is a render-time decision, which pose-conditioned video generation happily accommodates.

The standard benchmark, incidentally, is AIST++: 5.2 hours, 1,408 sequences, ten genres, multi-view with known cameras — worth knowing both as a corpus and as the substrate most music-to-dance generation is trained on.7

docs.title: The clever part: making it move like a person
docs.text:
Raw output from every one of these systems shares a look: feet that skate, joints that jitter, poses that are individually fine and collectively boneless. The repair techniques are where the field has gotten genuinely clever, and they sort into three tiers by what the fix can see — a tiering worth internalizing because it recurs everywhere in this territory.

Tier one: geometric patches. Detect foot-contact frames from velocity and height, then pin the foot with inverse kinematics for the contact's duration; filter the jitter. Cheap, local, ships as a checkbox in commercial tools ("foot locking"). It fixes the single most visible artifact and nothing else — and a pin that fights the data can buy you a knee pop in exchange for the slide.

Tier two: learned priors — denoising by projection. Train a generative model of how humans actually move — VPoser for single poses, HuMoR for whole trajectories, motion-diffusion models as the current generation — then pull noisy estimates toward what the model believes.8 Readers of the latent-spaces chapter will recognize this instantly: it is the manifold, used as a repair strategy — off-manifold capture gets projected back onto the thin surface of plausible human movement. And it inherits the manifold's caveat with teeth: a prior is only as good as its corpus's coverage, so a prior trained on walking-heavy mocap will "correct" your floorwork toward standing. For dance, check what the prior was fed before letting it edit.

Tier three: physics — legalization by embodiment. The deepest fix, and the one most worth understanding. Train a reinforcement-learning controller that drives a simulated humanoid — mass, joint limits, friction, gravity — to track your noisy reference motion: the DeepMimic line (2018) through AMP to PHC (Perpetual Humanoid Control), the current workhorse, which tracks large noisy corpora robustly.9 The output is whatever the simulated body actually did — and therefore feet cannot slide (friction is real), momentum is conserved, balance is kept or visibly lost. Physics repairs what the other tiers cannot even represent: forces, weight, contact — precisely the fields the gamut chapter called the treacherous ones, and pedagogy's root cause of transition failure. Seen from this subject's angle, tier three is the legality graph gone continuous: simulation as a checker that cannot be argued with. The costs: an RL training loop, and a subtle one — the controller is itself a performer with an accent, and extreme stylization comes back slightly flattened. Sound familiar? It's the LifeForms lesson again: every tool's easy path shows up in the output.

The tiers compose — prior-then-physics is the strong pipeline — and choosing by failure mode keeps it cheap: skating feet, tier one; jitter and odd poses, tier two; impossible dynamics or contact-rich floorwork, tier three.

And there's an interactive version of the whole idea. Cascadeur — a standalone keyframe animator with a genuinely usable free tier — packages the priors inside the authoring loop rather than as after-the-fact repair: AutoPosing completes a natural pose from a few dragged handles (a learned pose prior as a direct-manipulation tool), and AutoPhysics nudges keyframed motion toward ballistic and momentum correctness while preserving the animator's intent.10 It is, in this subject's vocabulary, a human gate with a physics-literate assistant — worth knowing even if your pipeline is mostly generative, because it's the fastest way to hand-fix the ten seconds the pipeline got wrong.

docs.title: Stage five: retargeting, the quiet quality-killer
docs.text: Captured motion lands on your character through retargeting — mapping one skeleton's motion onto another's proportions — and this unglamorous step is where free pipelines usually lose their realism. Different limb lengths shift contact timing; a clean capture retargeted carelessly skates again. The free path is settled: Blender (with Rokoko's free plugin or native tooling) and Mixamo for auto-rigging; Cascadeur's retargeting sits in its paid tier. Budget a cleanup pass after every retarget, and treat rig choice as an aesthetic decision — proportions are style, as anyone who has watched the same motion on two differently-built dancers already knows.

docs.title: The free stack, summarized
docs.text:
Tool Stage What it does Cost MediaPipe / DWPose 2D keypoints; VACE control skeletons free GVHMR / WHAM / OnlineHMR 3D lift world-grounded SMPL(-X) from one video free (research code, GPU) FreeMocap 3D multi-cam webcams → triangulated 3D → Blender/FBX free, open source Pose2Sim 3D multi-cam biomechanics-grade kinematics free, open source Rokoko Vision cloud lift video → FBX, plugins for Blender/Unity/UE free ≤15 s clips DeepMotion cloud lift video → FBX, foot-lock modes free ~60 s/month Cascadeur assist/author AutoPosing, AutoPhysics keyframing free tier; Pro ~$396/yr Blender + Mixamo rig/retarget auto-rig, retarget, render free

(Caps and prices verified August 2026; this table is the rotting kind of knowledge — expect drift within a year.)

docs.title: What this opens
docs.text:
Two doors, both of which later chapters walk through. Capture turns footage into corpus — the raw material for learned movement spaces and for the unsupervised gesture-discovery program (chapter 10's research sweep, coming) starts as exactly these skeletons. And capture turns performance into control signal: a cleaned 3D take, re-rendered from any angle through the pose-conditioned video pipeline, is the bridge between a real dancer's phrasing and a synthetic dancer's body — the subject of the rendering chapter ahead.

Field notes

This chapter renders three commons notes researched for it on 2026-08-18 (the library's research-first rule: findings land in notes/ with sources, then render here): ml-video-to-3d-dance-pose-landscape, ml-physics-and-priors-motion-cleanup, data-free-mocap-tooling-2026.

  1. Scope note: this chapter covers markerless (video-based) capture, which is where the action and the zero budgets are. Optical marker systems (Vicon, OptiTrack) and IMU suits (Xsens, Rokoko Smartsuit) remain the studio-grade options — better data, four-to-six figures or a wearable, and out of scope here. ↩

  2. WHAM — Reconstructing World-grounded Humans with Accurate 3D Motion (CVPR 2024). ↩

  3. GVHMR — World-Grounded Human Motion Recovery via Gravity-View Coordinates (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024; TPAMI 2026); code. ↩

  4. FreeMocap — free, open-source markerless capture. ↩

  5. Pose2Sim — markerless kinematics to OpenSim. ↩

  6. Survey of 3D human pose and shape estimation for contemporary dance; BRACE — the breakdancing competition dataset. ↩

  7. AIST++ / AI Choreographer. ↩

  8. HuMoR (ICCV 2021) is the standard motion-prior reference; VPoser ships with SMPL-X (CVPR 2019). ↩

  9. DeepMimic (SIGGRAPH 2018) → AMP (SIGGRAPH 2021) → PHC (ICCV 2023), with guided-diffusion humanoid policies as the 2025–26 research edge. ↩

  10. Cascadeur — free tier for personal use; retargeting in Pro. ↩

docs.title: The pipeline, end to end
docs.text: Part VII has walked through the stages one at a time. This chapter puts them in a row, says who — human, rule system, model, simulator — owns each, names the budgets that bind across stages, and then adds the part that no single stage owns: composing for the camera, which turns out to be a design decision taken at authoring time, not a coverage decision taken afterward. It closes with one phrase walked through the whole chain.

docs.title: The stages, and their owners
docs.text:
• 1 · The gamut — a small, typed, hand-authored vocabulary with connectors and state-changing verbs first-class (Building a gamut); discovery models may propose candidates (Machine-discovered vocabularies), a human names and types them. Owner: human.
  • 2 · The sequencer — chance, rule, or model, owning an enumerated list of continuity dimensions and nothing else (Chance and rules); generators (Generating movement) are sequencers with a learned vocabulary, useful as proposal machines. Owner: system.
  • 3 · The legality check — the typed pre/post chain, window metric, symmetry quotiented out, one strongly connected component (The architecture). Owner: machine tier.
  • 4 · The gate — interest and performability, kept distinct; throughput budgeted; proposals rendered at the fidelity that fits the human's role. Owner: human tier.
  • 5 · Motion realization — a body performs it and is captured (The captured body), a generator emits it, or physics and objectives produce it (Locomotion without a choreographer). Owner: body, model, or simulator.
  • 6 · Cleanup — geometric patches, learned priors, physics simulation, chosen by failure mode and scored against the plausible-body rubric. Owner: machine tier, human spot-check.
  • 7 · Render — skeleton and keyframes into pixels; background pinned by envelope, pose on grey, motion budget set and matched between preview and final (Rendering the dancer). Owner: model, under conditioning.
  • 8 · Camera and cut — this chapter. Owner: human, at authoring time.

docs.title: The budgets that bind
docs.text:
Several quantities are spent across stages and are easy to overspend because no single stage sees the whole bill:

  • The motion budget — in the renderer, literally the high-noise step count; upstream, the one-beat-per-clip rule. Camera motion and character motion draw on it together; a pinned background takes the set out of it.
  • The keyframe budget — every pin is a still that must agree with its neighbors on light, palette, and framing; more pins forbid more shortcuts and leave less for the model to invent.
  • The gate's throughput — candidates per hour a human can actually judge; the generator's output is sized to it, and the machine tier keeps anything obviously invalid from reaching it.
  • Camera-move slots — deterministic 2D moves are cheap to make and still cost a slot in the shot grammar; a locked camera is the default and a move is spent, not free.
  • Level-changing units — the expensive transitions in rehearsal and in rendering; keep them a minority of the vocabulary and rate-limit them per phrase.

docs.title: Compose for the camera at authoring time
docs.text:
Here is the stage-to-screen inversion that the rest of this part has been building toward. Humphrey's stage rule — movement looks slower and weaker from the house, so scale it up — runs backward on camera: the lens magnifies. A passage built on breath, a hand, a face is viable material on screen and simply isn't on stage. Which means shot size is a parameter of the composition, not a coverage decision:

  • Wide carries travel, floor pattern, level change, jumps — and loses face and hands.
  • Full (body fills frame) carries whole-body line — the documentation default — and loses the environment.
  • Mid carries torso-led movement, gesture, weight shift — and crops the feet, so footwork and travel vanish.
  • Close carries face, hands, feet, breath — "micro-choreography" — and nothing spatial.

Two design rules follow. Match material to frame when you author it: pathway-rich and level-rich phrases only pay in wide coverage; gaze- and gesture-rich phrases want mid or close; floor material wants a floor-height camera, because high angles flatten floorwork into a pattern on the ground. And scale counterpoint is a form — alternating macro sections (travel, level, wide) with micro sections (hands, face, breath, close) is screen-native, has no stage equivalent, and is the solo performer's substitute for the textural contrast an ensemble gets for free. The shoot rule that falls out: plan three frames — wide, mid, close — and shoot (or render) each phrase at two or more of them, so every moment exists in more than one size. That redundancy is what supplies the edit's cut points; it isn't a hedge against a bad take. For a generated pipeline the same logic decides what a generation is asked to contain: a wide shot asks the model for whole-body travel, a close-up for a face and a hand — very different reliability propositions, and a reason to keep one moving region per clip.

Lens facts worth carrying: wide and normal lenses close to the performer preserve toward-and-away dynamics; telephoto compresses depth and kills them — save the long lens for faces and detail, and shoot Z-axis material wide and close in.

docs.title: Author the cut points into the material
docs.text:
Editing is usually done to finished material. The stronger move is to schedule the cut points into the performance — roughly one every phrase or two — as a constraint on the generator. Five performed events double as edit licenses:

  • A hold or stillness — tolerates a cut anywhere inside it; the most permissive edit point there is, and the reason stillness earned first-class status in the vocabulary.
  • An accent or hit — cut on the impact; the eye tracks the action across the join and the cut disappears.
  • A turn or spin — a rotation resets the eye-line, which licenses a camera-position change that would otherwise read as a jump. Turns are edit enablers, not just spatial variety.
  • A pass through neutral — weight centered, standing: any two takes align there.
  • An exit from frame — total freedom about what enters next.

Two structural properties extend the list. Loop closure: a phrase whose final pose matches its opening in shape, weight, facing, and near-zero velocity is loopable and re-orderable — the transition-legality condition applied to one phrase reflexively; make at least the recurring phrase a perfect loop and the edit can repeat or reorder it at will. And Deren's principle, from A Study in Choreography for Camera (1945): temporal continuity survives spatial discontinuity — a movement begun in one location can complete in another, the movement carries the cut while the space goes free. That is the license to shoot one phrase across locations, sets, wardrobe states, or generated backdrops, and in a rendered pipeline it's why a continuous action is the safest thing to place across a background change. Her other line generalizes further: the compositional unit is "whatever is in the frame, including the space," not the body.

The discipline that still applies: cut on the beat but not on every beat (off-rhythm shot changes read as a palpable disconnect; constant cutting disorients); long takes of fifteen seconds and up read as respect for the movement, fast cutting masks technique; the 180° line still flips a performer's direction; and Astaire's rule — either the camera dances or the performer does — means one mover per moment. And the fallback that keeps it all honest: any sequence that passes the legality check is performable in one take, so coverage buys options; it never rescues a join that was illegal.

docs.title: One phrase, through the chain
docs.text:
An eight-count phrase, start to finish:

  1. Gamut. Units drawn from the vocabulary — a travel, a reach to apex, a turn, a pass through neutral, a hold — each with its signature; the turn and the hold chosen partly because they are edit licenses.
  2. Sequence and check. The sequencer orders them; the legality graph confirms the chain — facing relative, momentum honored, the weight transfer into the turn complete. The transition into the reach starts on count six of the previous unit, as transitions do.
  3. Gate. Of several candidate chains, a person picks the one that reads as necessary, and confirms a body could do it in the space.
  4. Motion. A dancer performs it and is captured (GVHMR from the footage, or a two-webcam FreeMocap rig) — or a generator proposes it over the same units; either way it's cleaned: contact pinned, a prior for the jitter, physics if the floor is involved.
  5. Skeleton and keyframes. The cleaned motion becomes a DWPose control track composited onto grey inside a binary envelope mask; the background plate repeats outside it, pinned. One interior keyframe at the reach's apex forbids the shortcut. Three stills — opening, apex, close — agree on light, depth of field, and the planted foot.
  6. Render. VACE-Fun, 81 frames, a static shot stated in the prompt and the prompt spent on the motion arriving at the apex; motion settings identical between the iteration pass and the final; steps raised at finals to scrub the skeleton ghost.
  7. Frame and cut. The phrase exists at wide and at mid, so the travel reads in one and the reach in the other; the edit cuts on the turn into the mid shot, holds through the stillness, and — because the phrase closes its loop — can repeat it under the chorus.

Every stage in that walk is one of this part's chapters, and every budget is spent in view.

docs.title: What this part leaves open
docs.text:
The pipeline is complete from gamut to frame, but the frame isn't finished: the dancer wears something, stands somewhere, is lit somehow, and moves to music. Those are Parts VI and IV, and the plausible-body rubric is the only piece of them the pipeline already holds. The synthetic dancer, in other words, now has a body, a vocabulary, a system, and a camera — and is waiting on a costume, a stage, and a score.

Field notes

This chapter renders theory-shot-size-selects-movement-scale and theory-edit-affordances-in-the-material (the composing-for-camera pair) and wan22-vace-character-motion-control (keyframe-first, control-track-second), and synthesizes the rest of Parts II, V, and VII.

docs.title: The plausible body
docs.text:
Every synthetic dancer is graded against a rubric the audience never writes down: the physics and anatomy of actual bodies, which every viewer has carried since learning to walk. The captured-body chapter showed the repair machinery — priors, simulation — that pulls generated motion back toward that rubric. This chapter writes the rubric out, because you cannot evaluate, prompt, or gate for plausibility without knowing what plausibility consists of, and because the list turns out to double as a design tool: it's the set of things a body does that a skeleton-in-a-video-model has no idea about.

The reader of Part II will notice that most of what follows is the state that the gamut chapter insisted on typing — support, balance, momentum, weight — now stated as physics rather than as annotation.

docs.title: The body is an instrument with ranges
docs.text:
Joints move within ranges, and trained dancers extend those ranges without abolishing them. The specific numbers matter less than the shape of the constraint:

  • Every joint has a range of motion, and ranges couple: hip flexion with a straight knee is limited by the hamstrings, so a high leg in front costs differently from one to the side; turnout is external hip rotation, trained far past the untrained default but still bounded, and faked below the hip (at the knee) exactly the way audiences can see.
  • The spine is segmented, not a hinge: flexion, extension, lateral bend, and rotation distribute across vertebrae, which is why a contraction in Graham technique reads as a wave and a rendered torso that bends at one point reads as a cardboard box.
  • Shoulders float — the shoulder girdle moves on the ribcage before the arm moves in the socket, so a real reach starts in the back; a reach that starts at the elbow is a puppet's.
  • Proportion is identity. Anthropometric ranges are narrow, and the eye is exquisitely tuned to them — limb-length ratios, head size, hand size. Retargeting captured motion onto a differently proportioned figure shifts contact timing (the capture chapter's warning), and a video model asked to animate a stylized figure with a realistically proportioned skeleton is being asked to resolve exactly this conflict.

docs.title: Balance: the center over the base
docs.text:
A standing body is a controlled fall. Its center of mass must stay above its base of support — the footprint, or whatever is touching the floor — or it must be moving in a way that will bring a new base under it in time. Everything choreographic about weight lives here:

  • Weight transfer is the fundamental act, and incomplete weight transfer — a step that never fully commits — is the named root cause of most transition failures in pedagogy and of most "floaty" synthetic movement. A body mid-transfer is off-balance by definition, and the next movement must resolve that or the body falls.
  • Suspension (Humphrey's arc) is the instant at the top of a rise where vertical velocity is zero and the body hangs; it is legible precisely because it is brief and physically specific — hold it a frame too long and it reads as levitation.
  • Off-balance is a state, not an error. Falls, tilts, leans are material — but they write a debt (momentum, a shifted center) that a subsequent movement must pay. A generated body that leans without consequence is the uncanniest thing it can do.

docs.title: Momentum: the air is not negotiable
docs.text:
Once the feet leave the floor, nothing about the trajectory of the center of mass can change — only the shape of the body around it. This single fact governs every jump and most turns:

  • Flight time is set at takeoff. A vertical jump of thirty centimeters is airborne for roughly half a second; no rendered dancer should hang for two. Apex height and flight time are locked together by gravity, and the eye knows the curve.
  • Angular momentum is conserved in the air: a turning jump speeds up when limbs pull in and slows as they open — which is also how a pirouette is controlled on the ground, through a pivot that adds friction torque. Spotting — the whip of the head — exists to manage perception, and its absence in a generated turn is legible even to viewers who couldn't name it.
  • Acceleration has a cost. Muscles produce bounded force, so sudden movements have ramp shapes: a "punch" (in the effort vocabulary) is a ballistic launch and then a deceleration, never a constant-velocity slide. Uniform easing — constant speed between poses — is a named pathology of interpolation precisely because no real limb moves that way.

docs.title: Contact and friction
docs.text:
Feet on floors obey friction. A foot that is bearing weight does not translate; a foot that translates is not bearing weight — and the moment a rendered foot does both, the viewer sees foot-skate, the signature artifact of synthetic motion and the thing an entire tier of cleanup machinery exists to fix. Beyond feet:

  • Contact is bidirectional. A hand on a floor, a partner, or a prop supports weight and changes what the rest of the body may do; two bodies in contact share a balance problem.
  • Ground reaction shapes the body. Landing from a jump flexes knees and hips in proportion to the height fallen; a body that lands stiff either broke or is weightless.
  • The floor is a surface with a height. Floorwork — rolls, slides, inversions — is the region where capture, priors, and generators fail most, and the plausibility test is simple and brutal: which parts of the body are the floor holding up right now, and does the movement honor that?

docs.title: The eye reads bodies from almost nothing
docs.text:
Here is the finding that should reorganize how you think about fidelity. In 1973, Gunnar Johansson attached small lights to the joints of walkers and filmed them in the dark: from a dozen moving dots and nothing else, viewers instantly perceived a walking person — and, in the studies that followed, could read gender, mood, effort, even identity of a friend, from the dots alone.1 Biological motion perception is a dedicated, fast, exquisitely sensitive system, and it works on skeleton dynamics, not on appearance.

Two consequences for anyone rendering a dancer:

  • The skeleton carries the performance. A DWPose stick figure already contains most of what a viewer will feel about the movement; a beautifully rendered body on a wrong skeleton is a beautifully rendered wrong. Spend the fidelity budget on motion before pixels.
  • Dynamics, not poses. Johansson's dots are meaningless as stills. Timing, acceleration shape, the lag of a limb behind the torso — that is what the system reads, and it is exactly what interpolators get wrong while getting every individual frame right.

docs.title: Secondary motion and the breathing of stillness
docs.text: Real bodies are never still, and nothing attached to them moves in sync. Hair, cloth, and soft tissue lag — they arrive a beat after the skeleton and overshoot. A held pose breathes: the ribcage moves, weight shifts between feet in slow sway, the head makes small corrective motions. Animation codified this generations ago as follow-through and moving holds; generated video gets it for free when it gets it at all, and its absence is the "frozen" look — a pose that stopped instead of a body that paused. The rendering chapter returns to this when it discusses what a video model does with a held frame.

docs.title: The checklist
docs.text:
Everything above, as the rubric it really is — the list to score a generated dancer against, by eye or by machine:

  • Support — which surfaces bear weight right now, and does the movement honor that?
  • Weight transfer — committed or incomplete? (Incomplete is the first suspect.)
  • Balance — center over base, or moving toward a new base in time?
  • Momentum — does the airborne trajectory obey gravity? Do turns conserve spin?
  • Acceleration shape — ballistic ramps, not constant-velocity slides.
  • Contact — planted feet stay planted; landings flex; hands that touch, hold.
  • Joint ranges — nothing beyond the envelope, and nothing faked below it.
  • Proportion — stable, human, and consistent with the motion's timing.
  • Skeleton first — would this read as a person as Johansson dots?
  • Secondary motion and breath — does stillness still live?

The captured-body chapter's three repair tiers map onto this list almost item for item — geometric patches for contact, learned priors for ranges and proportion, physics for balance and momentum — which is the real argument for knowing the rubric: it tells you which machinery to reach for when a dancer looks wrong, and, better, what to ask of the generator so it looks right the first time.

Field notes

No commons notes rendered directly — biomechanics and perception from general knowledge, per the sourcing policy; the rubric is the human-facing face of the state fields in structure-typed-composable-primitives / structure-transition-legality-graph and the repair tiers of ml-physics-and-priors-motion-cleanup.

  1. Gunnar Johansson, "Visual perception of biological motion and a model for its analysis," Perception & Psychophysics 1973 — the point-light walker; the later gender/identity results (Kozlowski & Cutting, 1977; Cutting & Kozlowski, 1977) are the classic follow-ups. ↩

docs.title: Rendering the dancer
docs.text:
Everything upstream — a gamut, a sequence, a gate, a captured or generated skeleton, a cleaned trajectory — becomes visible in exactly one place: the render. This chapter is about that last stage as it actually behaves in mid-2026, using the open-weights stack a working pipeline most plausibly runs on — WAN 2.2 and its VACE control branch — as the worked case. The particulars are WAN's; the structural lessons (motion is a budget, conditioning beats tuning, the preview must match the final) are not.

A fair warning about this chapter's texture: it is the most hands-on in the subject, because the commons learned most of this at the bench, and the bench is where details earn their keep. The numbers here are kept on purpose.

docs.title: The stack, and which checkpoint you're really choosing
docs.text:
WAN 2.2 remains the open-weights ceiling as of August 2026 (aggregator sites claiming "Wan 2.7" or "3.0" are fabricating; the official Hugging Face org is the only source of truth). It ships in shapes that matter:

  • TI2V-5B — dense, text- and image-conditioned in one checkpoint, runs a five-second 720p clip on an 8 GB-class card. Iterate here; practitioners report it gets ~90% of composition right.
  • A14B — a mixture-of-experts (two experts, ~14B active per step) needing a 24 GB card at 720p; separate, non-interchangeable T2V and I2V checkpoints. Finish here.
  • The Fun branch — task-specialized A14B checkpoints: -InP (start/end frames), -Control (canny/depth/pose/MLSD + trajectory), -Control-Camera (camera codes), and VACE-Fun, which unions the first two with reference images — and explicitly not camera control.

That last fact is a structural choice, not a footnote: picking a checkpoint picks which controls you may combine in one generation. For character-driven work you stay on VACE-Fun and buy camera moves another way (below); true camera codes cost you the reference and endpoint conditioning a dancer's identity depends on.

docs.title: One protocol under every VACE trick
docs.text:
VACE looks like a pile of features — first/last frame, inpaint, outpaint, pose-drive, reference injection. It is one conditioning protocol, and knowing it is worth more than knowing the recipes:

  • control_video — a full-length frame sequence carrying what you already know. Grey (127 / 0.5) is the literal zero of the control signal — the node subtracts 0.5 from every frame — so grey means "nothing specified, generate from prompt and references." Real pixels pin a frame's appearance; preprocessed frames (pose skeletons, depth, edges) pin structure.
  • control_masks — where control may act: white = regenerate, black = preserve. One mask frame broadcasts; a sequence lets the editable region move over time.
  • reference_image — VAE-encoded and prepended to the control latents (hence the trim_latent output you must honor downstream).
  • strength — how literally to obey, independent of LoRA weights; the first dial to lower when control fights identity.

Hard constraints: dimensions divisible by 16, frame counts of the form 4n+1 (81, 97, 121). Once the protocol is clear, the "features" collapse: first/last-frame is real pixels at frames 0 and N with grey between; keyframing is the same at any indices; outpainting is grey beyond the original frame with the mask white there; pose-driving is skeletons all the way through. You aren't choosing a mode — you're choosing what to paint and what to leave grey.

docs.title: Keyframes: the acting lives in the stills
docs.text:
With first/last-frame conditioning, both stills are enforced as ground truth inside the diffusion — genuine generative in-betweening, not optical-flow interpolation — and the model treats every difference between the two frames as something to explain with motion. Mismatched key light becomes an invented lighting change; mismatched depth of field an invented focus pull; a wide first frame and a tight last frame an invented camera move. So the craft is upstream: make the pair agree on everything except the intended motion.

And because the model has no notion of intent, only correspondence, the keyframes carry the acting. Classic posing craft exists to make a single drawing unambiguous, and that is all the model has. The checklist for a generated pair:

  • Match key-light angle and depth of field/framing explicitly between the stills.
  • Anchor contact points identically — a planted foot sits in the same place in both frames unless it is meant to travel.
  • Pose the eyeline in both; gaze is content the model can only interpolate, never infer.
  • Prompt the arrival, not just the departure — the model prioritizes prompt coherence and will otherwise ignore your endpoint.

Then the ceiling: keyframe pose distance has a plausibility limit, past which interpolation morphs. In-betweeners take the shortest path through pixel space; articulated, non-rigid motion — limbs, running, a dancer — breaks first; far-apart poses morph rather than move. (In the latent-space chapter's terms, a straight line between two valid frames cuts through invalid space, and morphing is what leaving the manifold looks like.) The working rules: one clear beat per generation, within three to five seconds (81 frames ≈ 3 s, 121 ≈ 5 s); prompt the easing explicitly, because constant-velocity easing reads as robotic; separate camera motion from character motion.

The highest-leverage move, though, is the generalization: VACE pins keyframes at any index — grey everywhere, real frames where you want them, mask black there — and an interior keyframe doesn't merely add control, it geometrically forbids the shortcut, because the cheap path no longer satisfies the constraints. One pin at the apex of a beat — the top of a reach, the extreme of a turn — converts the distance ceiling from a cap into a budget: two hops of forty percent instead of one of eighty. Costs: each keyframe is another still that must agree with its neighbors (the mismatch rule applies to each gap independently), and more pins leave less room for the model to invent the connective motion you actually wanted.

Keyframes beat chaining for the same span. A single long shot is made by seeding clip N+1 with clip N's last frame — extracted before VAE decode, never from the compressed video — but nothing crosses the seam: no velocity, no momentum; generators decelerate toward their own last frame, so naive joins stutter; and drift (color, lighting, identity) is directional and compounds, because each segment builds on the previous output, not the original reference. Keyframes inside one generation carry momentum across the pins. When you must chain: describe continuous low-magnitude motion across the seam, trim the deceleration tail, re-ground on the original reference periodically — or cut instead, which resets drift for free.

docs.title: The motion budget is a number
docs.text:
WAN 2.2's two experts are not halves of one thing. The high-noise expert runs the early steps and decides composition and motion; the low-noise expert refines detail. The handoff is by signal-to-noise, not step index — a trained boundary at sigma 0.875 (T2V) or 0.900 (I2V) — so shift plus total steps decide how many steps land above the boundary: your literal motion budget. The ComfyUI default template (shift 8, 20 steps) splits 10/10; the popular 4-step accelerated recipe splits 2/2 — all of a clip's motion planned in two sampling steps.

That is the mechanism behind the best-known complaint about the lightx2v speed LoRAs: they cut render time ~5× and measurably flatten motion and camera movement (maintainer-acknowledged; the model card claims otherwise — trust the issue tracker). Community mitigations are starting points, not settled numbers: asymmetric strength (~0.6–0.8 on the high-noise expert, 1.0 low), eight steps split 4+4, real CFG (~2–3.5) on the high pass only. And one project rule falls out with force: the preview must share the final's motion settings — LoRA strengths, steps, shift, CFG — or every motion judgment you made while iterating was made on a different film. Either bench with final settings, or accept that previews tell you about framing and identity and nothing about motion.

docs.title: Prompt for change, not appearance
docs.text:
WAN was trained against cinematically labelled data, so film vocabulary is a real control surface. In an image-conditioned pipeline the stills already carry subject, costume, palette, and set — spend the prompt on what changes: motion and camera. The vocabulary it answers to:

  • Moves — dolly in, pan left/right, tilt, pull back, tracking, arc, crane, handheld.
  • Lock — "static shot" / "fixed shot." Say it. Omitting camera language does not yield a locked camera; it yields an unconstrained one, and drift toward invented movement is the default.
  • Shot sizes, angles, lenses — the standard film lexicon, all of it live.
  • Speed and direction verbs — "slowly, toward camera" beats generic action words; staged phrasing ("begins with minimal movement, gradually increases") works.
  • Selective locking — "face and eyes remain still, only hair moves."

Source hygiene matters here: the SEO layer around WAN fabricates parameters — a "motion guidance strength" dial, CFG 7.0–7.5 recommendations — that correspond to no real node input. If advice doesn't name an actual node field, it's invented.

docs.title: The background and the dancer draw on one budget
docs.text:
Background drift — the set slowly sliding, warping, swimming under a nominally locked camera — is structural, not a tuning failure: the model has no 3D awareness, so "the camera moved" and "the world changed shape" explain the same pixels, and it picks either. It compounds with length (regularly past ~8 s). And the tension to internalize: there is no separate subject-motion and background-motion control. Every knob that buys a livelier dancer — more high-noise steps, higher shift, lower speed-LoRA strength — buys it for the whole frame. Fix a listless dancer and you've given the wall permission to breathe. Prompt patches bias the split; they don't partition it.

So decouple by conditioning, not tuning. The objection "my subject is dancing, I can't mask it" assumes the mask must trace the subject. It doesn't: make the control video your background plate repeated every frame, and the mask black everywhere except one generous white region containing the subject's whole range of motion. You are reserving territory, not cutting a silhouette — authored once per camera setup, reused across every clip that shares the framing. Everything outside the envelope is real pixels and cannot drift; inside it, push motion as hard as the shot wants. Costs: the subject can't leave the region; include the floor-contact zone; and a pinned plate forbids a camera move by construction.

When that envelope also carries a pose skeleton inside it — the combination a dancing character actually needs — one more rule, learned the hard way: a pose patch must sit on grey, not its native black. Black isn't background in a control video; it's a strong instruction meaning dark content here. Full-frame pose videos get away with black because the whole frame reads as one modality; a mixed control video doesn't, and the symptom is unmistakable — a crisp dark frame tracing the envelope boundary. Re-composite the skeleton onto grey 127, and keep the envelope mask binary — a feathered edge is half-specified dark content at half-preservation weight, rendered as a soft dark ring. Residual skeleton hues can still ghost onto the subject (teal torso lines on white fabric; the skeleton's pink eye dots as makeup); what works is CFG ~3 on the high-noise pass plus negatives naming the artifacts, and more denoising steps at finals — safe here because the pose rail specifies motion externally. What does not work: dimming the lines toward grey (tracking degrades before ghosting disappears) and desaturating the palette (hue encodes limb identity on a near-symmetric skeleton — you buy left/right errors, not cleanliness).

docs.title: Sparse control over dense; keyframe before control track
docs.text:
VACE-Fun accepts canny, depth, pose, MLSD, and trajectory control in the same checkpoint as reference images and endpoints. They are not equivalent for a stylized dancer:

  • Pose (DWPose skeleton) — sparse; transfers timing and articulation only. The driving source can be phone video of yourself, or a posed rig. The risk is proportion: an adult skeleton drives adult proportions and timing onto whatever figure you're rendering.
  • Depth / canny / MLSD — dense; they transfer the driving footage's shapes, rendering, and volume — actively harmful when the look is chosen to be forgiving of noise.
  • Trajectory — the lightest contract: where a thing goes without dictating how the body gets there. Path constrained, articulation invented.

And the sequencing rule: keyframes pin where the body is; a control track governs how it gets between them. Reach for the keyframe first — it costs a still, not a performance — and add a control track only when the in-between is what's failing.

docs.title: The camera, by rungs
docs.text: Seven mechanisms, ordered by determinism and integration cost: prompt words; the move encoded in the keyframe geometry; VACE canvas/outpaint; community camera LoRAs (Wan 2.1-era); the Control-Camera checkpoint's actual presets; trajectory instructions; 3D-grounded re-rendering. The highest value per effort is rung two, and it's an inversion of a hazard: a framing delta between the two stills is an invented camera move when accidental and a deterministic one when constructed — generate the still with headroom, derive the end frame as a tighter or shifted crop, and the push or pan is arithmetic rather than obedience. The limit is parallax: these are 2D moves. And the checkpoint split above means rung five is a model swap that surrenders reference conditioning — reserve it for shots with no identity burden.

docs.title: Identity: the LoRA, and the loss that lies
docs.text: A character LoRA for WAN wants 25–40 images across five-plus angles, three lightings, three expressions; a reported 12 GB recipe is rank 32, ~10 epochs, 512 px. Two traps: T2V and I2V LoRAs are not interchangeable — train on the checkpoint type you'll run; and training loss is pixel reconstruction, not identity — low loss does not mean the character looks right. Visual spot-checks every few epochs are the real gate.

docs.title: What the eye demands of the frames
docs.text: Finally, the perceptual floor any render must clear. Apparent motion is a cortical correspondence computation, not retinal persistence: small per-frame displacements relative to the moving shape read as smooth; past a threshold, a slower feature-tracking process takes over and motion reads as judder — so keep displacement small relative to the object, not just the frame rate high. Pin-sharp frames look stroboscopic at any rate; real motion blur is a shutter-angle property (the 180° convention), and generated footage that lacks it needs it added deliberately. Spinning material past half its repeat unit per frame aliases — the wagon-wheel effect — which is a live hazard for turns. These are the reasons a dancer can be perfectly posed in every frame and still look wrong in motion.

docs.title: Two routes, one choice
docs.text:
Everything above is the explicit route: motion first, then pixels, with a gate between and a skeleton you can inspect. The generation chapter introduced its alternative — Wan-Dancer and MACE-Dance generating dance video directly from music. Convenience and temporal coherence on one side; control, editability, and a choreographer's hand on the keyframes on the other. For a pipeline built on authored material and delegated continuity, the explicit route is native and the direct route is the benchmark to beat. How the whole chain assembles, end to end, is the last chapter of this part.

Field notes

This chapter renders eighteen commons notes from the WAN 2.2 / VACE bench work: vace-control-video-and-mask-protocol, vace-keyframes-at-arbitrary-positions, vace-mixed-control-pose-on-grey, vace-pin-background-with-motion-envelope-mask, wan22-flf2v-keyframe-conditioning, wan22-motion-lives-in-the-high-noise-expert, wan22-speed-lora-motion-tax, wan22-motion-prompt-vocabulary, wan22-clip-chaining-drift, wan22-variant-selection-2026, wan22-character-lora-training, wan22-vace-character-motion-control, wan22-camera-control-ladder, wan22-camera-move-encoded-in-the-keyframe-pair, background-drift-shares-the-motion-budget, anim-keyframe-distance-ceiling, anim-keyframes-carry-the-acting, and theory-motion-perception-for-visuals.

docs.title: Chance and rule-based choreography
docs.text:
In the early 1950s, Merce Cunningham began deciding parts of his dances by tossing coins. It remains one of the most misunderstood acts in twentieth-century art — misread then as abdication, misread now as a quaint precursor to "generative art." What Cunningham actually built, and what Trisha Brown, Lucinda Childs, Anna Halprin, and the Fluxus artists built after him, was a body of working generative systems with documented mechanisms, documented sizes, and documented failure modes — a seventy-year experimental record on exactly the question every generative practitioner faces: which decisions do you keep, and which do you hand to the system?

The record has a shape. Learn the shape and you can skip a decade of rediscovering it.

docs.title: Cunningham: chance decides continuity, never material
docs.text:
Cunningham's procedure, developed with John Cage and stabilized by Suite by Chance (1953), ran on charts. Before any randomness entered, he composed charts of movement material by hand — one chart of phrases, and separate charts for the questions he was willing to let chance answer: sequence, duration, direction, which dancer, how many. Then coin tosses (later hexagrams from the I Ching, later dice and card draws) indexed into the charts.1

The division of labor is the whole point, and Cunningham stated both halves in the same breath. The famous axiom — "it is possible for anything to follow anything else" — is remembered; the constraint that made it work is not: the charts, he was explicit, were not made by chance. The movement in each cell was chosen. Chance was permitted to decide continuity — order, duration, spacing, assignment — and was never once, in the entire half-century record, permitted to invent material.

The mature works show the system at scale. Torse (1976) draws its title from its method: sixty-four phrases — the I Ching's number, which became his default gamut size — expanded from five torso positions, with hexagram draws determining sequence and spatial distribution. Canfield (1969) dealt its structure from the card game of the same name, fifty-two motions for fifty-two cards. The numbers matter, and here is the first structural regularity of the whole tradition: every gamut in the record is counted in dozens. Three phrases and one operator in Brown's Solo Olos. Twenty-seven points in Locus. Thirty movements in Primary Accumulation. Sixty-four in Torse. Hundreds is not a bigger version of this — it is a different and worse thing. When Forsythe once built a 135-item alphabet for a single solo, keeping it usable required the kinesphere itself as a memory palace.

docs.title: The systems generation: Brown, Childs, Halprin, Fluxus
docs.text:
The choreographers who came out of Judson Dance Theater in the 1960s kept Cunningham's architecture and swapped the stochastic layer for deterministic rules — and in doing so demonstrated that the architecture never depended on randomness at all.

Trisha Brown made the rule itself the dance. Accumulation (1971): perform gesture 1; then 1, 2; then 1, 2, 3 — an additive list executed with the patience of a proof. Locus (1975) encoded a paragraph of autobiography as numbers (A=1 … Z=26) mapped onto twenty-seven points of an imaginary cube around her body; the text drove which point she gestured toward. Same two layers as Cunningham — a small authored gamut, a mechanical sequencer — but the sequencer is a readable algorithm rather than a coin.2

Lucinda Childs fixed nearly everything and permuted the little that remained. Calico Mingling (1973): forty six-count phrases over a vocabulary of essentially one step, walked through path permutations across four dancers — canon, phase, interference, the Steve Reich move performed by bodies (and a decade before she and Reich shared a stage with Einstein on the Beach's creative orbit).

Anna Halprin, on the West Coast and a generation earlier than Judson (she taught several of its founders on her outdoor deck), contributed the meta-system. The RSVP Cycles, formalized with her husband, landscape architect Lawrence Halprin: Resources (the material available), Scores (instructions of deliberately chosen openness), Valuaction (a scheduled stage for judging what the score produced), Performance — then cycle.3 Two ideas here outlived the acronym: that a score's openness is a dial — Halprin placed every score explicitly on an open↔closed continuum — and that evaluation is a named, scheduled stage of the system rather than something that happens ambiently. The next chapter builds its human gate directly on that second idea.

Fluxus supplied the limit case of openness. George Brecht's event scores — cards from the Water Yam box, often one line ("Drip Music: a source of dripping water and an empty vessel are arranged so that the water falls into the vessel") — are scores pared to almost pure frame, to be realized "publicly, privately, or negatively." Movement-prompt decks in use today (fifty-six to seventy cards is the standard range) are this idea, commercialized.

docs.title: The architecture all of it shares
docs.text:
Line the systems up and one architecture appears in every single one:

A gamut — a finite, named, human-authored set of units — plus a sequencer that decides only continuity: order, duration, tempo, placement, facing, assignment, density, entrances and exits.

Three design decisions, made separately, define every system in the record:

1. The unit list, by hand. Crisp boundaries, each unit masterable in isolation, none requiring a particular predecessor. (How to build that list well is the gamut chapter.)

2. Exactly which dimensions the sequencer owns — enumerated in advance. This is the deepest lesson, and the least obvious. Cunningham pre-wrote, per work, the list of questions chance would be asked; the list varied, and the variance was the composition. And every strong system randomizes few dimensions and fixes the rest: Cunningham fixed the units, freed continuity; Brown fixed the sequence rule, freed body-part choice; Childs fixed everything but the path permutation; Halprin fixed the frame, freed everything inside it. Each dimension handed over multiplies unfamiliarity — when Cunningham stacked independent draws per body part, the resulting material was, in his own account, nearly impossible, and cost months of rehearsal to weld. Free every dimension and you haven't built a more generative system — you've built improvisation. That isn't a sneer: the Grand Union (the improvisational collective that emerged when Judson veterans loosened every constraint at once) is the documented instance of the transition, and the point at which the practice stops being composition in any repeatable sense.

3. When the draw happens. At authoring time, frozen thereafter — Cunningham's default: chance composed the piece, then the piece was rehearsed and toured as fixed repertory. Or live at showtime — his Field Dances gave dancers in-performance choices, and that is a different genre with different failure modes, not a braver version of the same one.

The claim underneath all three, and the tradition's central finding: a generator's leverage comes from the separation, not from the randomness. Chance, rule, algorithm, model — the sequencer technology changed four times across the record, and it never much mattered. What mattered was that material stayed authored, small, and bounded while continuity stayed free.

docs.title: Can the audience read the rule?
docs.text:
Set two of these systems side by side and a second design axis appears. Watch Accumulation for sixty seconds and you get it — the additive rule becomes legible, and from then on you're watching two things at once: the movement, and a composition materializing in real time (plus a third: the performer's visible labor of memory). Watch a Cunningham chance sequence and no amount of attention reveals a rule, because the generating structure is statistical — what observers report instead is strangeness: sequences that feel, in a way audiences struggled to articulate, inevitable rather than arbitrary, freed as they are from a choreographer's habits of what should follow what. And Yvonne Rainer's Trio A (1966) is the tradition's control experiment: a dance built to refuse every compositional recursion at once — no repetition, no accumulation, no climax, deliberately uniform dynamics — and with it, the audience's perceived structure drops to zero, on purpose.4

So: rule legibility is a per-section design decision, independent of quality. A legible rule buys a second layer of audience attention — disproportionately valuable when the surface is thin (one dancer, one voice, one instrument, one screen). An opaque rule buys inevitability and strangeness, and asks the surface to carry all the interest itself. Make the choice by default and generative work reads as arbitrary; that's usually the actual diagnosis behind the complaint.

The legible mechanisms, usefully, are the cheap ones — additive and subtractive lists, retrograde, rotation, phase, exhaustive permutation of a tiny lexicon. And the tradition's answer to their predictability is not added noise, which destroys readability immediately, but layering a second legible system: Accumulation with Talking runs two accumulations and two spoken stories simultaneously; the group Accumulation phase-shifts one material across four bodies. Two readable rules interfere; interference is interesting; readability survives.

docs.title: Scores that are deliberately incomplete
docs.text:
There's a third lever, subtler than the other two, that this tradition pulls constantly: emit an unfinished instruction, and let the performer finish it.

Brecht's one-line cards are the pure case, but the move is everywhere. Laban's own Motif Notation — the stripped-down cousin of Labanotation, using Guest's Movement Alphabet — exists precisely to record only the leading intention ("travel, then turn, ending enclosed") and leave every other dimension free: a score that is literally a program with free variables. The contemporary systems make the purpose explicit. Scuddle (2011) evolves "movement catalysts" — a body position, a height level, effort qualities, and deliberately no path between them — scored by Laban-derived heuristics, with the stated goal of breaking the choreographer's habits. Kate Sicchio's Terpsicode projects keyframes and leaves the dancer to tween them.

Why this is the cheapest robust pattern in the whole toolkit: the three hardest problems in recombining movement — legal transitions, stylistic coherence, physical feasibility — are delegated in a single move to the one person who was going to execute the result anyway. Nothing else solves three problems with one decision.

But the record is equally clear about when it pays, and the conditions bite:

  • The axes you do specify must collide with habit. Under-specify along dimensions the performer is fluent in and they hand you their defaults back — novelty pressure has to land where the habits live, which is Scuddle's entire design.
  • Openness is a dial, set per section — Halprin's continuum, or Nancy Stark Smith's Underscore (the contact-improvisation frame), which sets the dial differently in each of its twenty-plus named phases.
  • It trades machine control for human competence. The pattern needs a performer whose completion beats your rule. With no performer in the loop — a fully synthetic pipeline — this lever mostly isn't available, and everything it delegated comes back on the system's plate.

docs.title: Old news, in the best way
docs.text:
One closing reframe. This chapter's architecture — a fixed, checkable frame; a free, skilled realization inside it — is not a 1950s invention. It is how much of the world's music has always specified itself: a jazz standard's changes against the solo, a raga's grammar against the alap, flamenco's compás against the cante, a dub riddim against its versions. Traditions discovered again and again that you don't specify the piece — you specify a space of performances, as a constraint system plus a convention for filling it. Cunningham's charts and Halprin's scores are dance finding the same split, and stating it unusually plainly.

Which is encouraging, if you're building such a system: you are not imitating a mid-century avant-garde experiment. You are implementing one of the oldest architectures in performance — with, for the first time, a sequencer that can check its own work. How it checks is the next chapter.

Field notes

This chapter renders the commons notes structure-gamut-plus-sequencer (the two-layer finding, gamut sizes, dimension discipline, draw timing), structure-legible-rule-as-content (legibility as a per-section axis; Trio A as control; layering legible systems), interaction-deliberate-under-specification (Scuddle/Terpsicode/Motif; the three delegated problems; the paying conditions), theory-open-form-improvisation-frameworks (frame vs realization across musical traditions), and theory-variation-development-strategies (variation as distinct mechanisms — the operator-catalog connection).

  1. The primary scholarship this account leans on is Carrie Noland's Coping and Choreography, which reconstructs the chart procedures from Cunningham's notes and Remy Charlip's and Carolyn Brown's first-hand accounts. ↩

  2. Brown's own gloss on this period of her work: "choreography as a system that makes dance happen" — she considered the three system families (accumulations, mathematical procedures, and equipment pieces) distinct instruments. ↩

  3. Lawrence & Anna Halprin, The RSVP Cycles: Creative Processes in the Human Environment (1969) — written as a general theory of scoring for any collaborative process; dance was its proving ground. ↩

  4. Rainer's accompanying "No Manifesto" (1965) — "No to spectacle no to virtuosity…" — is the position paper; Trio A is its executable. ↩

docs.title: Computational choreography: a history
docs.text: title: Computational choreography: a history summary: Thirty-five years of choreographers composing with computers — LifeForms to AISOMA — and the five patterns that held the whole way through. covers: - ml-aisoma-living-archive-lineage - interaction-proposal-fidelity-imitate-vs-interpret

docs.title: Computational choreography: a history
docs.text: The chance chapter made a claim worth testing against the record: the sequencer technology — coin, rule, algorithm, model — changed repeatedly across seventy years and never much mattered, because the leverage was always in the separation of authored material from delegated continuity. This chapter is the test. It follows choreographers into the computer, from the first keyframed stick figure in 1989 to a public AI tool trained on one man's archive in 2025, and asks what actually changed each time the tools did.

docs.title: 1989: the stick figure enters the studio
docs.text:
The computer arrived in choreography as a drawing tool. LifeForms — developed at Simon Fraser University through the late 1980s by Tom Calvert's group with dancer-technologist Thecla Schiphorst, later commercialized (and later still renamed DanceForms) — let a user pose and keyframe an articulated figure and play the result back.1 Its famous adopter was Merce Cunningham, then seventy, who took it up in 1989 and premiered the first dance composed with it, Trackers, in 1991. He kept composing with it for the rest of his life.

Two things about LifeForms matter more than its feature list. First, it gave Cunningham a proposal medium that suited his system exactly: a figure that could be asked to do anything, with no opinion about whether a body could. Sequences the software rendered happily turned out to be impossible on dancers and had to be re-solved in rehearsal — the architecture chapter's point that a convincing preview defers the feasibility check rather than performing it. Second, and more consequential: the software's avatar was divided into fourteen sections you keyframed independently, which made per-limb layering the cheapest operation in the tool — and critics can date Cunningham's work of that era on sight by its angular arm material running in counter-rhythm to the legs. Nobody chose that style. The tool's easy path became the house idiom over a decade of work. It is the cleanest documented case of an affordance leaking into art, and every later tool in this chapter is implicated by it.

docs.title: 1999–2001: the captured body as decor
docs.text: The next move was capture, not composition. For Biped (1999), Cunningham had his dancers motion-captured and the data handed to Paul Kaiser and Shelley Eshkar — the digital artists who would become OpenEndedGroup — who rendered it as hand-drawn figures projected on a scrim in front of the live dancers: the captured body as a second, ghostly cast.2 Loops (2001) went further inward — motion-capturing only Cunningham's hands performing his 1971 solo of that name, then rendering the data as abstract drawn forms. The compositional system was untouched; what computation added was a new kind of performer — one made of data — and a question that hasn't closed since: what does a captured dance look like when you stop rendering it as a person?

docs.title: 1994–2013: Forsythe makes the thinking visible
docs.text:
William Forsythe's digital projects took a different road: not composition, not decor, but analysis rendered public. Improvisation Technologies began as an in-house training tool in 1994 and was published by ZKM in 1999 as a CD-ROM in which Forsythe, on video, draws his operations — lines, folds, extrusions — as white graphics over his own moving body.3 The gamut chapter treated those operations as an API; here they are an artifact — a choreographer externalizing his literacy so others can acquire it.

Synchronous Objects (2009), made with Ohio State's Advanced Computing Center for the Arts and Design, took one dance — One Flat Thing, reproduced — and generated a suite of data-visualizations from it: cueing networks, movement density, alignment annotations, the dance's "counterpoint" drawn as a system.4 And Motion Bank (2010–2013) extended the method to other choreographers, producing online scores for Deborah Hay, Jonathan Burrows and Matteo Fargion, Bebe Miller, and Thomas Hauert.5 Behind all of it sits Forsythe's essay Choreographic Objects (2008), whose central formulation is worth carrying around: a choreographic object is "a model of potential transition from one state to another" — which is to say, a choreographic idea detached from a body and made available to other media.6 That sentence licenses this entire subject.

docs.title: 2000s–2019: the machine proposes
docs.text:
The computer started proposing movement in earnest through OpenEndedGroup's long collaboration with Wayne McGregor. The Choreographic Language Agent, developed across the 2000s with his company, generated choreographic suggestions and — the design decision that survives every model change since — rendered them as animated points, lines, and planes rather than as an anatomical avatar, because dancers imitate a figure but must interpret a sketch. Fidelity of the proposal sets how much the human contributes: low fidelity for completion, high for selection.

The learning era followed quickly:

  • Scuddle (2011) — an evolutionary system generating deliberately pathless "movement catalysts" to break choreographers' habits (the under-specification lever of the chance chapter).
  • chor-rnn (2016) — a recurrent network trained on one choreographer's mocap, generating continuations in her style.
  • Beyond Imitation (2019) — Mariel Pettee's variational autoencoders as an improvisation partner, trained on her own movement.
  • Living Archive (2019) — McGregor with Google Arts & Culture: a model trained on twenty-five years of the company's video, visualized as a navigable map of his movement, proposing continuations from a dancer's pose; the dancers selected.7

In parallel, an academic track built the datasets and models for music-to-dance generation — AIST++ (2021) as the benchmark corpus, Bailando (2022) with its learned choreographic memory, EDGE (2023) with diffusion — the work the discovery chapter and Part VII examine in depth. The two tracks barely cite each other and are solving the same problem: the artist's track wants a collaborator, the research track wants a benchmark score, and both keep building a codebook plus a sequencer.

docs.title: 2025: the gate goes public
docs.text:
The most recent move is the second generation of McGregor's collaboration. AISOMA (2025) rebuilt Living Archive on better capture — nearly four million poses extracted from hundreds of archive videos, now in 3D rather than 2D — and changed the interface: a user dances a short phrase at their device's camera, and the system extends it with original phrases in McGregor's vocabulary.8 McGregor used it privately first, to "expand, challenge, and interrogate" existing sequences; then it was released publicly alongside Wayne McGregor: Infinite Bodies at Somerset House (October 2025 – February 2026), so that anyone could co-create with the archive of one choreographer. Dancers who use it describe the output as stimulus to interpret, not steps to copy — the Choreographic Language Agent's lesson, now at consumer scale.

The 2019-to-2025 delta is the telling thing. The compositional idea didn't change at all: propose from a corpus, human selects. What changed was capture quality — two dimensions to three — and who sits at the gate: a public tool makes every user their own valuaction stage.

docs.title: The five patterns
docs.text:
Thirty-five years, a dozen systems, and the record is consistent enough to state as rules:

  • The material stayed authored. LifeForms keyframed Cunningham's choices; chor-rnn, Pettee, Living Archive, AISOMA all learned from one artist's corpus. Computation never once supplied material from nowhere; the corpus is the gamut.
  • The human gate never left. Cunningham refined LifeForms output in rehearsal; McGregor's dancers select from proposals; AISOMA's users interpret. Every system that produced kept work has a person choosing.
  • Proposal rendering is a design decision. Points and lines when you want interpretation; a realistic figure when you want selection. OpenEndedGroup understood this in the 2000s and nobody has improved on the principle.
  • Affordances leak into style. LifeForms' fourteen sections became a decade of counter-rhythm arms. Audit the easy path of any tool as an aesthetic choice.
  • The real progress has been capture. From hand-keyframed figures, to mocap as decor, to learned archives in 2D, to learned archives in 3D: each leap in what could be recorded changed what could be proposed. The compositional architecture has been stable since 1953.

Which is exactly what the chance chapter predicted, and why the latent-spaces chapter could check that architecture against the continuous world and find it intact. The computers changed everything about the studio and nothing about the split. Part VII takes up the capture story where the progress actually is.

Field notes

This chapter renders ml-aisoma-living-archive-lineage (researched 2026-08-18) and interaction-proposal-fidelity-imitate-vs-interpret (the CLA and LifeForms findings); the rest is documented history written from general knowledge.

  1. Thecla Schiphorst's SFU master's thesis documents LifeForms' design and Cunningham's adoption; the software lives on as DanceForms (Credo Interactive). ↩

  2. Biped (1999): choreography Cunningham, music Gavin Bryars, digital decor Paul Kaiser & Shelley Eshkar (Riverbed, later OpenEndedGroup). ↩

  3. William Forsythe, Improvisation Technologies: A Tool for the Analytical Dance Eye (ZKM, 1999). ↩

  4. Synchronous Objects — Forsythe with Norah Zuniga Shaw and Maria Palazzi, OSU ACCAD (2009). ↩

  5. Motion Bank (2010–2013), a Forsythe Company research project; its online scores remain available. ↩

  6. William Forsythe, "Choreographic Objects" (2008), published on his website and widely anthologized. ↩

  7. Living Archive: Creating Choreography with Artificial Intelligence — Studio Wayne McGregor × Google Arts & Culture (2019). ↩

  8. Wayne McGregor's AISOMA (Google Arts & Culture, 2025); Google's announcement. ↩

docs.title: Locomotion without a choreographer
docs.text:
Every chapter in this part has had an author of motion somewhere in the loop. Cunningham's coins sequenced units he had made; Brown's rules ordered gestures she had chosen; the learned archives of the computational-choreography chapter proposed from a corpus a human had danced. This chapter drops the author. Its subject is motion that nobody writes — that falls out of a body, a physics, an objective, a rule — and the question of what such motion is good for when the body in question is a humanoid, and when it's something stranger.

Three reasons a dance library cares. Synthetic dancers will increasingly move by these methods, because capture and keyframing don't scale and priors only reproduce what was recorded. Non-human performers are already on stage — a quadruped robot with its own choreography tool, an industrial arm in a duet, wind-driven linkages on a beach. And it is the purest case of the commons' deepest motif: emergence, watched in a body.

docs.title: Seven places motion comes from
docs.text:
Each source below has a canonical exemplar and a lesson that travels. They aren't exclusive; modern systems stack them.

  • Mechanics alone. Tad McGeer's passive dynamic walkers (1990): an unpowered pair of legs, set on a gentle slope, walks down it with an eerily human gait — no motor, no controller, no program. The gait is a property of leg length, mass distribution, and gravity. Theo Jansen's Strandbeests are the art-world twin: twelve-bar linkages whose proportions — Jansen's "eleven holy numbers," found by evolutionary search on a home computer — turn wind into a walking foot-curve.1 The lesson has a name, morphological computation: put the motion in the body and the controller can shrink toward nothing.
  • Oscillators. Animals walk on central pattern generators — networks of coupled oscillators in the spinal cord that produce rhythmic motion without brain-level commands; the lamprey is the textbook case. Auke Ijspeert's salamander robot (2007) reproduced the trick: one drive signal, and the body switches from swimming to walking as the oscillator network changes mode.2 A gait, in this view, is a limit cycle, and its parameters are frequency, phase relationships, and amplitude — precisely the LFO-and-phase logic of a modular patch, applied to legs. Oscillator-plus-learning hybrids are current practice.
  • Evolution. Karl Sims's Evolved Virtual Creatures (1994) remains the founding image: block-bodied creatures whose morphology and neural controllers were co-evolved to swim, walk, jump, and follow — and which famously exploited bugs in the physics simulator when that was cheaper than walking.3 The line runs to Evolution Gym (2021), a benchmark for co-designing voxel soft robots in a mass-spring simulator fast enough to train in minutes, and on to 2026 work driving co-design with graph neural networks and continuous material stiffness (stiffer bodies evolve better land gaits; softer ones do better in water).4 But the sobering result is from 2025: brain-body co-optimization consistently fails to select for morphological potential — bodies lock in before their controllers can reveal what they could have done, and the search converges prematurely; novelty search yields far more diverse morphologies than fitness does.5 Read that as a rule: for emergence, diversity pressure beats fitness pressure.
  • Optimization. Igor Mordatch's contact-invariant optimization (2012): specify a goal and the physics, and a trajectory optimizer discovers gaits, climbing, getting up off the floor — with no motion data at all.6 The motion is the solution; the author wrote only the problem.
  • Objectives (reinforcement learning). DeepMind's 2017 parkour humanoids — flailing, knees-high, unmistakably emergent — showed locomotion arising from rich terrain and a forward-progress reward alone.7 The legged-robot era made it precise and, surprisingly, biological: minimizing energy consumption makes natural gaits emerge; so do barrier-shaped "style" rewards with no motion capture whatsoever (bounding appears on its own); quadrupeds trained without references discover pace and gallop as speed rises; humanoid controllers now walk, hop, and stand on one leg from a single policy.8 The lever here is the environment: when a behavior won't emerge, change the world before tuning the reward — the self-play and affordance-ladder lesson — and when you want a range of behaviors, co-evolve terrains with the walker, admitting only terrains that are neither trivial nor impossible (POET's minimal-criterion gate, which the commons found to be the load-bearing part).
  • Rules. Craig Reynolds's boids (1987): three local rules — separation, alignment, cohesion — and a flock appears that no one choreographed.9 Drone-swarm shows and crowd simulation are boids made commercial: collective locomotion defined entirely by rule.
  • Repertoires. Quality-diversity turns all of the above from "find a gait" into "find every gait." The canonical demonstration is Cully et al. (2015): MAP-Elites fills a behavior grid with some thirteen thousand distinct hexapod gaits, and when the robot is damaged it searches that map for a compensating gait in minutes.10 That is a machine-made gamut of locomotion — a finite, indexable vocabulary of ways to move — which is where this chapter rejoins the rest of the part.

docs.title: Humanoid versus not
docs.text:
The same emergent gait means two different things depending on the body that performs it, and the difference is perceptual, not technical.

On a humanoid, emergence reads as error. The architecture chapter carried a finding from motion-graph research that bites here: everyone is an expert on walking, so tolerance for wrongness in human gait is near zero. The 2017 parkour humanoid is funny because it is a person-shape doing it wrong; a physically plausible but uncanny walk is worse than stylized animation. Which is why humanoid locomotion defined by objective gets paired with priors or physics cleanup before anyone sees it.

On a non-humanoid body, emergence reads as character. No one knows how a six-legged voxel blob should walk; there is no ground-truth gait to be wrong against, so whatever the system discovers is, by default, how that creature moves — which is why Sims's creatures have been loved for thirty years, why a dancing quadruped robot charms instead of unsettling, and why a Strandbeest on a beach reads as an animal rather than a mechanism. The design rule falls straight out: use emergent definition most freely where nobody knows what correct looks like. Novel morphologies are not a complication for these methods — they are their natural home.

docs.title: Non-human bodies on stage
docs.text:
Which brings the chapter to the stage, where non-human performers already work, and where how their motion gets defined turns out to recapitulate this entire part.

  • Spot, and the Choreographer. Boston Dynamics ships a public tool for dancing their quadruped: a drag-and-drop timeline of moves — a built-in library of pre-validated primitives (steps, body poses, turns, kneels, arm gestures), each with parameters and a beat-length — laid against music and, recently, synced to SMPTE timecode so the robot cues like a lighting rig.11 Their stated goal is that a user works "like a choreographer instructing a dancer rather than an engineer programming a robot," and the famous "Do You Love Me" routine was in fact made by one — Monica Thomas, a human dance-maker.12 Look at the structure: an engineer-authored gamut, a human sequencer — the chance chapter's two layers verbatim — with one genuinely new feature: transition legality lives in the firmware. Every move is something the balance controller can always execute and chain, so the choreographer never meets an illegal join. The legality graph, solved once, shipped in the body.
  • KUKA, and Huang Yi. The Taiwanese choreographer has danced duets with an industrial robot arm since the early 2010s, programming every trajectory himself — roughly ten to twenty hours of programming per minute of choreography.13 No gamut, no sequencer: hand-keyed motion, and the human is the adaptive layer, fitting his body and timing to a machine that cannot improvise.
