It is the human gate run in reverse, and the tenderness of the piece comes from exactly that asymmetry.
  • Strandbeests perform wherever they are set down; the choreography is the choice of beach and wind.
  • Drone swarms are choreographed at the level of formations — the authored layer is trajectories for the group; local rules keep the thousand agents from colliding.
  • Pilobolus, Momix, and the puppeteers go the other direction: non-human forms made of human bodies or operated objects — several performers sharing one creature — where the thing that reads as alive (breath, weight, hesitation) is precisely what no single operator controls. War Horse's three-person horse is the textbook case.

docs.title: What it means for the synthetic dancer
docs.text:
The synthetic dancer of Part VII does not have to move by capture. Its motion can be defined by a body and an objective and allowed to emerge — and for a humanoid that is a risky choice requiring priors and physics to stay presentable, while for any stranger form it is the best choice available. The human gate returns, as it always does, one level up: not "is this step legal" but "which of the thirteen thousand gaits reads as dance." And the most interesting creative territory this chapter opens may be the least explored: choreographing for bodies that have never existed, whose way of moving is discovered rather than known — the one place where the generator genuinely gets to invent material, because there was no tradition to author it.

Field notes

This chapter renders emergence-locomotion-without-a-choreographer and theory-nonhuman-performers-motion-definition (both researched 2026-08-18), together with three existing commons notes: ml-quality-diversity-map-elites (repertoires over optima), ml-poet-environment-agent-coevolution (the admission gate as the load-bearing part of terrain–walker co-evolution), and ml-curriculum-and-self-play (change the environment before the reward).

  1. Tad McGeer, "Passive Dynamic Walking," IJRR 1990; Theo Jansen's Strandbeests are documented on his own site and in The Great Pretender (2007). ↩

  2. Ijspeert et al., "From Swimming to Walking with a Salamander Robot Driven by a Spinal Cord Model," Science 2007. ↩

  3. Karl Sims, "Evolving Virtual Creatures," SIGGRAPH 1994 — the video is still worth watching. ↩

  4. Evolution Gym (NeurIPS 2021); GNN-driven co-design and EvoGymCM (2026). ↩

  5. Evolutionary Brain-Body Co-Optimization Consistently Fails to Select for Morphological Potential (2025). ↩

  6. Mordatch, Todorov & Popović, "Discovery of Complex Behaviors through Contact-Invariant Optimization," SIGGRAPH 2012. ↩

  7. Heess et al., "Emergence of Locomotion Behaviours in Rich Environments" (DeepMind, 2017). ↩

  8. Energy-minimization gait emergence (Fu et al., 2021); barrier-based style rewards (ICRA 2025); gait emergence without motion references (2025); HugWBC (2025) — see the curated awesome-rl-for-legged-locomotion list. ↩

  9. Craig Reynolds, "Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model," SIGGRAPH 1987. ↩

  10. Cully, Clune, Tarapore & Mouret, "Robots that can adapt like animals," Nature 2015. ↩

  11. Boston Dynamics — Choreographer developer guide; Spot Takes the Stage. ↩

  12. Dance Magazine — Meet the Choreographer Behind Those Dancing Robots. ↩

docs.title: The gamut+rules architecture
docs.text: The previous chapter read seventy years of generative choreography as a record; this one reads it as a specification. Suppose you accept its findings — material authored and small, continuity handed to a sequencer, dimensions enumerated — and set out to build such a system today, with a typed gamut in hand. Three problems remain, and they are where the real engineering lives: what makes a chain of units legal, who judges whether a legal chain is any good, and — least obvious — what form the system's proposals should take. Each has a documented answer.

docs.title: Transitions are the hard part — and they are content
docs.text:
Start with the pedagogy's blunt correction to how engineers instinctively frame this. Transitions are not glue between the real material. Dance teaching is explicit that a transition is material — it can be a breath, a weight shift, or an entire traveling passage whose job is repositioning — and Cunningham went further: "dynamics in movement come from the continuity." The joins are where the expressive interest concentrates, not where it's absent.

Two practical facts ride along with this reframe. First, the expensive transitions are the ones that change level or support — floor to standing, standing to air. They dominate rehearsal time in the human case and failure rates in the synthetic one, so keep level-changing units a minority of the gamut and rate-limit them per phrase. Second, transitions start early: in an eight-count phrase the transition typically begins around count six or seven — the last beats of a unit are already preparation for the next. A system that treats units as sealed blocks meeting at instantaneous boundaries has mismodeled the material from the start.

Structurally, the consequence is that a vocabulary should partition into content units and connector units — weight shifts, pivots, breath suspensions, rises and lowers, rolls — whose declared job is satisfying somebody else's preconditions. Hold that thought; it becomes the fix of choice below.

docs.title: Three transition policies
docs.text:
Any system that recombines authored units makes a policy decision about joins — usually by accident. The record contains exactly three policies, and the crucial fact about them: they are per-section choices, not system-level ones.

1. The legality graph. Annotate every unit's entry and exit state; generate only legal walks. Smooth, scalable, the animation industry's default, and the only policy that works with no human in the loop. Cost: the annotation work, plus one system-level check covered below.

2. The neutral hub. Define a common neutral — a stand, a home position — and route every join through it. Always legal, zero annotation. This is what movement-prompt decks and accumulation practice do implicitly. Cost: every join has the same shape, the result is rhythmically flat, and the hub becomes a visible tic. (You have heard this failure: it is the generative-music equivalent of returning to the tonic between every phrase.)

3. Illegal by design. Cunningham's position, held deliberately: anything may follow anything, and solving the impossible joins in rehearsal is the expressive content. The costs are documented with unusual precision — Changeling took months; dancers mastered units in isolation and then welded them; Carolyn Brown described the only viable coping strategy as "absolute concentration on each single moment." So is the payoff: audiences reported chance sequences over a good gamut as reading inevitable, where conventionally structured work "looks contrived." Choose this policy knowingly, and cap unit difficulty so the welds stay humanly solvable. With synthetic dancers, note, the rehearsal room where impossible joins get solved does not exist.

docs.title: Mechanics of the legality graph
docs.text:
For policy 1, the definitive recipe comes from an unexpected direction: Motion Graphs, the SIGGRAPH 2002 paper that taught game animation how to stitch mocap clips.1 Its four mechanics transfer to any system that concatenates authored units — the paper is about pixels, but the findings are about joins.

Compare a window, not an instant. Naive per-frame pose distance fails, because a good join must match velocities and accelerations, not just positions. The paper's fix: compare the material over a window of roughly a third of a second, which makes the derivatives implicit in the comparison. General form: define the join metric over a window of the signal and derivative continuity comes free.

Quotient out what the domain leaves free. A motion clip is the same motion anywhere on the floor and facing any direction, so the distance is minimized over that free transform before comparing. Consequence for your gamut's type signatures: facing is stored relative, never absolute — only rotational momentum genuinely constrains a successor. Every domain has such a symmetry (in music it is transposition), and failing to quotient it out means rejecting valid joins and duplicating your library to compensate.

Set thresholds by audience expertise, not globally. The paper's own example: walking demands exacting joins because every viewer is an expert on walking; ballet is more forgiving because they aren't. Read that twice — it means join tolerance is a perceptual parameter, per category of material. Pedestrian connectors (walk, stand, turn) need the cleanest joins in your entire set; stylized material grants slack.

Prune to the largest strongly connected component. Pairwise legality is not enough: a graph can be locally correct and still contain sinks — states with legal entries and no legal exits — where generation stalls. Keep only the largest strongly connected component, and when it comes out too small, add connector units rather than loosening the metric. A gamut of brilliant content units with no connectors fails this check no matter how good the units are; the fix is never to redefine legality, it is to hire more of the units whose job is joining.

One adjustment when the executor is human rather than a renderer: a dancer out-blends any interpolator, so tune the thresholds permissive and let the performer legalize marginal joins. The structure transfers; the numbers don't.

docs.title: The human gate
docs.text:
Here is the finding the generative-art literature keeps treating as an embarrassment, restated as the load-bearing component it is: every system in the seventy-year record that produced kept work has a human accept/reject gate. Cunningham "almost always" refined what chance handed him. Halprin's RSVP Cycles schedules the gate as a named stage — valuaction — which is precisely what makes it a cycle rather than a one-shot generator. Wayne McGregor's Living Archive (the machine-learning collaboration with Google) proposes thirty continuations per pose; the dancers select. Curation is designed in. It is not a confession that the generator is weak.

Cunningham's gate is worth studying in detail, because he stated his criteria, and they are two different kinds of check: aesthetic interest — does the sequence read as a necessary, integral form — and practicality — can human beings perform it, in this space. A candidate can be interesting-but-impossible or performable-but-dull, and knowing which gate rejected it tells you which knob to turn upstream. Keep the criteria separate in your own gate, even if one person applies both.

The architecture that falls out is a clean two-tier split:

  • The machine tier checks whatever is stateful and enumerable. For movement: the support/level/balance/momentum/facing chain — the legality graph above. Cheap, exhaustive, and blessedly tasteless.
  • The human tier judges quality and interest — plus everything the domain defines as a performance target rather than a measurable. Effort qualities are the clean example: no checker can verify a "wringing" quality, and pretending otherwise just launders taste through a metric.

Blurring the tiers fails in exactly two directions, both worth naming. Train a learned "is-it-good" scorer and start optimizing against it, and you get the classic Goodhart collapse — the score improves while the work degrades. Or keep tightening the mechanical checker to encode taste it cannot see, and it starts rejecting joins a performer would have absorbed without noticing. The machine tier's job is to be strong and dumb: strict about state, silent about quality.

And a budgeting rule that sounds trivial and decides projects: a gate is only load-bearing if somebody sits at it. Cunningham filtered every draw; RSVP schedules valuaction; a proposal stream nobody selects from is a firehose, not a system. Size the generator's output to the number of candidates a human can actually judge, and let the machine tier guarantee nothing obviously invalid ever reaches them.

docs.title: The proposal is an interface
docs.text:
The last finding is the one nobody expects, and it may be the most transferable: the representation a system proposes in carries the same design weight as the model doing the proposing.

Exhibit one. The Choreographic Language Agent — built by Marc Downie's OpenEndedGroup for Wayne McGregor's company — renders its choreographic proposals as animated constructions of points, lines, and planes, deliberately not as an anatomical avatar. The stated reason: dancers imitate a realistic figure literally, but are forced to interpret an abstract sketch. Fidelity of rendering directly sets how much the human contributes. Want the human's job to be selection? Render high-fidelity, so they judge the real thing. Want their job to be completion — the under-specification lever — render deliberately lossy, and lossy in the dimensions you want them to own.

Exhibit two, the cautionary one. Cunningham spent his last two decades composing with LifeForms, early choreography software whose avatar was divided into fourteen independently keyframeable sections. Critics can date works of that era on sight: angular arm material running in counter-rhythm against the legs — because independent per-limb layering was the cheap operation, and the tool's easiest path quietly became the house style. Nobody chose that. Whatever your tool makes one-click will show up in the artifacts; audit the easy path as a style decision, not a convenience.

Corollary, for high-fidelity previews: they defer the feasibility check, they don't perform it. LifeForms happily rendered sequences that were physically impossible, and the impossibility surfaced downstream, on dancers, in rehearsal. A convincing preview moves the reckoning later — budget for it there.

docs.title: The assembled architecture
docs.text:
The whole synthesis fits in a paragraph. A small, typed, hand-authored gamut (content units plus connectors, state-changing verbs first-class). A sequencer owning an enumerated list of continuity dimensions and nothing else. A machine tier enforcing transition legality — window metric, symmetry quotiented out, expertise-scaled thresholds, one strongly connected component. A human gate with stated criteria, interest and feasibility kept distinct, throughput budgeted. A proposal medium chosen for the role you want the human to play. Seventy years of practice, one working diagram — and nothing in it that stops applying when the dancer is made of pixels, except the rehearsal room where policy 3 got solved.

Field notes

This chapter renders the commons notes structure-transition-policies (the three policies, connective material as material, level/support cost, early transitions), structure-transition-legality-graph (the Motion Graphs mechanics and their movement instantiation), eval-split-checkable-from-judged (the two-tier gate, Cunningham's criteria, throughput budgeting), and interaction-proposal-fidelity-imitate-vs-interpret (CLA's abstraction choice; the LifeForms fingerprint).

  1. Lucas Kovar, Michael Gleicher & Frédéric Pighin, "Motion Graphs," SIGGRAPH 2002 — the paper that made mocap libraries walkable as graphs; its window metric and strongly-connected-component pruning are described in the chapter body. ↩

docs.title: Choreographing in latent spaces
docs.text:
Everything in this part so far has been discrete: named units, finite gamuts, legality graphs with countable edges. The obvious question — obvious now, anyway — is whether any of it survives when movement is represented the way modern ML actually represents it: as a point moving through a continuous learned space, where between any two movements there are infinitely many others, and "vocabulary" seems to dissolve entirely.

People have choreographed this way. Some of them used autoencoders. Some of them, remarkably, did it decades before the mathematics existed — and the pre-mathematical versions turn out to illuminate the learned ones. This chapter takes the continuous position seriously, traces both lineages, and then asks the structural question: how much of the gamut+rules architecture survives the loss of the unit?

docs.title: The learned movement space
docs.text:
The framing, briefly, for the one reader who hasn't built one. Train a model to compress motion data — sequences of joint rotations — through a bottleneck and reconstruct them, and the bottleneck's coordinates become a latent space: a compact space in which every point decodes to a motion, nearby points decode to similar motions, and directions acquire meaning no one programmed. Movement operations become geometry: interpolation is a line between two points, blending is averaging, "more like this" is a direction you can keep walking.

For motion specifically, the founding demonstrations are Daniel Holden's mid-2010s graphics work — convolutional autoencoders over large mocap corpora, yielding a "motion manifold" on which synthesis, interpolation, editing, and style transfer all became latent-space operations.1 Dance arrived almost immediately. chor-rnn (2016) trained a recurrent network on five hours of one choreographer's mocap and generated novel continuations in her style — the space was implicit, but the compositional act ("start here, let the model continue, curate") was already latent-space choreography.2 Mariel Pettee — a particle physicist and dancer — built the explicit version: Beyond Imitation (2019) trained variational autoencoders on her own improvisation, then used sampling and interpolation as an improvisation partner, generating phrases she then learned back into her body.3

The flagship remains Wayne McGregor's Living Archive (2019, with Google Arts & Culture): a model trained on twenty-five years of McGregor's company archive, its movement space visualized as a navigable map, generating continuations from a dancer's live pose. You met its gate in the architecture chapter — thirty proposals per pose, dancers selecting. Note what the dancers were navigating: not "dance" in general but a learned space of McGregor — his archive, his style, made spatial.4

docs.title: Where the manifold bites
docs.text:
The seduction of the continuous picture is interpolation: infinite movement between any two movements, no transition problem, no legality graph. The trap is one of the deepest recurring findings in the commons, and it has a dance-specific bite.

Valid movement is a thin manifold in a vast space. The space of all joint-angle sequences is astronomically larger than the space of possible human movement — almost every point in it is a body doing something no body can do. Learned motion spaces are useful precisely because training bends them toward the valid manifold; they are dangerous because nothing guarantees it. Walk a straight line between two legal points and the midpoint can be quietly illegal — which is what foot-sliding, floating pivots, and impossible weight shifts in generated motion are: the visible symptom of a path that left the manifold and came back.

The audio world learned the design lesson in a directly transplantable form: naive interpolation between two synth presets in raw parameter space sounds terrible, because a straight line through parameters is not a straight line through timbre — and the fix is to regularize the latent during training so that its geometry matches perceptual distance, after which interpolation stays musical. The motion translation: a movement latent is choreographically useful in proportion to how much the geometry you navigate matches the space that matters — physical validity, and beyond it style. Distance in a good movement latent should mean "a body can get there from here credibly," which is, of course, exactly what the transition legality graph computed discretely. Same requirement, new substrate: the legality graph becomes the metric.

docs.title: The pre-mathematical lineage
docs.text:
Now the part that should permanently change how you see the effort chapter. Choreographers built navigable movement spaces by hand, long before anyone could learn one — and the constructions are good enough to be read, without squinting, as designed latent spaces.

Laban's choreutics is the strongest case, and one of the least-told stories in this subject. The same Laban who factored effort spent decades on what he called space harmony: a geometry of the kinesphere — the sphere of reach around a standing body — structured by inscribed polyhedra, most famously the icosahedron, whose vertices define standard directional points. Movement, in this system, is a trajectory through the structured space, and Laban composed scales — the A scale, the B scale, prescribed circuits visiting the icosahedron's points in order — explicitly analogized to musical scales, with sequences of directions treated as consonant or strained the way intervals are.5 Sit with what that is: a hand-built coordinate system for movement, with named positions, canonical paths, a notion of distance, and a notion of harmonic relation between regions. Dancers trained the scales daily, which is to say: they practiced navigating the space. It lacks only the word "latent."

The effort cube is the quality-space version — three bipolar factors as axes, eight named corners, adjacency as similarity, diagonals as contrast. And it was made continuous the moment EMOTE implemented the factors as dials in [−1, +1]: at that point "punch" and "float" are regions, not categories, and a phrase can trace a curve through quality space. A designed, interpretable, three-dimensional latent for movement dynamics — from the 1940s.

Forsythe's operations are directions. Extension, folding, extrusion, compression — each is a continuous transformation applicable to any material by degrees, which is precisely what a meaningful direction in a learned latent is (the "smile vector" of face models, the style axes of motion models). A dancer literate in the operations is doing vector arithmetic on their own material, kinesthetically.

And Gaga speaks in directions, not positions. Float, quake, melt are not shapes to reach but qualities to move toward, by degrees, from wherever you are — instructions of the form "walk this way in sensation space." The anti-vocabulary of the technique chapter is, in this light, a navigation convention for a space with no landmarks: only vectors, never coordinates.

docs.title: The architecture, translated
docs.text:
So: does the two-layer finding — authored material, sequenced continuity — survive the continuous world? Check it against the actual practice, and the answer is: almost entirely, in translation.

  • The corpus is the gamut. Living Archive learned McGregor's archive; chor-rnn learned one choreographer's five hours; Pettee's VAEs learned her own improvisation. In every documented case the material is still human-authored, bounded, and personal — chance still never invents material; it now interpolates it. The authoring moved from writing the unit list to curating the corpus, but it did not disappear, and its size discipline echoes too: a space distilled from one artist stays navigable and stylistically coherent the way a 64-phrase gamut does, where "all of mocap" is the latent version of the 135-item alphabet.
  • The walk is the sequencer. Which dimensions the system owns is still the composition: Pettee choosing where to sample, McGregor's dancers choosing when to consult; a latent walk's step size and direction policy are Cunningham's "list of questions chance will answer," re-parameterized.
  • Staying on the manifold is the legality graph — argued above.
  • The gate persists, unchanged. Thirty proposals, dancers select. Pettee learning phrases back into her body is valuaction. Nothing about continuity removed the human gate; if anything the firehose got wider, making the gate's throughput budget bind harder.

What genuinely changes is the loss of the unit boundary, and it cuts both ways. The transition problem dissolves — there are no joins, only paths. But with it go the edit points: the held stillness, the phrase seam, the moment the gamut chapter called the most useful cut on camera. A latent walk is all middle. And rule legibility — the chance chapter's second axis — collapses toward the opaque pole: an audience can read an accumulation in sixty seconds, but no one reads a latent walk; strangeness is the only register it offers. The continuous world, in other words, buys smoothness with structure, and the price is exactly the structures the discrete tradition knew how to spend.

Which is why the most interesting position is the hybrid one — and why it's so satisfying that Laban got there first. A discrete gamut of authored units, each placed in a continuous quality space that modifies and interpolates its rendering: that is choreutics plus the scales, it is effort dials over a movement alphabet, and it is, roughly, where the strongest current systems are converging — discrete tokens or graph nodes for material and editability, continuous latents for quality, blending, and style. The state of that art, and what it means for a working pipeline, is Part VII's business — the movement-generation chapter's research sweep will take the inventory.

Field notes

This chapter renders the commons notes manifold-of-valid-artifacts (valid artifacts as a thin submanifold; navigate along it, don't sample the void) and data-timbre-regularized-latent (SPINVAE-2's lesson: train the latent so distance = perceptual distance, or interpolation cliffs), transplanted to movement. The historical and ML material is confident general knowledge; current-SOTA inventory is deferred to the ch. 25 research sweep.

  1. Daniel Holden, Jun Saito & Taku Komura, "Learning Motion Manifolds with Convolutional Autoencoders" (SIGGRAPH Asia 2015) and "A Deep Learning Framework for Character Motion Synthesis and Editing" (SIGGRAPH 2016). ↩

  2. Luka & Louise Crnkovic-Friis, "Generative Choreography using Deep Learning" (ICCC 2016) — trained on choreography by Louise Crnkovic-Friis. ↩

  3. Mariel Pettee et al., "Beyond Imitation: Generative and Variational Choreography via Machine Learning" (ICCC 2019). ↩

  4. Living Archive: An AI Performance Experiment, Studio Wayne McGregor × Google Arts & Culture (2019); the trained tool fed material for McGregor's stage work of the same year. ↩

  5. Rudolf Laban, Choreutics (written 1939, published posthumously 1966; issued in the US as The Language of Movement). The icosahedral scales are still taught in Laban-lineage training programs. ↩

docs.title: Ballet: the long history
docs.text: title: Ballet: the long history summary: Court spectacle to Romantic ballet to Petipa to the Ballets Russes to neoclassicism to today's companies — how the lexicon was codified, how the schools became dialects, and what ballet is now; with deep dives on the Ballets Russes and the pointe shoe. covers: []

docs.title: Ballet: the long history
docs.text: Ballet is the only dance tradition with four centuries of continuous institutional history — a lexicon, schools, companies, a repertory, and a paper trail — which makes it both the best- documented dance in the world and the one most often mistaken for dance in general. This chapter tells the history at the depth the syllabus assigns (detailed, not exhaustive), with two deep dives where the material earns them: the Ballets Russes, the twenty years that made ballet modern, and the pointe shoe, the one piece of dance equipment that is unambiguously a technology. The codified-vocabularies chapter covers the lexicon itself; the costume history covers the tutu; the composing chapter covers Tchaikovsky and Stravinsky. Here is the spine they hang on.

docs.title: The court: 1580–1760
docs.text:
Ballet is born in the Italian Renaissance courts — Domenico da Piacenza's treatise (c. 1455) is the first dance manual in Europe — and grows up in France, where Catherine de' Medici's Ballet Comique de la Reine (1581) is conventionally the first ballet: a court spectacle of dance, verse, music, and machinery, performed by nobles for nobles. Under Louis XIV it became a state art. The king danced (the Ballet de la nuit, 1653), founded the Académie Royale de Danse (1661) to codify the technique, and his dancing master Pierre Beauchamp fixed the five positions of the feet that every ballet class still begins with. When the Académie Royale de Musique — the Paris Opéra — opened in 1669, dance moved from the court to the professional stage; women professionals appeared in 1681; and the Beauchamp-Feuillet notation (the notation chapter) recorded the repertory of a technique that was, at this point, turned out, upright, precise, and danced in heeled shoes and heavy costume.

The eighteenth century's reforms were the costume history's removals and one idea: the ballet d'action. Jean-Georges Noverre's Lettres sur la danse (1760) argued that ballet should tell stories through expressive movement rather than decorate operas with divertissements; Gasparo Angiolini made the same argument in Vienna; Jean Dauberval's La Fille mal gardée (1789) is the oldest ballet still in the repertory in any form. The virtuoso male dancer (Auguste Vestris, the dieu de la danse) reigned; Charles Didelot took French technique to St Petersburg and hung dancers on wires.

docs.title: Romantic ballet: 1830–1850
docs.text: Within two decades the art changed sex and subject. Marie Taglioni's La Sylphide (Paris, 1832; choreography by her father Filippo) made the ballerina the center, the supernatural the subject, and rising onto the toes — pointe — the signature: a trick became the image of weightlessness. Giselle (1841; Jean Coralli and Jules Perrot, for Carlotta Grisi) is the Romantic ballet that survives whole: a peasant girl, a betrayal, madness, death, and a second act of vengeful spirits in white — the ballet blanc — whose corps de ballet in moonlit unison is still the test of a company. Perrot's Pas de Quatre (1845) put four rival ballerinas on one stage. In Copenhagen, August Bournonville built a parallel tradition — his own La Sylphide (1836), Napoli (1842) — whose light, bounding, buoyant style and strong male roles the Royal Danish Ballet has preserved almost intact, a living dialect from the 1840s. Everywhere else the male dancer faded; by mid-century in Paris men's roles were sometimes danced by women en travesti, and ballet's image as a feminine art dates from here.

docs.title: Petipa and Imperial Russia: 1850–1910
docs.text:
The center moved east. Marius Petipa, a Marseillais, arrived in St Petersburg in 1847 and ran the Imperial Ballet for half a century, creating or revising the works that define classical ballet: Don Quixote (1869), La Bayadère (1877 — the Kingdom of the Shades, thirty-two ballerinas descending a ramp in arabesque, the purest abstraction in the nineteenth-century repertory), The Sleeping Beauty (1890), The Nutcracker (1892, staged mostly by his assistant Lev Ivanov), Swan Lake (the 1895 revival with Ivanov that rescued Tchaikovsky's score from its failed 1877 premiere), Raymonda (1898). Petipa's contribution was structure: the full-evening ballet as an architecture of mime scenes, character dances, ensembles, and the grand pas — entrée, adagio, variations, coda — whose grammar the composing chapter describes from the composer's side. The Italian virtuosas of the 1880s and 90s (Virginia Zucchi, Pierina Legnani and her thirty-two fouettés) brought a technique the Russians absorbed; Enrico Cecchetti taught them; and the Imperial school's training, systematized in the Soviet era by Agrippina Vaganova (Basic Principles of Classical Ballet, 1934), became the Vaganova method — the most influential of the schools.

The schools matter, because ballet's lexicon is one language with dialects: Vaganova (Russian: expansive back, high extensions, plastique arms), Cecchetti (Italian: anatomical rigor, set daily exercises), Bournonville (Danish: light, quick, the arms low), the French school (Paris Opéra: elegance, speed, petite batterie), the Royal Academy of Dance syllabus (English, 1920), and Balanchine's (American: speed, attack, off-balance, the "neoclassical" line). A dancer's schooling is audible in the body the way an accent is in a voice.

docs.title: The Ballets Russes: 1909–1929
docs.text: Then Serge Diaghilev. The Ballets Russes — a touring company of Imperial-trained dancers, based in Paris and Monte Carlo, that never performed in Russia — made ballet a modern art in twenty seasons, and its story is told at length in the deep dive. In brief: Michel Fokine's reforms (Les Sylphides, The Firebird, Petrushka, expressive one-act ballets with every element unified); Nijinsky's three shocks (L'Après-midi d'un faune, 1912; Jeux and The Rite of Spring, 1913); Massine, Nijinska (Les Noces, 1923), and the young Balanchine (Apollo, 1928; Prodigal Son, 1929); scores by Stravinsky, Debussy, Ravel, Satie, Prokofiev, Poulenc; designs by Bakst, Benois, Picasso, Matisse, Chanel. When Diaghilev died in 1929 the company dissolved and its people founded the twentieth century: Ninette de Valois's Vic-Wells Ballet (1931, later the Royal Ballet), Marie Rambert's company (1926), Balanchine and Lincoln Kirstein's School of American Ballet (1934) and New York City Ballet (1948), Serge Lifar at the Paris Opéra (1930–58), the various Ballets Russes de Monte Carlo touring America. Ballet's worldwide company system is the Diaghilev diaspora.

docs.title: Neoclassicism and the twentieth century: 1930–1990
docs.text: Balanchine in America made plotless ballet the century's central form: Serenade (1934, the first work for his American students), Concerto Barocco (1941), The Four Temperaments (1946), Agon (1957), Jewels (1967) — the music visualized, the vocabulary sped up and pulled off its axis, the tutu replaced by practice clothes (the costume history's leotard ballets). Ashton in England made the lyrical, épaulement-rich English style — Symphonic Variations (1946), La Fille mal gardée (1960), The Dream (1964) — and Kenneth MacMillan the dramatic, psychologically raw full-evening ballet: Romeo and Juliet (1965), Manon (1974), Mayerling (1978). Jerome Robbins moved between Broadway and NYCB (Fancy Free, 1944; Afternoon of a Faun, 1953; Dances at a Gathering, 1969). The Soviet ballet built its own canon — the drama-ballet, Yuri Grigorovich's Spartacus (1968) at the Bolshoi, Vaganova's school at the Kirov — and exported it through defections (Nureyev 1961, Makarova 1970, Baryshnikov 1974) that transformed Western companies. In Europe: John Cranko's Stuttgart (Onegin, 1965) and his heirs John Neumeier (Hamburg) and Jiří Kylián (Nederlands Dans Theater); Maurice Béjart's populist spectacles (Boléro, 1961); Mats Ek's reimagined classics (Giselle, 1982, set in an asylum); and from 1984 William Forsythe at Ballett Frankfurt, taking the Balanchine line to its deconstructive limit (Artifact, 1984; In the Middle, Somewhat Elevated, 1987) — the hinge to the technique chapter and to Part V. Arthur Mitchell's Dance Theatre of Harlem (1969) answered the art form's whiteness with a classical company of Black dancers.

docs.title: Now
docs.text: Ballet in the 2020s is a repertory art in a company system: the great houses — Paris Opéra, the Royal Ballet, the Bolshoi and Mariinsky, New York City Ballet, American Ballet Theatre, the Royal Danish, La Scala, Stuttgart, Hamburg, San Francisco, the National Ballet of Canada, the Australian Ballet, Dutch National, and dozens more — each mixing the classics, Balanchine, Forsythe, and new work. Its choreographers are a recognizable set: Christopher Wheeldon and Alexei Ratmansky (whose reconstructions from Stepanov notation are the notation chapter's vindication); Wayne McGregor as the Royal Ballet's resident since 2006; Crystal Pite; Justin Peck at NYCB; Akram Khan's Giselle (2016) for English National Ballet; Cathy Marston, Pam Tanowitz, Alonzo King. Its arguments are about its inheritance: the racial and gender assumptions of the canon (pointe shoes in skin tones arrived only in 2018), the body standards, the nineteenth-century ballets' orientalism and their revision, the Russian companies' isolation after 2022, and the blur between contemporary ballet and contemporary dance — whether "ballet" names a technique, a repertory, or an institution. The best short answer is that it names all three, and that the technique is the durable part: a lexicon four centuries deep, taught in every city on earth, that every other form in this subject positions itself against.

docs.title: What ballet is, structurally
docs.text:
For the rest of the library, the facts to carry:

  • The lexicon — several hundred named French terms for positions, movements, and qualities; the oldest codified movement vocabulary in continuous use, and the codified-vocabularies chapter's central case.
  • Turnout, the outward rotation of the legs from the hip, the technique's defining physical premise and the source of its line and its injuries; the plausible-body chapter treats the anatomy.
  • The schools as dialects of one language, audible in the body.
  • Pointe, the technology that made Romantic ballet's image — the deep dive.
  • The grand pas and the full-evening architecture, Petipa's form, which the music was written to fit.
  • The company-and-school system, Diaghilev's diaspora, which makes ballet the most institutionally reproduced dance in the world.
Field notes

No commons notes rendered — confident-knowledge writing. Ballet's lexicon, costume, music, and pointe technology are treated in their own chapters and deep dives.

docs.title: The modern revolt and after
docs.text: This is the spine of the library's core tier — the lineage from which nearly every idea in Parts II and V comes, and on which the shelf's reference pages hang. It is told here as a lineage because that is how the field tells it: teacher to student, company to splinter, each generation defining itself against the last. The technique chapter covers what these people taught their dancers to do; the costume and props chapters cover how they dressed and staged it; the shelf covers the individuals at length. This chapter is the map between them.

docs.title: Before: the soloists
docs.text:
Modern dance begins as a refusal of ballet by women dancing alone. Loie Fuller's Serpentine Dance (1892) — silk, wands, colored light — made the dancer a moving image and the stage a light-box; Isadora Duncan, from around 1900, danced barefoot in a Greek tunic to Chopin, Gluck, and Beethoven, in a vocabulary of runs, skips, and gestures from the solar plexus, and declared in The Dance of the Future (1903) that ballet was deformed and nature was the model. Both were Americans who succeeded in Europe; both claimed the body's "natural" movement as a value; both were, in the first chapter's terms, inventing concert dance outside the only existing concert tradition. Behind them stood two systems of expressive movement — François Delsarte's gesture analysis and Émile Jaques-Dalcroze's eurhythmics — that gave the revolt a pedagogy.

Ruth St. Denis (Radha, 1906) brought an exoticist, spiritual orientalism to the American stage, and with Ted Shawn founded Denishawn (Los Angeles, 1915–31): the school and company through which American modern dance's second generation passed. Denishawn's repertory was eclectic and its "music visualizations" literal, but its graduates — Martha Graham, Doris Humphrey, Charles Weidman — left it in revolt, and Shawn's all-male company and his farm at Jacob's Pillow (1933) gave modern dance its first festival.

docs.title: Germany: Ausdruckstanz
docs.text: A parallel revolt in German-speaking Europe produced the Ausdruckstanz, expressive dance. Rudolf Laban — the movement theorist of the effort chapter and the notation chapter — ran movement choirs, built a movement analysis, and taught Mary Wigman, whose Hexentanz (1914; the masked 1926 version) and solos of the 1920s were dark, weighted, earthbound, and entirely unballetic; her Dresden school (1920) trained a generation, and its New York branch under Hanya Holm seeded the American line. Kurt Jooss's The Green Table (1932), the anti-war ballet with its masked diplomats, is the one Ausdruckstanz work in the permanent repertory; his school at the Folkwang in Essen is where Pina Bausch later trained. The movement's entanglement with and destruction by the Nazi period — Laban's exile in 1937, Wigman's compromises — broke its continuity, and its deeper influence ran underground until Tanztheater resurfaced it in the 1970s.

docs.title: The Graham generation: 1926–1960
docs.text:
American modern dance proper begins with Martha Graham's first independent concert (1926) and consolidates at the Bennington School of the Dance (1934–42), the summer program where the founders taught and premiered side by side. Four lines:

  • Graham built a technique on the breath — contraction and release, the spiral, the fall — and a repertory that moved from austere abstraction (Heretic, 1929; Lamentation, 1930; Primitive Mysteries, 1931) through Americana (Frontier, 1935; Appalachian Spring, 1944) to the Greek myth cycle (Cave of the Heart, 1946; Night Journey, 1947; Clytemnestra, 1958). Her composer-adviser Louis Horst taught composition to the whole generation; Noguchi built her sets; she danced until 1969 and choreographed until 1990.
  • Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman (company 1928–44) built the other technique — fall and recovery, the body as a pendulum between the two deaths of standing still and lying down — and a repertory of ensemble works (Water Study, 1928; The Shakers, 1931; the New Dance trilogy, 1935–36). Humphrey's The Art of Making Dances (1959) is the craft chapter's canon; her protégé José Limón carried the line (The Moor's Pavane, 1949) and his company survives.
  • Hanya Holm brought Wigman's German weight to America and then to Broadway (Kiss Me, Kate, 1948 — the first copyrighted choreography).
  • The Black modern lineage, too often told as a sidebar and in fact central: Katherine Dunham, anthropologist of Haitian and Caribbean dance, built a technique and a company (Tropics and Le Jazz Hot, 1940) that fused them with modern and ballet and trained a generation; Pearl Primus (Strange Fruit, 1943) did for African and African-American material what Dunham did for the Caribbean; Lester Horton in Los Angeles built a technique (still taught) and a company whose dancers included Alvin Ailey and Carmen de Lavallade; Talley Beatty and Donald McKayle (Rainbow 'Round My Shoulder, 1959) made the repertory; and Alvin Ailey founded his company in 1958 and made Revelations (1960), the most-performed modern dance work in the world. Anna Sokolow's Rooms (1955) and the New Dance Group (1932) carried the period's political strain.

docs.title: Cunningham's break: 1944–
docs.text: Merce Cunningham danced for Graham (1939–45), gave his first solo concert with John Cage in 1944, founded his company at Black Mountain College in 1953, and broke with everything modern dance had assumed: that dance expresses, that music and movement are related, that the stage has a front and a center, that the choreographer chooses. His chance procedures decided continuity; music, décor, and dance were made independently; any point in the space was a center; and the technique — a long, erect, balletic spine over fast, complex legs — produced a body ready for any sequence. The "Events" (from 1964) recombined repertory excerpts for non-theatre spaces; the visual artists (Rauschenberg, Johns, Warhol, Stella) made the company a crossroads of the New York avant-garde; LifeForms (1989) made him the first choreographer to compose on a computer. He worked until his death in 2009. Beside him, Paul Taylor (from Graham and Cunningham; Aureole, 1962; Esplanade, 1975) built the great mid-century American repertory company, and Alwin Nikolais and Murray Louis the total-design theatre.

docs.title: Judson and the postmodern turn: 1962–1980
docs.text:
Cunningham's composition teacher Robert Dunn ran a class (1960–62) applying Cage's methods to dance; its students began showing work at Judson Memorial Church in Greenwich Village in 1962, and the Judson Dance Theater (1962–64) became the name for a generation that stripped dance to walking, running, task, and rule. Yvonne Rainer's Trio A (1966), four and a half minutes of continuous, unaccented, unrepeated movement performed with the gaze averted, is the emblem, and her "No Manifesto" (1965) the creed. Steve Paxton made walking pieces (Satisfyin Lover, 1967) and then invented contact improvisation (1972), the duet form of shared weight that became a worldwide practice. Trisha Brown made equipment pieces on walls and rooftops, then the accumulations (1971), then — with Rauschenberg and Laurie Anderson — Set and Reset (1983), the liquid, released, sliding vocabulary the technique chapter describes. Lucinda Childs moved from Street Dance (1964) to the pattern-permutations of Dance (1979) with Glass and LeWitt. Simone Forti's Dance Constructions (1961), David Gordon, Deborah Hay, Meredith Monk, and the Grand Union (1970–76, an improvisation collective) complete the core. Sally Banes's Terpsichore in Sneakers (1980) named it postmodern and is still its standard account.

The 1980s turned back toward spectacle, virtuosity, and content. Twyla Tharp crossed over — Deuce Coupe (1973) for the Joffrey, Push Comes to Shove (1976) for Baryshnikov — and made the pop-score, rigorously structured, loose-bodied style that fed Broadway and ballet alike. Mark Morris (company 1980) restored music and narrative. Bill T. Jones and Arnie Zane made identity, illness, and race the subject (Still/Here, 1994, and its critical firestorm). Pilobolus (1971) and MOMIX made collaborative body-sculpture; Elizabeth Streb made impact; Garth Fagan, Stephen Petronio, Molissa Fenley, Bebe Miller filled the downtown decade.

docs.title: Tanztheater and the European wave: 1973–2000
docs.text:
In Wuppertal, from 1973, Pina Bausch made something that was neither dance nor theatre — Tanztheater: evening-length pieces built from questions put to the dancers, assembled from repeated gestures, speech, song, social dance, and cruelty, on stages of earth, water, and flowers, in evening clothes. The Rite of Spring (1975), Café Müller and Kontakthof (1978), 1980, Nelken (1982), and some forty more made her the most influential European choreographer of the century's last quarter; the Folkwang line (Reinhild Hoffmann, Susanne Linke) and Johann Kresnik's political "choreographic theatre" surrounded her.

Belgium produced the next wave: Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker (Rosas, 1983; Fase, 1982; Rosas danst Rosas, 1983 — the mathematical minimalist), Wim Vandekeybus (Ultima Vez, 1986 — risk and impact), Alain Platel (les ballets C de la B — outsider bodies, chaos), Jan Fabre, and later Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui. France's nouvelle danse of the 1980s, funded through the decentralized Centres Chorégraphiques Nationaux — Maguy Marin (May B, 1981), Dominique Bagouet, Jean-Claude Gallotta, Régine Chopinot, Angelin Preljocaj, Philippe Decouflé — made France the most densely subsidized dance culture in the world. Britain had Richard Alston and Siobhan Davies in the Cunningham line, Michael Clark's punk ballet, Lloyd Newson's DV8 (Dead Dreams of Monochrome Men, 1988) founding physical theatre, and Matthew Bourne's all-male Swan Lake (1995). And in Japan, a parallel revolt: butoh — Hijikata Tatsumi's Kinjiki (1959), Kazuo Ohno's Admiring La Argentina (1977), Sankai Juku (1975) — the white-painted, slow, grotesque, inward body that is the makeup chapter's limit case and the shelf's.

docs.title: The contemporary now: 2000–
docs.text:
"Contemporary dance" names a field, not a style, and its geography has widened past the transatlantic axis. A map by region, each entry a door to a shelf page or a tradition:

  • Israel — Batsheva (Graham's 1964 foundation) under Ohad Naharin from 1990: Gaga, the anti-vocabulary, and Decadance's touring fragments; Sharon Eyal's pulsing, DJ-driven unison; Hofesh Shechter's percussion- scored mass choreography (Political Mother, 2010), now British.
  • Britain — Akram Khan's kathak-contemporary (Zero Degrees, 2005, with Cherkaoui; Desh, 2011; his Giselle, 2016); Wayne McGregor's hyper-articulate bodies and computational collaborations; Russell Maliphant; the hip-hop theatre of Boy Blue and Botis Seva.
  • Canada — Crystal Pite's Kidd Pivot (Betroffenheit, 2015; Revisor, 2019) and her ballets (Flight Pattern, 2017); Édouard Lock's La La La Human Steps; Marie Chouinard.
  • The conceptual turn in continental Europe — Jérôme Bel (The Show Must Go On, 2001; Véronique Doisneau, 2004), Xavier Le Roy (Self Unfinished, 1998; Retrospective, 2012), Boris Charmatz's Musée de la danse (2009), La Ribot, Tino Sehgal, Meg Stuart's Damaged Goods — dance about dance, in galleries as often as theatres.
  • Africa and its diaspora — Germaine Acogny's École des Sables in Senegal and the Acogny technique; Faustin Linyekula (Kisangani), Gregory Maqoma and Dada Masilo (Johannesburg — her Swan Lake, 2010), Qudus Onikeku, Nora Chipaumire; in America Kyle Abraham, Camille A. Brown, Ralph Lemon, Okwui Okpokwasili, and Trajal Harrell's fusion of voguing with Judson.
  • Asia — Lin Hwai-min's Cloud Gate (Taiwan, 1973; Moon Water, 1998; Songs of the Wanderers, 1994, danced on tons of rice), Tao Ye's numbered abstractions (Beijing), Shen Wei (New York), Padmini Chettur and Chandralekha's post-bharatanatyam minimalism (India), Eko Supriyanto (Indonesia).
  • Latin America — Grupo Corpo (Belo Horizonte, 1975), Deborah Colker (Rio), Tânia Pérez-Salas (Mexico).
  • The United States — Pam Tanowitz, Faye Driscoll, Justin Peck in ballet, Rennie Harris's Puremovement (1992) bringing the street to the concert stage.

docs.title: The blur
docs.text:
Two boundaries have dissolved in the last twenty years, and both matter for this subject. Contemporary and ballet: McGregor, Pite, Forsythe, Khan, and Ratmansky move between companies freely; a ballet company's "contemporary" program and a contemporary company's are often the same choreographers; "contemporary ballet" is a settled category. Contemporary and commercial: television competition formats since 2005 made "contemporary" a named style — lyrical, emotive, acrobatic, a hybrid of jazz, modern, and ballet — taught in every suburban studio and danced in music videos, and Gaga classes "for people" made Naharin's method a fitness practice. The concert lineage this chapter traced is now one stream among several that share a name, and the street styles of the next chapter are a third — which is the present state of the territory, and the reason the shelf matters: the lineage is where the ideas are, and the ideas are what the rest of this library is about.

Field notes

No commons notes rendered — confident-knowledge writing. The lineage's ideas (chance, technique, the gamut, the operator vocabulary, Gaga) are rendered in Parts II and V; the individuals are on the shelf.

docs.title: Street and club styles
docs.text:
The styles in this chapter were invented in the last sixty years by young people in American cities, with no school, no company, no notation, and no choreographer — and they are now among the most widely practiced dance forms on earth, with named vocabularies as precise as ballet's, international competitive circuits, and, since 2024, an Olympic event. That makes them the counter-case to ballet's four centuries of institutions and the live demonstration of the codified-vocabularies chapter's claim that a canon can form without an academy. They are also, for this library's generative project, the dance forms most completely shaped by their music's structure, which the commons happens to hold in detail.

The usual division is hip-hop styles (breaking and its East Coast party dances), funk styles (popping and locking, West Coast and older than hip-hop), and club styles (house, waacking, voguing), with krump as a later, separate birth. The division is cultural as much as formal, and practitioners defend it.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text: Breaking was born in the Bronx in the early-to-mid 1970s, where DJ Kool Herc isolated and extended the percussion break of funk records — the section where the band drops out and the drums run — and dancers invented a form to fill it. The name is the music's: b-boys and b-girls dance the break. The vocabulary divides into toprock (standing footwork and posture, the entry), downrock or footwork (the six-step and its family, hands and feet on the floor), power moves (windmills, headspins, flares, airflares — the rotational, gymnastic material that television loves and purists rank below footwork), and freezes (held poses on the hands or head, the punctuation). Crews formed — the Zulu Kings under Afrika Bambaataa's Zulu Nation (1973), the Rock Steady Crew (1977) — and the battle, crew against crew in a cypher (the circle of onlookers who are also participants), became the form's native institution. Three films (Wild Style, 1983; Flashdance, 1983; Beat Street, 1984) took it global; Europe and Asia developed scenes that soon outran New York's; Battle of the Year (from 1990) and Red Bull BC One (from 2004) became the world championships; and Paris 2024 put it in the Olympics, with a judging system (technique, vocabulary, originality, execution, musicality) that the culture debated as both recognition and capture.1

docs.title: Popping and locking: the funk styles
docs.text: Locking is the older: Don Campbell in Los Angeles around 1970, the "Campbellock," a vocabulary of locks (sudden freezes), points, wrist rolls, knee drops, and comic timing, danced to funk; his group The Lockers (1973, including Toni Basil and Fred "Rerun" Berry) took it to Soul Train and national television, in the striped socks and apple hats the dressing-the-genre chapter described. Popping came from Fresno in the mid-1970s — Boogaloo Sam and the Electric Boogaloos — and is built on the hit or pop, a sudden contraction of the muscles on the beat, combined with boogaloo's rolling isolations and a family of illusions: the robot, waving, tutting (right-angled arm and hand geometry), animation, strobing. Popping is the most "mechanical" of the styles and the most obviously mappable to a beat grid; it is also a precise vocabulary with named sub-styles and ancestral credit, and practitioners are unforgiving about conflating it with breaking (the 1980s media label "electric boogie" lumped them and is still resented).

docs.title: The club styles
docs.text: House dance grew in the Chicago and New York clubs of the late 1980s — the Warehouse, the Paradise Garage — to house music: fast, intricate footwork (the "jack" — the torso's pump — over loose, skating, lofting steps), done for hours, in a loose community of dancers (Ejoe Wilson, Brian "Footwork" Green, Marjory Smarth are the names the scene credits) rather than in battle. Waacking came from the gay Black and Latino clubs of 1970s Los Angeles — whipped, rotating arm movements, posing, and a glamour that quotes Hollywood's divas — danced to disco (Tyrone Proctor, Viktor Manoel); it too reached Soul Train. Voguing is Harlem's: the ballroom scene of Black and Latino gay and trans communities, organized into houses (House of LaBeija, 1972; Xtravaganza; Ninja) that compete in balls across categories, many of them realness categories judged on passing as the named thing. The dance — lines, poses, and arm-work quoting fashion magazines — divides into Old Way (1980s: lines, symmetry, precision), New Way (1990s: flexibility, contortion, the arms' geometric illusions), and Vogue Fem (the dramatic elements: catwalk, duckwalk, hands, floor performance, spins and dips). Willi Ninja and Paris Dupree are the canonical figures; Paris Is Burning (1990), Madonna's "Vogue" (1990), and the series Pose (2018) carried it out of the ballroom and into the mainstream, with the usual argument about what was lost.2

docs.title: Krump and the rest
docs.text: Krump was born in South Central Los Angeles in the early 2000s (Tight Eyez and Big Mijo), out of Tommy the Clown's hip-hop clowning: chest pops, stomps, arm swings and jabs, an intensity — buck — that reads as rage and is practiced as release; the documentary Rize (2005) introduced it. Around and after these, the map keeps filling: Memphis jookin (the sliding, gliding footwork Lil Buck brought to concert stages), Chicago footwork to juke at 160 bpm, Detroit jit, Oakland turfing, Brooklyn flexing (the "bone-breaking" contortions of Storyboard P), Harlem litefeet; the long line of hip-hop party dances — the Running Man, the Cabbage Patch, the Harlem Shake, the Dougie, the Milly Rock, and the TikTok era's fifteen-second sequences; Jamaican dancehall's own lineage; and the African street styles (azonto, gwara gwara, the amapiano dances) that now travel the same viral routes. Each is a vocabulary with a place, a music, and a set of originators the culture can name.

docs.title: How a canon forms without an academy
docs.text:
The codified-vocabularies chapter asked what codification costs and buys; this chapter's traditions show how it happens in the absence of every mechanism ballet used. The pieces:

  • Naming by practitioners. Moves are named by the people who invent them, often after the inventor, and the names spread through the cypher. A vocabulary exists when its terms are shared.
  • Foundation. Each style has a recognized core — breaking's toprock/footwork/freeze, popping's hit, locking's lock and point — that a dancer must demonstrate before originality counts. "Foundation" is the street's word for the closed vocabulary, and its guardians are the OGs, the originators and elders whose authority is historical rather than institutional.
  • The sin of biting. Copying another dancer's signature material without transformation is the culture's central offense. The rule enforces variation on the closed vocabulary — the operator logic of Part II as an ethic.
  • Transmission by circle and by tape. The cypher teaches by exposure; video (VHS in the 1980s, YouTube from 2005) made global transmission possible without a single school. A breaker in Seoul learned from tapes of New York, and then New York learned from Seoul.
  • Codification by competition. Battles need judges, judges need criteria, and criteria harden the vocabulary. The Olympic system made this explicit and institutional — which is exactly the moment a practitioner canon becomes an academy's, and exactly the moment the culture feared.

The result is a set of vocabularies as precise and as teachable as ballet's, produced by peer legitimacy instead of by a king, in a fraction of the time. The machine-discovery chapter should be read with this in mind: an unsupervised system that clusters movement into units is doing mechanically what a cypher does socially, and the cypher's extra ingredient — the biting rule, which forces each unit to be used differently — is the part the clustering lacks.

docs.title: The music's grammar is the dance's
docs.text:
Every style above is inseparable from a music, and the commons describes two of those musics in terms that explain the dance.

Hip-hop runs two temporal ontologies at once: the instrumental is a cyclic loop — a two-to-four-bar drum-and-sample pattern with little internal change — and the MC's flow over it is linear and narrative; form is bar-counted (sixteen-bar verse, eight-bar hook) and punctuated by the sample-flip (variation by recontextualizing a fixed source) and the beat-switch, a hard, wholesale replacement of the instrumental at a structural boundary.3 Read the dance against that. The b-boy's break is the loop laid bare — the section that is only the cyclic drums — and breaking's structure (toprock to footwork to power to freeze, then the next dancer) is a set of short, self-contained sequences sized to the loop's cycle, with the freeze as a beat-switch in the body. The biting rule is the sample-flip as an ethic: take the foundation, flip it.

House and techno are loop-grid music — a one-or-two-bar four-on-the-floor pattern as the state — whose sections are not new material but which layers are active, carved by muting and filtering, with phrase changes landing on eight-, sixteen-, and thirty-two-bar boundaries almost as a hard rule, because dancers and mixing DJs both need the boundary to be predictable.4 House dance is shaped by that precisely: continuous, non-sectional footwork that rides the loop for hours, with the dancer's own variation (the jack's amplitude, the footwork pattern, the lofting) doing the work that layer changes do in the music, and the phrase boundary as the place to change. It is participatory dance to music designed for participation, and it is the closest the contemporary world comes to the social function in its original form: the point is that everyone is dancing, and the music is built so that they can.

For the generative project the lesson is blunt. These dances are grid-native in a way concert dance never was — their units are sized to the loop, their changes land on the phrase line, their variation is governed by an explicit rule against repetition — and a system that modeled the music's loop-and-bar grammar first would find the dance's structure already given. The music-to-dance generators trained on AIST++ (ten genres, most of them street) are closer to this than they know.

Field notes

Renders theory-genre-hiphop (cyclic loop vs. linear flow; bar-counted form; sample-flip and beat-switch) and theory-genre-techno-house (loop-grid state; sections as active layer subsets; 8/16/32-bar boundaries because dancers and DJs need them). The style histories and the canon-formation analysis are confident-knowledge writing.

  1. Breaking's Olympic debut was Paris 2024; it is not on the Los Angeles 2028 program. The judging system weighs technique, vocabulary, originality, execution, and musicality. ↩

  2. The ballroom scene's history — houses, categories, realness — is documented by its own participants and in Paris Is Burning; its dance vocabulary's three eras are the scene's own periodization. ↩

  3. Schloss's ethnography of sampling and Krims's flow taxonomy are the commons note's scholarly anchors; the beat-switch as a formal category is documented in journalism rather than peer-reviewed analysis. ↩

  4. The commons' techno/house note: four-on-the-floor at genre tempo, sections as layer presence, boundaries on 8/16/32, the DJ set as a second linear form layer above the track. ↩

docs.title: What dance is; what choreography is
docs.text:
Every subject in this library opens by saying what its thing is, and dance resists the exercise more than most. The usual definition — rhythmic movement of the body, organized for its own sake or for expression — admits the wrong things (a marching band; a child skipping) and, more seriously, excludes the right ones: the Sufi whirler is not expressing, the ballroom competitor is not moving for its own sake, and a good deal of contemporary concert dance is neither rhythmic nor, in any obvious sense, organized. The working definition this subject uses is framing: dance is movement that a community treats as dance — watches, learns, names, evaluates, and transmits as dance. That sounds evasive and is in fact the most useful thing anyone has said about it, because it turns the question "what is dance?" into the question "what does this community's framing do?" — and the answer varies enormously, in ways that decide everything downstream.1

This chapter lays out the basic ontology — the nouns every later chapter assumes — and then the lens Ryan asked for: the functions of dance, which the world atlas groups geographically and which this chapter treats as the primary way to understand any dance you meet.

docs.title: The nouns
docs.text:
The dancer is the instrument and the performer at once — the one fact that makes dance unlike music, where a violin is not a violinist. Everything the dancer is (trained, tired, tall, injured, sixty) is in the dance, and every vocabulary in Part II is, at bottom, a way of making one dancer's movement repeatable by another.

The choreographer is a recent invention. The word comes from Feuillet's Chorégraphie (1700), where it meant dance-writing; by the nineteenth century it meant the composing of dances, and the figure of the choreographer as author — a named person whose work is the dance — consolidated with the ballet masters of Romantic and Imperial ballet and hardened into a profession only in the twentieth century. Most of the world's dance has no choreographer in this sense. It has tradition, teachers, lead dancers, master drummers, ritual specialists, and communities who all know the steps; the authored work is a Western concert convention, and this library's generative project inherits the convention wholesale (a system that composes dances is, structurally, a choreographer). It is worth remembering how local that is.

The work, the score, the performance. Is a dance the thing that happened on Tuesday night, or the thing that happens every time it is performed? Philosophers of art distinguish autographic works, identical with a physical object (a painting), from allographic ones, which exist as a type realized in many performances (a symphony) — and Nelson Goodman's observation was that dance is allographic only if it has a notation that fixes what counts as a correct performance.2 The notation chapter explains why it mostly doesn't; the practical consequence is that dance works are held in bodies and tradition — a répétiteur who knows Giselle, a company that knows its Bausch — and that a score, where one exists, may be a Labanotation manuscript, a video, a set of rules, or an instruction to improvise. The chance chapter is largely about scores that deliberately under-specify the performance, which is only possible once the distinction is clear.

Improvisation versus set material is a spectrum, not a switch. At one end, Swan Lake's second act is set to the count; at the other, a contact-improvisation jam has no material at all. In between lies most of the world: structured improvisation (a score, a task, a frame within which the dancer chooses — a raga's grammar, a flamenco palo's compás, a cypher's conventions), and the universal studio reality that "set" material was improvised into existence last month. The distinction the chance chapter draws between a frame (checkable constraints) and a realization (what happens inside them) is the precise version, and it applies across the whole spectrum.

docs.title: The four functions
docs.text: Now the lens. Dance is done for something, and four functions recur across every culture — ritual, social, concert, and competitive. They are not genres; the same steps can serve different functions (and often migrate between them), and the function changes who watches, who may join, what counts as good, how the dance is taught, how it relates to its music, and — the point for this library — what a machine would be asked to do. The ethnomusicologist Thomas Turino's distinction between participatory performance (everyone present takes part; there is no audience; the goal is the maximum number of people dancing) and presentational performance (a prepared performance by some for others) cuts across the four and is the single most useful tool for reading them.3

docs.title: Ritual: dance as efficacy
docs.text:
Ritual dance is done to accomplish something — to honor, to heal, to induct, to invoke, to mark a passage — and its criterion is efficacy, not beauty. The Mevlevi sema, the whirling of the Sufi dervishes, is a form of dhikr, remembrance of God; Haitian Vodou and Cuban Santería dance to summon specific spirits, each with a characteristic rhythm and movement; Balinese sanghyang is trance-dance in which the dancer is understood to be possessed; Japanese noh descends from shrine ritual; the powwow's grand entry is a ceremony before it is a contest. A few features follow. Ritual dance is usually participatory or semi-participatory: the congregation moves, or the dancer moves for them in a way that requires their presence. Its vocabulary is conserved — correctness matters because efficacy is believed to depend on it — and transmission is often restricted to initiates. And its relation to music is not aesthetic but functional: the drum calls the spirit, the repetition carries the dancer somewhere.

Which raises the one claim about ritual dance that everyone repeats and that the commons has checked: that rhythm induces trance. The honest reading is split. That a steady beat entrains the nervous system is solid and replicated — EEG shows neural phase-locking to a musical beat and meter, enhanced at the beat frequency even when the sound doesn't emphasize it — and the finding that moderate syncopation is rated more pleasurable and more move-inducing than either none or maximum is equally solid. But the specific claim that drumming at particular tempi drives the brain into trance traces to a 1960s "auditory driving" hypothesis and a large anthropological literature, and the most direct recent test found entrainment correlating only weakly and inconsistently with altered-state reports — with a live competing hypothesis that predictable rhythm may cause the auditory cortex to suppress input rather than lock onto it. Real entrainment is not the same claim as induced altered consciousness; treat the second as unresolved. What the ritual traditions reliably achieve is sustained, entrained, communal engagement, and that is already a great deal.4

docs.title: Social: dance as participation
docs.text: Social dance is done with others, for its own sake and for the sake of the relationship — the circle and line dances of the Balkans, the Levant, and Greece (kolo, horo, dabke, hora); the partner dances of the European-derived world (waltz, polka, tango, swing, salsa); the club floor from Harlem to Chicago to Berlin; the wedding, the céilí, the quinceañera. It is participatory by definition: the point is that you dance, and a good social dance is one that the maximum number of people can join at the level they have. That shapes the movement profoundly. Social dances have low entry floors and high ceilings (anyone can waltz; few can waltz well); they run on shared, simple, cyclic structures (the eight-count, the compás, the four-on-the-floor) so that strangers can synchronize; and they are conserved by use, not by institutions — the steps survive because people keep doing them. Their relation to music is entrainment: the music exists so that bodies can share time. And they are the great reservoir from which every other function draws: ballet's court dances were social; the Lindy Hop was social before it was theatrical; breaking was social and competitive at once.

docs.title: Concert: dance as a work
docs.text: Concert dance is presentational: prepared by some, watched by others, and — the decisive feature — organized around the work, an authored object with a beginning, a shape, and an end, which can be good or bad, revived, interpreted, owned. This is ballet and modern and contemporary dance, the core of this library's subject and the tier it treats at full depth, and it is a small and recent slice of the world's dancing: a few centuries old, a few cultures' invention, exported everywhere through conservatories and touring. Its features invert social dance's. The floor is high (years of training), the vocabulary is elaborated for the eye rather than for participation, evaluation is aesthetic and critical, transmission runs through schools and companies, and the music relationship is composed — a designed choice, the choreomusicology chapter's whole subject. It is also the only function that produces choreographers in the authored sense, and therefore the only one whose logic a generative system straightforwardly reproduces. Everything in Part V and Part VII assumes the concert frame: a work, an author, an audience.

docs.title: Competitive: dance as contest
docs.text: Competitive dance is done to win, and the presence of judges changes the form as surely as the presence of a congregation does. The competitive world is large and old: the dance marathons and the Savoy Ballroom's contests of the 1920s and 30s, ballroom's DanceSport, the Irish feis, Highland games, powwow competitions with their categories and prize money, tap and jazz competitions, the television formats since the 2000s, and the street's battles — breaking's cyphers formalized into Battle of the Year (1990), Red Bull BC One (2004), and, in 2024, the Olympic Games. Three things happen to a dance when it is judged. Its vocabulary is codified so that it can be scored (the codified-vocabularies chapter on how street styles did this without an academy, and the anxiety when the Olympics imposed a rubric). Its movement is tuned for legibility at a distance under adverse conditions (the dressing-the-genre chapter on ballroom's floats and fringe). And its evaluation becomes an explicit selection pressure — which means that whatever the scoring rewards, the dance becomes, and whatever it cannot see, the dance loses. That is the oldest instance in the art form of the problem the evaluation thinking behind the synthetic dancer keeps meeting: a metric that is optimized stops measuring what it was meant to.

docs.title: Migration between functions
docs.text: Almost every dance worth knowing has moved. Bharatanatyam was a temple and court art (sadir, danced by hereditary devadasis) before Rukmini Devi Arundale and others reconstructed it as a concert form in the 1930s — ritual to concert, with the costume, the music, and the respectability transformed along the way. Hula went from sacred to tourist entertainment to the Hawaiian Renaissance's revival. The waltz went from village social dance to ballroom to the concert stage (and to competition). Breaking went from the Bronx block party to the battle to the Olympics in fifty years, and the culture's argument about what was lost at each step is the argument this section is about. The atlas pages track these migrations per tradition; the rule is that a dance's function is a fact about its present use, not its origin, and that a tradition can run several at once (a flamenco juerga, a tablao show, and a concert-hall ballet flamenco are three functions of one vocabulary).

docs.title: Why this matters for a system that makes dances
docs.text:
A machine that generates movement is asked, implicitly, to serve one of these functions, and they want different things. A ritual or social generator would be judged by participation and entrainment — can people join, does the pulse hold — and has no use for novelty. A concert generator is judged by the work: shape, surprise, coherence, the things the gamut+rules architecture was built for. A competitive generator is judged by a rubric, and will find the rubric's holes. The literature on dance generation treats "dance" as one thing; this chapter's claim is that there is no such thing as good dance, only good for what, and that the first design decision — before the vocabulary, before the model — is which function the output serves. The rest of Part I walks the territory with that lens in hand.

Field notes

Renders theory-repetition-trance-perception (entrainment and the syncopation inverted-U are solid; drumming-induces-trance is thin and contested). The ontology and the four-function lens are confident-knowledge writing; Turino's participatory/presentational distinction and Goodman's autographic/allographic one are cited from memory.
