The framing view is standard in dance anthropology — Judith Lynne Hanna's To Dance Is Human (1979) and Joann Kealiinohomoku's essay "An Anthropologist Looks at Ballet as a Form of Ethnic Dance" (1970), which dismantled the assumption that Western concert dance is the unmarked case, are the usual starting points. ↩

  2. Nelson Goodman, Languages of Art (1968), on autographic and allographic arts and on Labanotation as a notation system. ↩

  3. Thomas Turino, Music as Social Life (2008). His four fields — participatory, presentational, high-fidelity recording, studio audio art — apply to dance with the obvious substitutions. ↩

  4. Nozaradan, Peretz & Mouraux (2012) for beat entrainment; Witek et al. (2014) for the syncopation inverted-U; Neher's 1960s auditory-driving hypothesis and the 2025 Aparicio-Terrés study are the commons note's anchors for the contested trance claim. ↩

docs.title: The Ballets Russes
docs.text:
Deep dive off Ballet: the long history.

Between May 1909 and August 1929 a touring company of Russian-trained dancers, based in Paris and Monte Carlo and run by an impresario who neither danced nor choreographed nor composed, remade ballet as a modern art. It premiered most of the twentieth century's first great scores, brought the School of Paris into the theatre, produced four major choreographers in succession, and, when it dissolved on its founder's death, scattered the people who founded the company system the world still uses. No twenty-year span in dance history did more, and the reason is worth understanding precisely: the Ballets Russes was an institution for collaboration — a machine for putting the best choreographer, composer, and painter in one room and obliging them to make one thing.

docs.title: Diaghilev
docs.text: Serge Diaghilev (1872–1929) came to ballet sideways — through the Mir iskusstva (World of Art) circle in St Petersburg, art exhibitions in Paris, and a 1908 season of Russian opera there. The 1909 ballet season at the Châtelet, with Imperial dancers on leave — Anna Pavlova, Tamara Karsavina, Vaslav Nijinsky, Ida Rubinstein — and Fokine's repertory, was a sensation; from 1911 the company was permanent and independent of Russia; after 1917 it could not go back. Diaghilev's talent was taste, persuasion, and the will to unify: he chose the collaborators, paired them, overruled them, and paid for it all by charm and debt. He was also the first producer to make the total work — music, décor, movement conceived together — a practical rather than a Wagnerian ideal.

docs.title: Fokine: the reform, 1909–1912
docs.text: Michel Fokine arrived with a program, later set down as his "Five Principles": movement should suit the period and subject rather than the ready-made lexicon; mime should be expressive through the whole body, not a sign language; the corps should dance, not decorate; and music, design, and dance should be equal partners. The early repertory is the program enacted. Les Sylphides (1909, to Chopin) is the first plotless ballet — a Romantic ballet blanc with the plot removed, leaving mood. The Firebird (1910), Stravinsky's first ballet, and Schéhérazade (1910), Bakst's orientalist riot, made the company's name. Petrushka (1911; Stravinsky, Benois, Nijinsky as the puppet) is Fokine's masterpiece — a fairground, a love triangle of puppets, a death — where every dance is character and every character is movement. Le Spectre de la rose (1911) gave Nijinsky the leap through the window that became legend. Fokine's reforms are now simply what ballet is; in 1909 they were a revolution.

docs.title: Nijinsky: the three shocks, 1912–1913
docs.text: Vaslav Nijinsky was the greatest male dancer of his era and, for two years, a choreographer of a radicalism no one had anticipated. L'Après-midi d'un faune (1912; Debussy, Bakst) is twelve minutes of profile movement — heads and feet turned sideways as on a Greek vase, the body flattened, the faun's final erotic gesture over the nymph's scarf — with no ballet steps at all, made in over a hundred rehearsals. Jeux (1913; Debussy) put three tennis players in modern dress in a flirtation that critics found baffling. And The Rite of Spring (29 May 1913; Stravinsky, Roerich) — turned-in feet, stamping, hunched bodies, the Chosen One dancing herself to death to music of unprecedented rhythmic violence — provoked the most famous riot in the history of the performing arts. The counting crisis (the dancers counting aloud, Marie Rambert drilling the rhythm) is told in the composing chapter. Nijinsky's choreography was lost within a few years — the Rite survived only eight performances, and was reconstructed in 1987 by Millicent Hodson and Kenneth Archer — but the idea that ballet's vocabulary could be discarded entirely and a new one invented for one work was in the air from then on. He was dismissed in 1913 after marrying; his last years were spent in mental illness.

docs.title: Massine, Nijinska, Balanchine: 1915–1929
docs.text: Léonide Massine was the war years' and the 1920s' choreographer: Parade (1917; Satie, Cocteau, Picasso's Cubist costumes — the costume history's limit case), La Boutique fantasque (1919), Le Tricorne (1919; de Falla, Picasso), character dance and wit; later, in the 1930s, the symphonic ballets. Bronislava Nijinska, Vaslav's sister, made the company's two greatest works of the 1920s: Les Noces (1923; Stravinsky; Goncharova's brown-and-white peasant designs), a Russian wedding as a massed, stamping, architectural ritual, and Les Biches (1924; Poulenc; Marie Laurencin), the ironic, ambiguous house party that is the modern sensibility's first ballet. And George Balanchine, arriving from Petrograd in 1924, made Apollon musagète (1928; Stravinsky) — the birth of the god, the three muses, a clarity that taught him, he said, he could eliminate — and The Prodigal Son (1929; Prokofiev, Rouault), weeks before Diaghilev died. In Balanchine the company passed its inheritance to the second half of the century.

docs.title: The collaborators
docs.text: The list is the point. Composers: Stravinsky (Firebird, Petrushka, Rite, Pulcinella, Les Noces, Apollo), Debussy, Ravel (Daphnis et Chloé, 1912), Satie, Prokofiev, Poulenc, Milhaud, Auric, de Falla, Respighi. Painters and designers: Bakst, Benois, Roerich, Goncharova, Larionov, Picasso, Matisse, Derain, Braque, Miró, Ernst, de Chirico, Rouault, Laurencin, Chanel. Poets and librettists: Cocteau. Conductors: Monteux, Ansermet. Ballet had always used composers and designers; the Ballets Russes used the leading ones, and made the theatre a place where modern music and modern painting first met a mass public. The props chapter and the costume history follow the painters; the composing chapter the composers.

docs.title: Why the diaspora matters
docs.text:
Diaghilev died in Venice in August 1929, insolvent; the company could not survive him. Its dispersal is the founding of the modern company system:

  • Ninette de Valois (a company dancer) founded the Vic-Wells Ballet in London (1931) — the Royal Ballet from 1956 — and Marie Rambert the Ballet Rambert (1926): British ballet.
  • Balanchine went to America with Lincoln Kirstein: the School of American Ballet (1934), Ballet Society, New York City Ballet (1948): American ballet.
  • Serge Lifar ran the Paris Opéra Ballet (1930–58) and restored its dignity.
  • The Ballets Russes de Monte Carlo (de Basil's and Denham's rival companies, 1932 onward) toured America for two decades and seeded regional ballet across the continent.
  • Dancers and teachers settled everywhere — Australia, Canada, South America — and taught.

Ballet's worldwide network of national and civic companies, each with a school, a repertory mixing classics and new work, and a touring life, is this diaspora's shape. So is the expectation that a ballet is a collaboration among named artists — the thing Diaghilev institutionalized — and so, in a sense, is the shelf of this library: the idea that choreographers are authors whose works are studied is one the Ballets Russes made real.

Field notes

No commons notes rendered — confident-knowledge writing. Lynn Garafola's Diaghilev's Ballets Russes (1989) is the standard history.

docs.title: The pointe shoe as technology
docs.text:
Deep dive off Ballet: the long history.

Most of what a dancer wears is, in the costume history's terms, permission and signal. The pointe shoe is something else: a load-bearing device, the only piece of dance equipment designed to change what the skeleton can do, and the clearest case in the art form of a technology that produced the technique it serves. Romantic ballet's central image — the ballerina hovering on the tips of her toes — was a trick that the shoe made sustainable, then routine, then the foundation of a hundred-and-fifty-year vocabulary.

docs.title: From trick to technique
docs.text: Dancers were rising onto their toes by the 1810s and 20s, briefly, as a feat, in soft satin slippers whose toes they darned for grip and stiffness; Charles Didelot's wire rigs at the Paris Opéra had already shown the audience a dancer on her toes, suspended. Marie Taglioni's La Sylphide (1832) is conventionally the moment pointe became expression rather than stunt — the sylph's weightlessness — but her shoes were still darned slippers, and what she did on them was brief rises and poses, not the sustained balances and turns of later technique. The shoe hardened through the century: by the 1880s and 90s the Italian makers (Nicolini of Milan is the name usually cited) were producing a shoe with a stiffened box — layers of fabric and paste around the toes — and a firm sole that let Pierina Legnani and the Italian virtuosas perform the multiple fouettés and sustained pointe work that Petipa's ballets then built into the repertory. The technique followed the shoe: once a dancer could stand on a platform rather than a point, the vocabulary of pointe — relevé, piqué, bourrée, turns, hops, balances — could be codified and taught.

docs.title: Anatomy of the shoe
docs.text:
A modern pointe shoe has four working parts, and each is a decision:

  • The box — the hardened enclosure around the toes, traditionally built from layers of burlap, paper, and cardboard glued with paste (a papier-mâché construction, which is why the traditional shoe dies when wet and softens with wear). The vamp is the box's height up the foot; its length and taper decide how the toes are held.
  • The platform — the flattened tip, typically the size of a large coin, on which the dancer actually stands. Its width is the difference between a point and a stable surface; the whole technique balances on it.
  • The shank — the stiffened insole that supports the arch, traditionally leather or cardboard, in graded strengths. The shank's flexibility decides how the foot rolls through demi-pointe to full pointe, and dancers break it in (bending, cutting, hammering) to match their arch.
  • The sole, the ribbons, the elastic — the outer sole is leather; the ribbons are sewn on by the dancer, who also darns the platform in some traditions and bangs the box to quiet it.

Everything above is the dancer's personal engineering: shoes are fitted to the individual foot (width, length, box shape, vamp, shank strength — a maker like Freed has dozens of combinations and makers' marks for individual cobblers), then customized, then worn out. A principal in a classical company may go through a pair in a single performance; the traditional shoe's short life is the price of a construction that molds to the foot.

docs.title: Makers and materials
docs.text: Freed of London (founded 1929 by Frederick Freed) is the traditional standard — handmade, paste-and-fabric, with individual makers whose symbols dancers seek out. Russian, Italian, and American makers (Grishko, Bloch, Capezio) supply the rest of the classical world. The one real technological break came in 1993 with Gaynor Minden, whose shoes replaced the paste box and cardboard shank with elastomeric polymers — a shoe that doesn't break down, doesn't need breaking in, and lasts many times longer. The classical world's reception was a decades-long argument about feel, sound, and whether a shoe that doesn't soften is "cheating," and it is a textbook case of a technology whose adoption is governed by the technique's conservatism as much as its merits. In 2018 Freed released the first pointe shoes in shades of brown and bronze; until then the "flesh-colored" shoe was pink, and dancers of color dyed or pancaked their own — a small object carrying the art form's whole demographic history.

docs.title: What it does to the body
docs.text: Pointe work is performed on the talus — the ankle joint at full plantar flexion — with the body's weight through the metatarsals and toes onto the platform; it requires ankle mobility, foot strength, and a body whose alignment puts the weight directly over the small surface. Girls traditionally begin around eleven or twelve, once the foot's growth plates and the training allow; the injuries (stress fractures, bunions, tendinopathies, the general toll of standing on a coin) are the technique's known cost. Male dancers do not dance on pointe except in character, comedy, or deliberate reversal — the Trockadero's parody, the occasional contemporary piece — which is a cultural fact, not an anatomical one. The plausible-body chapter treats the joint limits; here the point is that the shoe shifts those limits, and that a synthetic dancer on pointe is a body under a specific mechanical constraint that the renderer must respect — the foot's full extension, the weight's narrow base, the ankle's line — or the eye will read the error instantly.

docs.title: Why it matters beyond ballet
docs.text:
The pointe shoe is the purest instance of a theme that runs through this whole subject: a constraint that creates a vocabulary. The shoe permits a single thing — sustained balance on the toes — and from that permission ballet derived an entire technical language, a body type, a training system, an aesthetic of weightlessness, and an image that the rest of the world recognizes as "ballet" before it recognizes anything else. The gamut chapter argues that a limited, typed vocabulary is what makes recombination possible; the shoe is the material proof, standing on a platform the size of a coin.

docs.title: Notation systems
docs.text: Music has had a durable written form for a thousand years; dance has had a dozen, none of them universal, and most dancers alive cannot read any. That asymmetry is the first fact about dance notation and the most revealing one: movement resists being written down not because nobody tried but because what to write is genuinely unclear. Every notation system that has survived more than a decade is, at bottom, a theory of what the unit of movement is — the named step, the direction-and-duration of a body part, the body's position at an instant, the rotation of a limb about a joint — and the systems disagree. That makes this chapter a companion to the gamut chapter and the machine-discovery chapter, which ask the same question from the maker's and the machine's side. Here it is asked from the archivist's.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Dance is the ephemeral art: it exists in performance, and until film it left nothing but memory, prose, and pictures. The consequences were severe. Repertoire died with its dancers; revivals were reconstructions from the bodies of those who had learned them; authorship could not be proven and so, for most of history, could not be owned. A notation promised three things — preservation (the work survives its makers), transmission (a stranger can learn it), and analysis (the work can be studied on paper, compared, decomposed) — and each system below is stronger at one of these than the others.

docs.title: Feuillet: the path and the step
docs.text:
The first real system is Chorégraphie, ou l'art de décrire la danse (Raoul-Auger Feuillet, 1700), recording the system developed under Pierre Beauchamp at Louis XIV's Académie Royale de Danse — which is why it is called Beauchamp-Feuillet. Its page is a map: a line traces the dancer's path across the floor, and along the path sit symbols for the steps — plié, élevé, sauté, cabriole, tombé, glissé, tourné — with small marks for the foot's position and bar lines tying the track to the music printed above. It is elegant and reads almost at sight once learned; hundreds of baroque dances survive in it, and reconstructions of them are the basis of everything we know about how the court danced.1

What it encodes is the floor pattern and the named step; what it drops is almost everything else — the torso, the arms (minimally marked), the face, the quality. It could do that because its unit was the codified step of a closed vocabulary: the reader already knew what a cabriole was, so the page needed only to say which and where. Feuillet notation is the gamut chapter's lesson in 1700: a vocabulary-level notation is only as good as the shared vocabulary, and when the vocabulary changed — Romantic ballet's new technique, the rise of the torso and arms — the system became unreadable within two generations.

The nineteenth century tried again repeatedly. Arthur Saint-Léon's La Sténochorégraphie (1852) and Friedrich Zorn's Grammatik der Tanzkunst (1887) used stick figures under the music; Vladimir Stepanov's Alphabet des mouvements du corps humain (1892) wrote movement on a musical staff, anatomically, by body part — and it is the one that mattered historically, because the Mariinsky used it to record the Petipa repertory. Those scores, taken to the West by Nikolai Sergeyev, gave the Royal Ballet its Sleeping Beauty (1939) and gave Alexei Ratmansky the basis for his reconstructions (Paquita, 2014; Sleeping Beauty, 2015) — a rare case of notation doing exactly the preservation job it was invented for, a century late.

docs.title: Labanotation: the direction, the level, the duration
docs.text:
Rudolf Laban published Schrifttanz in 1928, and the system — Kinetography Laban in Europe, Labanotation in America, developed by Albrecht Knust, Ann Hutchinson Guest, and the Dance Notation Bureau (founded 1940) — is the most complete movement notation that exists.2 Its logic:

  • A vertical staff, read bottom to top, so that time flows upward and the page's left and right are the body's left and right.
  • A center line dividing the staff: the innermost columns carry support (what the weight is on), then leg gestures, body, arms, head, outward.
  • Each movement is a symbol whose shape gives direction (nine basic directions), whose shading gives level (low, middle, high), whose length gives duration, and whose column gives the body part. Pins, hooks, and bows refine — contact, rotation, touch, the relation of one part to another.

The unit, then, is a body part moving in a direction, at a level, for a duration — finer than the step, continuous rather than positional, and independent of any particular vocabulary. That universality is the system's strength and its cost. It can record a Graham contraction and a Balinese agem with equal precision; a full score of an evening work takes hundreds of hours and a trained notator; few dancers read it fluently; and the Effort side of Laban's thinking — how the movement is done — needs a separate notation altogether (the effort chapter). Labanotation is the analysis system par excellence, which is why scholars use it and companies mostly don't.

Two things made it matter beyond the archive. It made choreography copyrightable: Hanya Holm's dances for Kiss Me, Kate (1952) were the first registered in Labanotation, and the US Copyright Act of 1976 named "choreographic works" explicitly — a fixed, written form being what the law needed. And its simplified cousin, Motif Notation (developed by Hutchinson Guest and Valerie Preston-Dunlop), records only the essential idea of a movement — a turn, a rise, a travel — leaving the rest to the performer. Motif notation is a gamut-level score: it writes the units and the operators and not the realization. The chance chapter's deliberately incomplete scores and the gamut chapter's unit layer have a notation already; this is it.

docs.title: Benesh: the position at the moment
docs.text:
Benesh Movement Notation (Rudolf and Joan Benesh, 1955) is the dancer's notation. Its staff is five lines like music's — top of head, shoulders, waist, knees, floor — read left to right in time with the score written above, and the notator marks where the hands and feet are, as seen from behind, at each significant instant, with small signs for bending, contact, and the direction of travel. The Royal Ballet and much of the ballet world use it; its practitioners are choreologists, and a company choreologist can notate at rehearsal speed.3

Its unit is the position at a moment — a frame. Benesh records the key instants and trusts the trained body to move between them, which is why it is fast to write and fast to read and why it is weak exactly where Laban is strong: dynamics, the path between positions, anything continuous. Readers of Part VII will recognize the architecture immediately: Benesh is keyframes and interpolation, sixty years before the pipeline — the choreologist draws the keyframes, and the dancer is the interpolator. Its assumptions (a trained ballet body, a known vocabulary that fills the gaps) are the assumptions of every keyframe system, and its failure modes are the same: where the in-between is the content, the notation is silent.

docs.title: Eshkol-Wachman: the limb as a rotating axis
docs.text: Eshkol-Wachman Movement Notation (Noa Eshkol and Avraham Wachman, 1958) is the mathematician's system. The body is a set of limbs, each a line segment rotating about the joint at its base; every movement is a rotation of that segment, written as numbers on a spherical coordinate grid — horizontal and vertical angles, amounts, and the kind of rotation (plane, conical, about the axis). The page is a table: rows for limbs, columns for time. It is entirely vocabulary-free and species-free — it has been used to notate animal behavior, sign language, and autism diagnostics as readily as dance — and it is the closest any notation comes to a joint-angle skeleton file. The capture chapter's BVH and SMPL representations are Eshkol-Wachman with a sensor instead of a notator. Its cost is legibility: nobody reads a movement off an EW score the way a pianist reads a chord; one computes it.4

docs.title: Four answers to one question
docs.text:
Set the systems side by side and they are four theories of the unit:

System Unit Strong at Silent on Feuillet (1700) the named step, on a floor path baroque repertory; floor pattern torso, quality, anything outside the vocabulary Labanotation (1928) body part × direction × level × duration analysis; any vocabulary; copyright speed of writing; quality (needs Effort) Benesh (1955) the position at a key moment ballet rehearsal; speed; music alignment the in-between; dynamics Eshkol-Wachman (1958) the limb's rotation about its joint precision; cross-species; computation human legibility Motif (1960s–) the essential idea (unit + operator) scores that leave realization open the realization itself

The table is the subject's map in miniature. Feuillet and Motif are gamut-level: they write vocabulary and leave the body to fill it in. Laban is description-level: it writes what the body does, finely. Benesh is keyframe-level. Eshkol-Wachman is skeleton-level. Every pipeline in Part VII passes through these same four levels — vocabulary, motion description, keyframes, joint angles — and the notators found each of them by hand, a generation before anyone asked a computer.

docs.title: Why notation never beat video
docs.text:
It is usually said that video killed notation, and the timing fits: portable video arrived in the 1970s, and within a decade the rehearsal tape had replaced the notator as a company's working memory (the craft chapter describes the habit). But the deeper reasons are structural and worth stating, because they are the same reasons a recording never replaced a score in music:

  • Cost. Notating is slow and expert; filming is instant and free. Preservation chose the cheap option.
  • Legibility. Few dancers read any system; all dancers can watch.
  • Completeness versus structure. Video captures appearance — everything, from one viewpoint, flattened, with no indication of what matters. Notation captures structure — what the dancer intends, at the level the notator chose, with everything else discarded. A video of Giselle tells you what one cast did; a score tells you what Giselle is. The Stepanov reconstructions were possible because the score had decided what the work was.
  • Transmission. Learning a role from video means copying a performer; learning it from a score means learning the work. Companies with a living tradition (the bodies that know it) need neither; companies reviving a dead one need the score.

The settled answer is that they do different jobs, and the next chapter is about the thirty-year attempt to build something that does both — a digital score that is video and structure. It ends where this chapter began: with the question of the unit, now asked of an algorithm.

  2. Ann Hutchinson Guest, Labanotation: The System of Analyzing and Recording Movement (4th ed., 2005), is the standard textbook; her Choreo-Graphics (1989) compares the systems side by side and is the best single survey of this chapter's territory. ↩

  3. Rudolf Benesh & Joan Benesh, An Introduction to Benesh Dance Notation (1956); the Benesh Institute (now within the Royal Academy of Dance) trains choreologists. ↩

  4. Noa Eshkol & Avraham Wachman, Movement Notation (1958). EW's use in animal-behavior research (Golani) and in early-autism movement studies (Teitelbaum) is the clearest evidence that it notates bodies, not dance. ↩

docs.title: Video, digital scores, and annotation practice
docs.text: The notation chapter ended with a standoff: video captures appearance without structure, notation captures structure without appearance, and dance needs both. This chapter is the thirty-year attempt to resolve it — first by living with video's limits, then by building digital scores that lay structure over footage, and finally by the everyday practice that grew out of those experiments: annotation, the time-coded labelling of rehearsal video, which turns out to be the most important unglamorous activity in the whole subject. It is also the one that connects most directly to the machine-discovery chapter, because an annotated video is exactly what an unsupervised segmenter is trying to produce without the human.

docs.title: Video as working memory
docs.text:
Portable video arrived in dance studios in the 1970s and became universal by the 1990s, and its first job was the humblest: memory. The craft chapter described the habit — film everything, because tomorrow nobody fully remembers today's material — and it is hard to overstate how completely this reorganized the making of dances. Material could be generated in quantity and curated later; tasks could be set and their results reviewed; a phrase made on Tuesday survived to Friday without a notator. The phone camera and cloud storage finished the job: a contemporary company's archive is a timeline of clips.

Video's second job was the archive — the Dance Division of the New York Public Library, the Jacob's Pillow collection, the company vaults — and its third was transmission: learning a role from the tape of the last cast. All three jobs share video's limits. One viewpoint, usually front-on, which flattens depth and hides the upstage body. No structure: nothing in the file says where the phrase begins, which part of the movement is the point, what was intended versus what happened. And no way to search: an hour of rehearsal footage is an hour, and the only index is a human who remembers. Annotation exists to fix the last two; the digital score was the ambitious attempt to fix all three at once.

docs.title: Forsythe: the thinking made visible
docs.text:
William Forsythe has been the field's great experimenter here, and his projects are stations on a single line of thought: can the structure of a dance — the decisions, the operations, the cues — be made as visible as its surface?

Improvisation Technologies: A Tool for the Analytical Dance Eye (CD-ROM, 1999, with ZKM Karlsruhe; developed from an in-house training tool of 1994) is not a recording of a piece. It is a lesson in a generative method: some sixty short films in which Forsythe demonstrates an operation — drawing a line in space and folding it, extruding a point, avoiding an imagined obstacle, collapsing a shape — while animated white lines are overlaid on his body to show the geometry he is thinking. The technique chapter called this an operator vocabulary; the CD-ROM is its notation — video plus a drawn layer that records intent rather than position. It taught a generation of dancers that a score could be a set of tools.1

Synchronous Objects for One Flat Thing, reproduced (2009, with Ohio State University's Advanced Computing Center for the Arts and Design) took a single piece — One Flat Thing, reproduced (2000), seventeen dancers and twenty tables — and extracted its hidden structure as data. The dancers' cues (who triggers whom), their alignments (moments of shared movement), and their movement density were annotated frame by frame, then rendered as twenty "objects": animated diagrams, generative drawings, a 3-D model of the cueing network, a statistical plot of density over time. The dance's counterpoint, which an audience feels but cannot see, became a visible graph. Forsythe's essay "Choreographic Objects" (2008) states the thesis: a choreographic idea can exist in forms other than a body, and making those forms is a way of knowing the dance.2 Synchronous Objects is also the clearest demonstration in the field that annotation is analysis — the objects were only as good as the schema the annotators had chosen (what counts as a cue? as an alignment?), and choosing it was the work.

Motion Bank (2010–2013, the Forsythe Company in Frankfurt, with funding to build online scores for other choreographers) generalized the idea. It produced web-based digital scores of Deborah Hay's No Time to Fly (Using the Sky, 2013 — seven recorded performances of a deliberately under-specified score, aligned so that the variation between them is the content), Jonathan Burrows and Matteo Fargion's counted duets, and Bebe Miller's and Thomas Hauert's working processes (Two). Each score was a different answer to "what is the structure of this work and how can footage carry it." And Motion Bank built the tool that outlived the project: Piecemaker.

docs.title: Piecemaker and the practice of annotation
docs.text:
Piecemaker began inside the Forsythe Company (David Kern, 2008) as the simplest possible thing: rehearsal video with time-coded notes typed during the rehearsal — "new phrase," "Fabrice's solo, version 3," "cut this" — so the company could find material again. That is annotation in its studio form: labels on a timeline. Motion Bank released a free, easy version (PM2GO) for studios and schools, and since 2016 the project, now at Hochschule Mainz, has been rebuilding it as Piecemaker 3 on the W3C Web Annotation standard — so that annotations are portable, linkable data rather than a closed file — integrated with MoSys, a cells-and-grids system for composing and presenting annotated material, and prepared for partners including the Pina Bausch Archive and the European repertoire-transmission project Dance On, Dream On, Pass On. The portable-data move is the one that matters: annotated rehearsal video becomes usable outside the tool — as an archive, as teaching material, or as data.3

What has emerged around these tools is a practice with three recognizable uses:

  • Rehearsal memory — the original use: find Tuesday's material on Friday; mark takes; log decisions.
  • Transmission and teaching — the annotated video as a teaching score: here is the phrase, here its unit boundaries, here what to attend to; the Pina Bausch Archive's interest is exactly this, for repertoire whose living carriers are aging.
  • Research — Motion Bank's own framing: annotation as a research practice, in which designing the schema (what categories exist, what counts as an event, what the layers are) is the intellectual contribution, and multimodal annotation — notation, video, text, and drawing on one timeline — is an active line of inquiry.

And one newer arrival, which the commons' sweep found real in capability and thin in evidence: pose-estimation feedback — estimators run on rehearsal video to compare a learner against a reference, segment a phrase automatically, or overlay a skeleton for correction. The estimators themselves are the capture chapter's subject and they work; the tools built on them for studios are, as of mid-2026, mostly student projects and vendor lists, with no peer-reviewed evaluation in working company practice. Treat the capability as available and the adoption claims as marketing until someone measures them.4

docs.title: What an annotation is
docs.text: Step back from the tools and look at the object. An annotation schema applied to a video produces a segmented, labelled timeline: intervals, each with a category from a fixed set, possibly layered (body part, quality, phrase, cue). Readers of Part II will recognize it. The fixed set of categories is a vocabulary — a gamut — and the intervals are a segmentation; the annotated video is a gamut plus a sequence, written by hand against footage. Which means two things. First, the notation chapter's question — what is the unit? — has not gone away; it has moved into the schema, where every annotator answers it anew, usually without noticing. Second, an annotated corpus is exactly the ground truth that machine gesture discovery is trying to produce unsupervised — and the reason that chapter's evaluation recipe is so hard is that the human schema it would be measured against is itself a design choice, not a fact about the movement. The dance world's thirty years of annotation practice are, seen from the machine side, thirty years of people hand-labelling the very structure the algorithms cannot yet find.

docs.title: Digital scores and the future of the record
docs.text:
The digital score's promise was video and structure in one object, and the record so far is honest: the experiments are brilliant and few, because each one took a research team, and the everyday practice that survived is the humble one — time-coded notes on a phone clip. Three developments are changing the calculus. Pose estimation makes the skeleton extractable from ordinary video, which is a free Eshkol-Wachman layer under every rehearsal tape. Portable annotation standards make the labels survive the tool. And the generative project on the other side of this subject — Wayne McGregor's Living Archive and AISOMA, which learned from a quarter-century of the company's footage — shows what a large annotated-or-extracted archive is for once it exists: a space to navigate, which is the latent-spaces chapter's subject, and a vocabulary to discover, which is the machine-discovery chapter's. The score that is also the footage that is also the data is no longer a research prototype's ambition; it is the default shape of a company's archive, waiting for the schema.

Field notes

Renders data-dance-annotation-tooling-landscape (the Piecemaker → PM2GO → PM3/MoSys lineage on W3C Web Annotation; pose-feedback tools as capability-real, adoption-unverified; a schema is a gamut). The Forsythe/Motion Bank history is confident-knowledge writing; the annotation-equals-gamut reading is this chapter's synthesis of structure-gamut-plus-sequencer and ml-unsupervised-gesture-discovery-landscape.
